title: Hacksmith's Peptalk Defintion
text:
hack·smith’s pep·talk /ˈhækˌsmɪθs ˈpepˌtɔːk/ noun 
 Where peptide conversations move from "what works" to why it works.
 Clear explanations. Better decisions. Fewer Mistakes. 
 This space is about learning and growing comfortable with peptides and health… ⚡️ The goal isn't just more information - it's better judgement. If you engage here, you'll know why you're doing something - not just what to take.

title: Why You're Here
text:
The quality of your decisions determines everything: how well you understand what you're taking
 how to choose the appropriate things for your goals
 how much time, money, and effort you don't waste
 The people who get the best results aren't guessing. They're learning from: patterns
 mechanisms
 shared experience
 and the why something worked (or didn't)
 ⚡️ This community works because people contribute what they learn, not just what 
 they want The strongest outcomes come from communities where:
 questions are thoughtful 
 data is shared clearly
 and mistakes are discussed openly
 This is the Hacksmith standard. 
 Now let's get you oriented.

title: Step 1:
text:
Everyone starts at Level 1, but our goal is to get you to Level 3 in this community. 
 What the levels actually do 
 Levels in the Skool Community reflect activity over time: 
 reading
 reacting
 asking questions
 sharing experiences
 They help conversations flow - they don't restrict access. 
 If you want to engage right away, start here: 
 👉🏽 Click me :) 
 Some ideas for your first post: 
 💪🏽 What's your primary goal right now?
 💉 Are you currently using any peptides? What's your stack?
 ⁉️ What's the most confusing thing about peptides for you so far?
 Lurking is fine. Jump in when it makes sense for you. 
 But why does engaging help? (Without pressure)

 surface better discussions
 improve answers you see
 make the community smarter over time
 Use the tools. Read the posts. Ask when ready. 
 That's how Hacksmith's Peptalk works. 
 Next course here: Step 2

title: You're Oriented
text:

title: ‍♂️ How to Best Use This
text:
Most people don't struggle because they lack information. 
 They struggle because they don't know where to look, what to ignore, or how to decide. 
 1️⃣ Start With Your Goal 
 Before asking what to take, be clear on what you're trying to change: 
 Fat loss / metabolic health
 Recovery or injury support
 Labs and biomarkers
 Cognitive performance
 Longevity / aging
 Once the goal is clear, everything becomes easier. 
 2️⃣ Use Search When Looking for Answers 
 Chances are, you might find a discussion thread for this. 
 Search helps you: 
 See multiple perspectives
 Spot patterns
 ..and if you don't find what you need, make a post! 
 3️⃣ How to Ask Questions That Get Good Answers 
 The best questions include: 
 your goal
 what you've already tried or researched
 any relevant context
 Vague questions get vague answers. 
 Clear questions get useful ones.

title: Step 2:
text:
You don't need to complete steps, earn points, or post on a schedule. 
 Use Hacksmith's Peptalk when: 
 something doesn't make sense
 you see conflicting information
 you're looking for perspectives
 you're deciding whether to do something at all. 
 Reading is fine. Asking is fine. Taking your time is expected. 
 What to do next (optional, not a task) 
 If you want direction: 
 browse recent discussions 
 explore cheat sheets 
 read a deep dive that matches your goals
 Good decisions don't come from urgency. 
 They come from understanding. 
 Next course here: Level 3

SS-31, MOTS-C, NAD+/NMN/NR, 5-Amino-1MQ, Humanin, Methylene Blue, Epitalon and FOX04-DRI sequencing, cycling, and stacking. 
 Should SS-31 be taken before MOTS-C, or the other way around, and what's the best general protocol for improving mitochondria?asked 4× 
 My position is SS-31 first. SS-31 stabilizes cardiolipin in the mitochondrial membranes and improves structural efficiency, while MOTS-C increases metabolic stress signaling and energy demand. You want to fix the damaged mitochondria first, then increase demand on it — stabilize the structure with SS-31, then optimize function with MOTS-C. That sequencing makes more physiological sense than the reverse, and it's the overwhelming consensus. In practice, you can either run SS-31 for several days before introducing MOTS-C, or finish the full 50mg total run of SS-31 first and then start MOTS-C — SS-31 is typically run until that total 50mg is completed, and MOTS-C is commonly run 4–6 weeks on. People tend to overcomplicate mitochondrial support, but for most people SS-31 followed by MOTS-C is going to be more than sufficient — start there before adding anything else. If you're also on NAD+, you can generally continue it alongside both unless you're feeling overstimulated or overly wired; there's no hard requirement to cycle NAD+, but if you've been on it 3 months straight, a short break wouldn't be unreasonable.

 Should I run MOTS-C daily at a lower dose or every other day at a higher dose, and is it okay to split the standard 5mg dose into smaller amounts?asked 4×

For insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial benefits, and fat oxidation, a few times a week can still be effective. It doesn't have to be daily at a lower dose; you really have to find the frequency and amount that works best for you — some people do well at 5mg daily, others do 1-2mg every other day. As for splitting the standard 5mg dose into smaller amounts like 2.5mg on back-to-back days, that's fine too. Trying lower is fine — some people respond well at lower amounts, and some have to work up higher.

title: GLP-1/Weight-Loss Peptides
text:
Semaglutide, Tirzepatide, Retatrutide and Cagrilintide dosing, switching, plateaus, side effects, and surgery timing. 
 Does microdosing Tirzepatide or Retatrutide (like 0.25–1mg) for inflammation, lipids, or longevity actually work if I'm not trying to lose weight?asked 3× 
 I think microdosing GLPs purely for lipid, inflammatory, or longevity benefits is often overstated. Some people may see improvement, but outcomes at very low doses are highly variable and not guaranteed - possibly helpful, but unpredictable. I'm honestly not a big believer in the micro-micro dose approach even when weight loss isn't the goal. At that low a dose it's also unlikely to cause issues like constipation, but not impossible. If what you're really after is anti-inflammatory support rather than weight loss, I'd lean toward something like KPV instead - it gives you the anti-inflammatory benefit with no weight loss potential, which is usually a better fit for that goal.
 Can I run Retatrutide for 3-6 months to lose weight and then stop without ending up hungrier than before I started?asked 2× 
 Yes, that's possible. If someone historically maintains well once their stress decreases, a 3-6 month structured run with proper tapering can work fine. The key is tapering off, not abruptly stopping - appetite signaling recalibrates much better when you reduce the dose gradually instead of quitting cold.
 📚 Covered in: Transitioning GLPs › Semaglutide to Retatrutide › Managing the Transition 
 When switching from Tirzepatide to Retatrutide, should I titrate down on Tirz while overlapping with low-dose Reta, or stop Tirz completely first?asked 2× 
 Personally, I like to come off completely rather than overlap the two - how would you know what type of suppression you actually get from Reta if you never give it a real chance on its own? Three weeks is generally enough time for Tirz levels to substantially decline given its half-life before starting Reta. I'd also be cautious about continuing other appetite suppressants, like low-dose Cagrilintide, during that washout window - it's not mechanistically dangerous, but stacking suppressants makes it a lot harder to assess your true baseline hunger and response to the new compound.
 📚 Covered in: Peptides for Specific Health Issues › Binge Eating / Appetite Control 
 How do I decide between Tirzepatide and Retatrutide, and when does it make sense to switch from one to the other?asked 2× 
 Both will likely work, but I think Reta tends to work a bit better overall - so if it's someone's first GLP, I'd usually choose Reta for max effectiveness if that's the goal. As for switching from Tirz to Reta, it makes sense if Tirz's suppression is too much for you, you're patient, you want something potentially more effective, or you just want to try it.

title: Growth Hormone Secretagogues and Fat-Loss Peptides
text:
CJC-1295, Ipamorelin, Tesamorelin, Sermorelin, GHRH/GHRP, AOD9604 and HGH dosing, cycling, timing, and side effects. 
 What is a safe/appropriate starting dose (and reconstitution) for Tesamorelin and Ipamorelin, and how should doses be adjusted as they increase?asked 5×from the feed 
 Good question, and it's actually part of why I don't love the fixed-ratio Tesa/Ipa blends — you lose the ability to dial each one in on its own. So let's break each one down separately.
 Tesamorelin: For reconstitution, whether you've got a 5mg or 10mg vial, add 1ml (100 units) of bacteriostatic water. From there, common dosages break down like this — on a 5mg vial, 500mcg is 10 units, 1000mcg is 20 units, 2000mcg is 40 units. On a 10mg vial, 500mcg is 5 units, 1000mcg is 10 units, 2000mcg is 20 units. Typical dosing runs 1-2mg, but you don't have to start there — I've said before that .5mg can be fine as a starting point for some people with tesa. So starting at 500mcg and working your way up toward the 1-2mg range as you see how you respond is a completely reasonable approach.
 Ipamorelin: Reconstitute a 5mg vial with 2ml (200 units) of bacteriostatic water, or a 10mg vial with 3ml (300 units). Common dosages on the 5mg vial reconstitution: 100mcg is 4 units, 150mcg is 6 units, 200mcg is 8 units, 250mcg is 10 units, 300mcg is 12 units. The typical range is 100-300mcg per day, best taken fasted, and it can be split into two doses (like 100mcg morning/100mcg night, or 150/150). As for schedule, 5 days on/2 days off is common, though daily or 6-on/1-off also works.
 As far as adjusting up: since these work on different pathways (tesa through GHRH, ipa through the ghrelin receptor), you want to be able to move each one independently rather than being locked into a blend ratio. Start at the lower end of each range, see how you respond, and increase from there within those typical dosing windows — that's the whole reason I recommend running them as separate injections timed together rather than as a combined blend.
 📚 Covered in: Consolidated Dose, Reconstitution, and Cycles › Tesamorelin › Cycle Length 
 How strict do I need to be about fasting before and after GH secretagogues like Tesamorelin, Ipamorelin, or CJC — does coffee or pre-workout break it, and how long do I need to wait around meals?asked 4× 
 General guidance is to space your dose at least 60-90 minutes before and after eating. Some people wait longer, but the real goal is just avoiding a significant insulin spike around injection time — insulin from food inhibits the GH benefit, and carbs spike insulin the most. If you have to eat in that window, keep it to fats or protein. If you're on a GLP like Reta, you don't need to wait a full 3 hours — 60-90 minutes is fine. Black coffee doesn't meaningfully break a fast in this context, so you can still have it in the AM with Ipa/Tesa. Powdered pre-workout generally doesn't affect efficacy either.

title: Reconstitution, Storage, and Injection Technique
text:
How to mix, store, and inject peptides — water types, shelf life, freezing, needle choice, and site reactions. 
 What gauge and length needle should I use for peptide injections?asked 3× 
 Most peptides will use a 30g 5/16" needle — that's my sweet spot at 8mm. For ones that go IM, I use a 30g 1/2". Remember, the smaller the gauge number, the thicker the needle is — a 22g is thicker than a 30g — and the thinner a needle is, the less long it can be. If you're hesitant about injections, a 30g half-inch is a fine place to start too; the actual length difference between a 5/16" and a half-inch 30g needle is minimal, and the sensation isn't really different — the visual size difference looks bigger than it feels. On the shorter end, something like 4mm can be a bit short and might leave you with a little lump, so I'd stick with 5/16" (8mm) as the sweet spot.
 📚 Covered in: Beginner Peptide Information › Supplies and Tools Needed 
 How long can a peptide stay potent after it's been reconstituted, and does storage length matter?asked 3× 
 Lyophilized peptides can stay stable for months when stored properly, but that changes once reconstituted. The bigger concern over time isn't the compound degrading — it's potential bacteria growth in the vial once it's mixed with liquid. Potency may not drop dramatically, but contamination risk goes up the longer a reconstituted vial sits. There's really no reason a reconstituted vial should be lasting longer than about 60 days, and I'd personally avoid going past 4-6 weeks once mixed. For something like L-carnitine and BAC water, room temperature storage with use within roughly 60-90 days is reasonable, and if the BAC water was refrigerated it's typically still fine even though manufacturer guidance says room temperature.
 📚 Covered in: Peptide Storage › How Long Are Reconstituted Peptides Good For? › How Long Are Reconstituted Peptides Good For? 
 Is it safe to use bacteriostatic water that's been refrigerated or accidentally frozen?asked 3× 
 Yes, that's all good. BAC water can be stored refrigerated — the benzyl alcohol preservative remains stable, so there's no issue using refrigerated BAC water to reconstitute a peptide, and you haven't wasted your blend. If your BAC water and a peptide froze overnight in the fridge but thawed out clear, you're fine — no need to toss them.
 📚 Covered in: Beginner Peptide Information › How to Reconstitute Peptides 
 Can I mix multiple peptides in the same syringe to cut down on shots, and are there any I shouldn't combine?asked 3× 
 Sometimes, but there's no blanket universal compatibility chart for every combination — the only real way to know for sure is compatibility testing, and visually you'll often see an issue if there is one. If a mixed solution clouds, gels, or precipitates, don't use it. If there's no clouding or precipitation, it's often tolerated, but visual clarity doesn't guarantee long-term stability. text:
Unexpected reactions, tolerance, interactions with medications/supplements, and why response varies between people. 
 Why do some people feel achy, fatigued, or flu-like after taking Glutathione?asked 2×

 Could skin irritation, welts, or itching at the injection site (or other intolerance symptoms) mean the body is rejecting the peptide?asked 2×from the feed 
 No, that's not your body "rejecting" the peptide. Injection site reactions like redness, itching, small welts, or mild soreness are basically just a local inflammatory response to the act of injecting itself, not necessarily a reaction to the compound. Mild redness, warmth, or a little small welt is pretty normal after a subcutaneous injection and usually goes away within 30-60 minutes. A small painless lump under the skin as the fluid absorbs is also normal and typically resolves within a few hours. I even get welts and itching myself sometimes, and it goes away the same day. Certain compounds are just more prone to this than others - things like amino acid blends, L-Carnitine, NAD+, glutathione, and MOTS-C tend to be spicier and can leave welts or soreness, while peptides like Tesamorelin or SS-31 often calm down and become more tolerable after a week or two of use as your body adjusts. Where it stops being "normal" and becomes something to actually worry about is if you see significant swelling, redness that's spreading outward, a lot of heat in the area, or pain that keeps increasing after 24 hours - that could point to infection or an allergic/systemic response and is worth getting checked out. Same goes for a hard, painful lump that lasts for days, which could be an abscess. But garden-variety itching, small welts, or soreness that fades on its own is just your skin's normal reaction to the injection, not your body rejecting the peptide.

 Is it safe/permitted to travel domestically or internationally (customs/TSA) with peptides, pens, or syringes without a prescription label?asked 6×from the feed 
 Short version: flying domestically is usually a non-issue. Crossing a border is where you need to be careful. 
 For flights inside the US — TSA is security , not the FDA. They're looking for weapons, not judging whether your vials are "approved." Syringes and needles are allowed in your carry-on, and that's where they should be, not in a checked bag. Bring your peptides in a cooler/insulated bag with ice or gel packs — medically necessary cold items are fine through the checkpoint, you might just get a second look. In my experience nobody's asking for a prescription, but understand that without a pharmacy label you've got no paperwork backing you up if someone does.
 International is a different animal. This is grey-market research material, and customs in another country can seize anything that breaks their import rules. Some countries are strict, some don't care. I wouldn't check it, wouldn't ship it ahead, and for a short trip I'd honestly weigh whether it's worth bringing at all versus just pausing your protocol for a few days.
 Bottom line: carry-on, keep it cold, and domestically you're fine the vast majority of the time. Cross a border and you're accepting a risk — that one's on you.

title: FAQs
text:
How do you determine how much BAC water to add? 
 The biggest thing to consider is how many units will you have to draw to get the appropriate dosage? If it’s under 5 units, it’s going to be very difficult to draw. So shoot for MINIMUM of 5 units for your dose. 10 is even better. The more concentrated something is, the more variance you can have in dosage if you draw an inaccurate amount of units. So less concentrated can mitigate issues from potential human error. 
 Do you dose based on overages listed in the COA? 
 Yes and no. Here’s the considerations that I take into account. What is my dosage? How much is the variance? For example, a 60mg vial while using a 5mg dose weekly is going to give you 12 doses. If the variance is 2mg over, you have to divide that 2mg overage across 12 doses. So if you don’t account for it, you’re only taking an extra 160mcg per dose. That’s very minimal and, in my opinion, not worth trying to account for. On the other hand, if I have a 10mg vial and my dose is 200mcg per day and the vial tests and 12mg, I just got myself an extra 10 days worth of doses out of it. Hopefully that makes sense on how I look at any overages and making that decision. Yes you always want to be as accurate as possible, but what if one vial was slightly higher than another and the vial you have might actually have a difference in variance? It’s hard to guarantee that all of them are exactly what the COA shows. 
 What are some common adverse effects of different peptides? 
 Please see this course . 
 GLPs: nausea, heartburn, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, bloating
 GH secretagogues: Water retention, joint pain. 
 All others: Some have flushing, some have injection site reactions (ISRs), etc. The course linked above will break these down more. 
 What peptides can you not take at the same time? 
 There’s not really a defined list of what 100% can and can’t be taken together in terms of peptides. However, I do think there is a reasonable amount of things that should be taken. title: Mechanisms and Metabolic Pathways
text:
Lipolysis What is it: 
 Lipolysis is the breakdown of stored fat (triglycerides) from the fat cells into free fatty acids and glycerol, which your body is then able to use for energy. 
 Why does it matter: 
 This is essentially the process that allows your body to "burn fat." It releases the fatty acids from the cells where your body can then burn them off. 
 Where this is used: 
 AOD-9604
 Growth Hormone Secretagogues
 Lipogenesis What is it: 
 Lipogenesis is the creation of new fat and can be due to excess carbohydrates, proteins, or alcohol. 
 Why does it matter: 
 It's basically the opposite of lipolysis. Things that can reduce insulin levels or improve insulin sensitivity can inhibit this process and potentially help prevent weight gain or things like fatty liver. 
 Where this is used: 
 5-Amino-1MQ
 MOTS-C
 GLPs
 AMPK Pathway (AMP-activated protein kinase) What is it: 
 AMPK is kind of like fuel gauge in your body. If your energy is low, it turns on fat burning and turns off fat storage. 
 Why does it matter: 
 It can help with weight loss, blood sugar control, and longevity. It's really one of the major pathways that gets targeted through some of the metabolic peptides. 
 Where this is used: 
 MOTS-C
 5-Amino-1MQ
 mTOR Pathway (Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin) What is it: 
 mTOR is a growth and repair signal in the body that can be triggered by things like protein, insulin, and IGF-1. It tells your body to build muscle and regenerate tissue. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Ideally, we're activating mTOR after workouts to help grow muscle. On the flipside, constantly elevating this can lead to faster aging and inflammation. 
 Where this is used: 
 IGF-1 LR3
 Growth Hormone Secretagogues
 Autophagy What is it: 
 Autophagy can be described as the body's clean-up system and will break down and recycle damaged cells, protein, and parts of the mitochondria. 
 Why does it matter: 
 This process helps keep the healthy cells in the body, can help prevent diseases, and can be a pretty big piece in slowing aging. 
 Where this is used: 
 Epitalon
 FOXO4-DRI
 Insulin Sensitivity / Resistance What is it: 
 Insulin sensitivity is how well your body responds to insulin, which is the hormone that helps to get the glucose out of your blood and into your cells. 
 Insulin resistance is when your cells aren't responding well to insulin and your body then has to make more of it to accomplish the same goal. 
 Why does it matter: 
 When you're insulin resistance, your fat loss is going to slow down, your blood sugar is going to stay high, and your energy levels are going to be in the dumpster. Peptides that improve insulin sensitivity can help lower blood sugar, reduce fat storage, and make it easier to achieve better body composition (less fat, more muscle). 
 Where this is used: 
 GLPs

 Glucagon is a hormone that raises blood sugar when levels are too low and causes fat to breakdown in the body.

title: Neuroendocrine and Brain-Related Terms
text:
BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) What is it: 
 BDNF is a protein that helps the brain grow new neurons and stronger connections and is important for memory and learning. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Low BDNF can lead to things like depression, anxiety, difficult focus, and cognitive decline. Some peptides can increase BDNF in the brain to help with these issues. 
 Where this is used:

 NGF (Nerve Growth Factor) What is it: 
 This helps to grow, protect, and repair nerve cells, particularly in peripheral nervous system (outside of the brain and spinal cord). 
 Why does it matter: 
 NGF can help with nerve regeneration and healing. It may help with things like neuropathy, pain reduction, and neurodegenerative diseases. 
 Where this is used: 
 P-21
 BPC-157
 Cerebrolysin
 Neuroplasticity What is it: 
 This is basically your brain's ability to rewire itself and do things like create new connections, learn, and adapt after stress and injury. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Some peptides can boost neuroplasticity and help with memory, focus, and mental recovery. 
 Where this is used: 
 Semax

 Neurogenesis What is it: 
 Neurogenesis is the creation of new neurons, typically in the hippocampus (memory center of the brain). 
 Why does it matter: 
 The more neurogenesis, the better the memory, mood, and cognitive health and is important in depression and brain aging. 
 Where this is used: 
 Semax
 Cerebrolysin
 Synaptogenesis What is it: 
 This is the formation of new synapses which are the places between brain cells where they communicate with each other. 
 Why does it matter: 
 The more synapses you have, the better the brain function.

 Dopaminergic Signaling What is it: 
 This is how your brain uses dopamine for motivation, reward, and drive. 
 Why does it matter: 
 If you have too little dopamine, you're going to have low motivation, brain fog, and cravings. If you have too much dopamine, you're going to have anxiety.

 Serotonin What is it: 
 Serotonin regulates mood, sleep, digestion, and overall emotion. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Low serotonin is tied to depression, irritability, and sleep issues, so peptides that can support serotonin levels can reduce anxiety and improve mood. 
 Where this is used:

 Oxytocin What is it: 
 Oxytocin is the love hormone and is released during bonding, trust building, and physical touch. 
 Why does it matter: 
 It helps with mood, emotional regulation, and social connection and can help with PTSD and anxiety. 
 Where this is used: 
 Oxytocin peptide
 HPA Axis (Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis) What is it: 
 This is your body's main stress-response system that links your brain and adrenal glands to help control cortisol release.

 Issues within the HPA axis can lead to chronic fatigue, anxiety, and hormonal balance.

title: Hormones and Growth Factors
text:
IGF-1 (Insulin-like Growth Factor 1) What is it: 
 IGF-1 is a hormone that is made mostly in the liver as a response to growth hormone (GH) in the body and can help with things like cell growth, tissue repair, and muscle building. 
 Why does it matter: 
 IGF-1 is a critical driver of muscle growth and recover and can also help with fat metabolism and supporting insulin sensitivity. 
 Where this is used: 
 IGF-1 LR3
 Growth Hormone Secretagoguges
 GH (Growth Hormone) What is it: 
 Growth hormone is made by the pituitary gland and can control growth, fat metabolism, and cellular repair. 
 Why does it matter: 
 It can promote fat loss, increase muscle, help with sleep and recovery, and help with collagen and skin. These levels will naturally decline with age, which is where supporting this as you age can be pretty beneficial. 
 Where this is used: 
 Growth Hormone Secretagogues
 GHRH (Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone) What is it: 
 This is a hormone that is released by the hypothalamus and tells your pituitary gland to release growth hormone. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Sermorelin, CJC-1295, and Tesamorelin can all mimic this hormone to naturally increase the release of growth hormone in the body. Essentially, they trigger this effect to cause your body to release more growth hormone.
 Where this is used: 
 Growth Hormone Secretagogues 
 GHRP (Growth Hormone-Releasing Peptide) What is it: 
 GHRPs mimic ghrelin to stimulate the release of growth hormone from the pituitary gland. 
 Why does it matter: 
 These can boost GH, but also support appetite and recovery.

 GnRH (Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone) What is it: 
 GnRH is a hormone that comes from the hypothalamus and tells the pituitary gland to release LH and FSH which are the hormones that control testosterone, sperm, and fertility. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Using peptides that stimulate this can help to restore hormone production without TRT and can be used for fertility, PCT, and HRT alternatives.

 LH (Luteinizing Hormone) What is it: 
 LH is released by the pituitary gland and tells the testes or ovaries to produce testosterone or estrogen/progesterone. In men, it signals the testes, in women it signals the ovaries. 
 Why does it matter: 
 This is important for natural hormone production and can help with libido, energy, and fertility. 
 Where this is used: 
 Kisspeptin
 Fertility peptides
 FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) What is it: 
 FSH works in conjunction with LH to help with fertility and helps sperm production in men and egg development in women. 
 Why does it matter: 
 FSH is very important for fertility and helps with overall hormone rhythm and reproductive health. 
 Where this is used: 
 Fertility peptides
 TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) What is it: 
 TSH is released by the pituitary gland and tells the thyroid to produce T3 and T4, which are very important metabolic hormones in the bod

 Telomeres are the protective caps on the ends of DNA (think of them like shoelaces). Telomerase is the enzyme that helps rebuild them. Shorter telomeres can lead to accelerated aging. 
 Why does it matter: 
 Preserving or lengthening telomeres can help with longevity and cellular function.

 Nitric oxide helps to relax blood vessels, increase circulation, and improve oxygen delivery to tissues within the body.

 More nitric oxide means that your body will have better blood flow, better pumps in the gym, and better recovery.

title: Immune Function and Autoimmune
text:
Th1 / Th2 Immune Balance What is it: 
 Th1 and Th2 are two pieces of your immune system. Th1 will help with cellular defense and take care of things like viruses and bacteria. Th2 will help with the humoral response and take care of things like allergies and parasites.
 Why does it matter: 
 If Th2 is overactive and Th1 is underactive, then you can have issues like allergies, autoimmune issues, and weak defenses against infections. 
 Where this is used: 
 Thymosin Alpha-1
 KPV
 Regulatory T Cells (Tregs) What is it: 
 Tregs keep your body from attacking your own tissues and help to shut off inflammation after an immune response is over. Think of these like peacekeepers within the immune system to prevent unnecessary fighting.
 Why does it matter: 
 Low or lack of functional Tregs can lead to autoimmune disease and chronic inflammation. 
 Where this is used: 
 Thymosin Alpha-1
 Thymalin
 Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs) What is it: 
 TLRs are sensors that exist on immune cells to identify danger with things like viruses or bacterial toxins. They essentially alert the immune system to those issues.
 Why does it matter: 
 If the TLRs are too sensitive or are constantly being triggered unnecessarily, then it can lead to chronic inflammation and autoimmunity. 
 Where this is used: 
 Thymosin Alpha-1
 VIP
 LL-37
 Macrophage Activation What is it: 
 Macrophages are immune cells that will go clean up damage, destroy pathogens, and give off signals to recruit more immune help from the body.
 Why does it matter: 
 Microphages are good during an infection or injury, but if there is overactivation, it can cause tissue damage and inflammation. 
 Where this is used: 
 Thymosin Alpha-1
 KPV
 Inflammasome What is it: 
 Inflammasomes are a protein complex inside of immune cells that can trigger the release of inflammatory cytokines.
 Why does it matter: 
 Overactive inflammasomes can cause autoimmune, chronic inflammation, and neurodegeneration. 
 Where this is used: 
 KPV
 Thymosin Alpha-1
 Mast Cell Activation What is it: 
 Mast cells release histamine and other inflammatory chemicals in response to different triggers like allergens, infections, and stress.
 Why does it matter: 
 If mast cells are overactive, they can cause different symptoms like fatigue, gut issues, itching, and brain fog. 
 Where this is used: 
 KPV
 LL-37
 Cytokine Storm What is it: 
 A cytokine storm is when the immune system has an overreaction and release way too many inflammatory signals at once and can cause severe tissue damage.
 Why does it matter: 
 This can cause dangerous inflammation when it comes to things like long-COVID and autoimmune flares. The goal is to regulate the cytokines before they can do damage. 
 Where this is used: 
 Thymalin
 Thymosin Alpha-1

title: What Are Peptides?
text:
Peptides are essentially just short chains of amino acids. You can think of them like little messengers in the body. They will travel to different places to tell your cells to do specific things like repair tissue, reduce inflammation, release growth hormone, or improve insulin sensitivity. Your body already produces peptides naturally, but supplementing with them gives you more control over what’s happening and the benefits and responses that are associated with them.
 They're not the same things as exogenous hormones, and they’re definitely not the same thing as TRT or steroids. Most peptides don’t replace anything in your body, they just signal your body to do something it already knows how to do and should be doing in a fully optimized state.
 Different peptides do different things depending on how they’re structured. Some help with joint healing, some support gut repair, some help burn fat more efficiently, and some improve cognitive function or sleep.
 Peptides typically come in powdered form and often times will need to be mixed with bacteriostatic water before you are able to use them. 
 Most of them are injected under the skin via subcutaneous injection (most common) or intramuscular injection. 
 Not all peptides will be felt immediately. Some might take days or weeks to build up the effects.

title: How to Reconstitute Peptides
text:
Most peptides are going to come in powder form in a small glass vial that may seem like it won't hold much liquid at all. These are 3mL (milliliter) vials, meaning they can hold up to 3mL of liquid (typically bacteriostatic water). Sometimes, you may find something that comes in a 5mL, 10mL, or 20mL vial. 
 A lot of people overcomplicate the reconstitution process. It may seem daunting, but all you are really doing is adding the right amount of liquid into a vial so the peptide dissolves and can be drawn into the syringe for use. 
 Reconstitution is the process of adding liquid to the freeze-dried powder in your peptide vial to create an injectable solution. The powder form is how peptides are shipped because it's stable at room temperature during transit. The reconstituted solution is what you inject.
 What you need: 
 Your peptide vial
 Bacteriostatic water (or other liquid solution that may be required)
 A 1cc or 3cc syringe with a 25-30g needle
 Alcohol swabs
 A stable surface
 The process: 
 Step 1: Let both vials come to room temperature. Cold BAC water injected into a cold peptide vial can shock the powder. Give both about 10-15 minutes out of the refrigerator. I personally do not store BAC in the fridge and I think it is best to store in a cool dark place, but some do. 
 Step 2: Wipe the rubber stopper of both vials with a fresh alcohol swab. Let it dry for 30 seconds.
 Step 3: Draw your BAC water into the syringe. The amount of BAC water you add determines the concentration of your final solution. Refer to the Reconstitution Cheat Sheet at in the classroom or use the Peptide Calculator to determine the right volume for your desired concentration.
 Step 4: Insert the needle into the peptide vial and slowly let the BAC water in. There is a good chance that there will be negative pressure that will basically suck the liquid into the vial. 
 Step 5: Remove the needle and gently swirl the vial. Most peptides dissolve within a minute or two. Some take longer. Gently rolling the vial between your palms can help.
 Step 6: The reconstituted solution should be clear and colorless. If it's cloudy, stringy, or won't dissolve something is wrong like wrong solvent, damaged peptide, or contamination. Do not inject it.
 Step 7: Store reconstituted peptides in the refrigerator. Label the vial with the date of reconstitution.
 How much BAC water to add: 
 This is where the Reconstitution Cheat Sheet and the Peptide Calculator are essential. The amount you add determines your concentration and therefore how many units you draw per dose.
 Use the Peptide Calculator and enter your vial size and desired dose and it does all of this for you.
 Shelf life: 
 Unreconstituted lyophilized peptide refrigerated or frozen: typically stable for 12-24 months, if not more depending on the compound.
 Bacteriostatic water after opening: typically 28 days at room temperature per the label. I personally use for 60 days at a time. There are some who run the same bottle of BAC

title: Supplies and Tools Needed
text:
This part trips people up because there are a bunch of syringe sizes, needle gauges, and random terms thrown around online. Here’s what supplies you'll need and what each thing is actually used for.
 Syringes You’ll commonly find two types of syringes:
 3cc syringe – This can be used for for reconstituting peptides, or for injections that require more than 1mL (100 units) for a dose. 
 1cc (insulin) syringe – This is for reconstituting or injecting the peptide . It has a super thin needle and shows dosing in "units" instead of mL, which makes it easy to measure small doses.
 Pro tip: Get U100 1cc insulin syringes with a 29–31 gauge needle, either 1/2” or 5/16” length. That’s what you’ll use for subcutaneous injections.
 Needles Needle gauge = thickness. Lower number = thicker needle.
 25G–27G needles for reconstitution (mixing bac water into your peptide vial)
 29G–31G needles for subcutaneous injections (less pain, small volume)
 You can also get combo packs where the needle is removable and swappable between drawing and injecting. This are commonly referred to as Luer Lock.
 Needle Lengths 1/2" or 5/16” is perfect for subcutaneous (belly fat, love handle, etc)
 1”+ is usually only for intramuscular, which most peptides don’t require
 Stick with 5/16" or 1/2” 30G insulin syringes if you’re injecting under the skin. That’ll work for 99% of things.
 Other Supplies Bacteriostatic water – What you’ll use to reconstitute the peptide
 Acetic Acid solution - Only used for AOD-9604
 Phosphate Buffered Saline - Only used for ARA-290
 Alcohol wipes – Wipe vial tops and skin to keep everything clean
 Sterile vials (if needed) – For blends, custom stacks, or transferring reconstituted peptides
 Sharps container – Or anything puncture-proof to safely toss used syringes

title: Understanding Dosages and Units
text:
This is the part that confuses a lot of people and it’s honestly where most dosing mistakes happen.
 This section is going to show you how to understand the math and make it simple.
 What the Units Actually Mean If you’re using a 1cc insulin syringe (which is most common), there are 100 units total on the syringe .
 100 units = 1mL
 50 units = 0.5mL
 10 units = 0.1mL
That’s it. All the units on the syringe are just a fraction or percentage of 1mL.
 Your peptide vial is reconstituted with a certain amount of bac water, typically somewhere between 1mL and 3mL, and that determines how concentrated it is.
 So when someone says “take 10 units,” that doesn’t tell you much unless you know how many mg or mcg of peptide are in each mL of liquid.
 Reconstitution Determines the Math Let’s say you’ve got a 5mg vial of a peptide. That means there’s 5,000 micrograms (mcg) of peptide in the vial. You choose how much bac water to add, and that’s what determines how strong each unit will be.
 Here are some examples:
 Example 1: You add 1mL of bac water to a 5mg peptide 5mg (5,000mcg) divided by 1mL = 5,000mcg per mL
 Each unit on the syringe = 50mcg (.05mg)
 10 units = 500mcg (.5mg)
 20 units = 1,000mcg (1mg)
 This is a more concentrated mix. You’ll be injecting a smaller volume to get your dose.
 Example 2: You add 2.5mL of bac water to a 5mg peptide 5,000mcg / 2.5mL = 2,000mcg per mL
 Each unit = 20mcg (.02mg)
 25 units = 500mcg (.5mg)
 50 units = 1,000mcg (1mg)
 This gives you more flexibility, especially if you want to start at a lower dose due to adding a higher volume of bac water. The math is cleaner, and it’s a lot harder to accidentally overdose yourself.
 How to Pick How Much Bac Water to Use Here’s the easiest way to think about it:
 You want to reconstitute your peptide in a way that makes the math clean, easy to scale, and gives you at least a 5-unit dose so you’re not messing around with tiny, hard-to-measure amounts.
 So instead of using a standard amount like 2 or 2.5mL, do this:
 Match the volume of bac water to the vial amount using decimal-based ratios. 
 Example:
 If it’s a 15mg vial , add 1.5mL or 3mL 
 If it’s a 12mg vial , add 1.2mL or 2.4mL 
 If it’s a 10mg vial , add 1mL or 2mL 
 If it’s a 5mg vial , add 0.5mL , 1mL , or 2mL 
 This helps the numbers stay clean and easy to divide, and the mcg per unit always comes out to something manageable and even.
 Why the 5-Unit Minimum Matters When you’re dosing with an insulin syringe (which shows 100 units = 1mL), you want your dose to be at least 5 units , ideally more if possible. Anything under 5 units is hard to measure accurately, and you’re more likely to either underdose or overshoot it.
 So when you’re deciding how much water to add:
 Think about the dose you’re going to be using 
 Make sure the math gives you at least 5 units per dose 
 This way, no matter what vial you’re working with, your math stays easy and you can draw accurate dosages

title: Injection Techniques and Locations
text:
Injecting yourself for the first time feels more intimidating than it is. For most people, once they do it for the first time, they realize it's not that difficult and are pretty confident. 
 Subcutaneous injection (the most common method): 
 SubQ injection goes into the fat layer just below the skin, not into muscle.
 Best sites for SubQ:
 Lower abdomen (most commonly used). Pinch an inch of skin and fat away from the belly button. 
 Outer thigh is good alternative.
 Back of upper arm is another spot, but personally this one is quite difficult for me to access.
 Love handle area.
 Rotate your sites. Using the same spot repeatedly may cause scar tissue to form which affects absorption and becomes uncomfortable. You have a lot of space on the abdomen and other sites where you can rotate quite easily to various spots. 
 How to inject SubQ: 
 Step 1: Wipe the injection site with an alcohol swab. Let it dry.
 Step 2: Draw your dose into the syringe.
 Step 3: Pinch a fold of skin and fat at your chosen site.
 Step 4: Insert the needle at a 45-degree angle (or 90 degrees if you have enough fat depth — 5/16" needle length at 90 degrees typically stays SubQ for most people).
 Step 5: Release the pinch. Push the plunger slowly and steadily.
 Step 6: Remove the needle at the same angle it entered. Apply gentle pressure with a clean swab if needed. 
 Step 7: Dispose of the needle in your sharps container immediately. For information on how to dispose of sharps in your state, visit safeneedledisposal.org . 
 What's normal after a SubQ injection: 
 Mild redness, warmth, or a small raised welt that resolves within 30-60 minutes.
 A small painless lump under the skin that disappears within a few hours.
 Occasional mild bruising may be normal, especially on thinner skin.
 What's not normal: 
 Significant swelling and increasing pain after 24 hours. Seek medical attention.
 Streaking redness spreading from the site. Seek medical attention immediately.
 If you see blood in the syringe: 
 You've nicked a small blood vessel. Remove the needle, apply gentle pressure, discard that syringe and draw a fresh dose. Do not inject into a vein. This is rare with SubQ injections but technically could happen.
 Intramuscular injection: 
 IM injection goes into muscle and is used less commonly for peptides but relevant for various aminos and for larger volumes.
 Common IM sites: glute (ventrogluteal preferred), outer thigh (vastus lateralis), shoulder (deltoid).
 Use a longer needle for IM, typically 1" at 25G for most sites. Inject at 90 degrees. No pinch needed. Some use the Z-track method for IM injections. 
 Intranasal administration: 
 For peptides like Semax and Selank that are administered intranasally you'll need a nasal spray bottle. Draw the reconstituted peptide into a syringe and transfer it into the nasal spray bottle. Tilt your head slightly forward, spray into one nostril while blocking the other, and breathe gently through your nose.

title: Peptide Cycles
text:
Most peptides are going to be ran in a cycle of various lengths. If you can understand why cycling is important, it can help you plan protocols correctly. 
 Why compounds are cycled: 
 Receptor desensitization: Some compounds may cause the receptor to become less responsive over time with continuous use. So taking a break can allow the receptor sensitivity to recover. 
 Important to note: GLP-1 compounds do not cycle for this reason. GLP-1 receptors do not significantly desensitize with continuous use. Things might "feel" different, but they still seem to respond in other ways. 
 Assessing response: If you had a few days of headaches, would you continue to take Tylenol or Ibuprofen daily after that? You wouldn't. With peptides, taking a break after a cycle can allow you to see if the issue was addressed and determine if additional cycles are even needed. 
 Cost and sustainability: Ultimately, you're going to save money when you cycle off. There are exactly zero people who wouldn't benefit from that. 
 For compound-specific cycle lengths, refer to the Consolidated Reconstitution, Dosage, and Cycle Lengths course in the classroom.

title: Your First Peptide - Where to Start
text:
When people do things the right, they are spending weeks and sometimes even months before making a decision and ordering things. That is the smartest way to do it but at some point your research will have to turn into a decision. 
 This section is going to give you a starting point based on your goal. It's not going to be an exhaustive list but it's a place to start to look into some things with one or two compounds that make sense for where you are right now, with realistic expectations for what you might experience and when. 
 The number one rule before anything else is to start with just one compound. You're not starting with a stack or three things at once. You're going to start with one compound and run it correctly for long enough to actually be able to assess it. This is how you learn what works for your body. It's going to keep costs manageable and know what is responsible if something goes wrong. 
 Once you have a baseline with one singular compound, then you can make an intelligent and informed decision in the future about what you might want or need to add later on. Until that point you're just guessing and hoping that the two things that you stack will work together or that you even still need a second or third thing. 
 Examples by Goal: 
 Healing - BPC-157
 Appetite-driven weight loss - GLPs
 Metabolic fat loss - MOTS-C
 Sleep and Recovery - Growth Hormone Secretagogues
 Cognitive / Anxiety - Selank
 Cognitive / No Anxiety - Semax
 Gut health - KPV
 Understand that in certain scenarios some things will have multiple areas in which they overlap and so you may be able to resolve multiple problems with just one thing.

title: How to Tell If It's Working
text:
This is something that I think people really struggle with and often times will continue using various compounds even when they're clearly not working. Usually it's because people don't understand what to even look for. 
 The most important thing to understand first: 
 Most peptides do not produce dramatic, immediately noticeable effects. If the first one you try is a GLP, you will likely be very disappointed in future peptides at first as you'll probably expect them to "hit" the way that the GLP did and give you very measurable results. But ultimately they work by enhancing the body's own processes which generally are more gradual. If you are expecting to feel something the first week the way you'd feel caffeine or a pre-workout you will more than likely think that nothing is happening even if something is. 
 The timeline depends on the compound and the goal. Here is a realistic expectation framework:
 BPC-157 and healing compounds: Week 1-2 - Possibly nothing noticeable. Week 3-4 - Reduced soreness, faster recovery between sessions, potential reduction in localized pain. Week 6-8 - Primary healing benefit should be clearly apparent if the compound is working.

title: Common Mistakes
text:
These are mistakes that I see come up over and over again. Most of them are avoidable. 
 Dosing in units without knowing mg/mcg: 
 "I'm taking 10 units of BPC-157" tells you nothing without knowing the concentration of your solution. 10 units at a 1mg/mL concentration =100mcg. 10 units at a 5mg/mL concentration = 500mcg. That's a 5x difference in dosage, even though it reads the same on a syringe. There is an entire course in the classroom on understanding dose, units, and concentration. 
 Starting multiple compounds at once: 
 If you start four compounds at once and feel great a few weeks in, what's doing it for you? There are many times where people don't even know what's responsible for what's happening to them. Start with one.
 Along with this, people think they HAVE to stack to get results, but you don't. 
 Expecting immediate results: 
 People either expect to see results the day they start or they expect to "feel" something immediately. Peptides don't work like stimulants. Most of them are going to take weeks to show meaningful effects / results. 
 Not knowing how a peptide works: 
 Somewhat in line with the previous point, people are expecting results that a specific compound won't do. If you don't take time to address the cause of your issue, figure out the mechanisms that can influence it, and directly tie a peptides mechanism of action to that, then you will likely not see results. Learn the peptides. 
 Not tracking anything: 
 People will have nothing written down or documented as a way to measure progress so they can't truly assess if things have changed. Write things down and take pictures. You'll be surprised the changes you see when you start doing that.

title: Overview
course: Slowing Aging: Everything to Fight Aging
text:
This course intends to cover the science of why we age and what can be done about it. It's going to pull together different threads you might have seen throughout other courses and put them together into one comprehensive framework while adding some things that other courses might not have covered. 
 This course isn't just a bunch of random anti-aging things thrown together. We will first define what aging is and break it down into biological components. Then, we'll go through and look at a full catalog of interventions like peptides, supplements, topicals, hormones, and daily practices and show which things each one targets, as well as the level of evidence to support it.

title: Course Video
course: Slowing Aging: Everything to Fight Aging

title: What is aging?
course: Slowing Aging: Everything to Fight Aging
text:
Before we can start to fight against aging, we have to define what it actually is. And this can be a bit complex. Aging is the progressive, time-dependent decline in the function and integrity of cells, tissues, and organs, leading to increased vulnerability to disease, and, ultimately, death. When we look at thing like heart disease, most cancers, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's, osteoporosis, etc they are not independent problems that happen in older people. Instead, they are downstream consequences of the same underlying aging processes. If we target the shared root (aging) as opposed to each disease separately, you may be able to delay or prevent many diseases at once. 
 By reframing this, we also can rename what we're changing. Instead of lifespan, we're focusing on healthspan. Lifespan is how long you live. Healthspan is how good you live in good health, free of chronic disease and disability. The goal of serious longevity work isn't just to extend life at the end (while we're still frail and sick) but to extend our heathspan by compressing the period of decline and disease into as short a window as possible at the end of a long, functional life. We want to stay as healthy and capably as possible for as long as possible, then decline rapidly at the end instead of enduring a long, drawn-out deterioration.

title: Biological Age vs. Chronological Age
course: Slowing Aging: Everything to Fight Aging
text: This is another important distinction we need to make. Chronological age is how many years you've been alive. Biological age is how old your body actually is when we look at the cellular and functional level. Two people of the same age can have very different biological ages depending on genetics, lifestyle, and state of aging hallmarks. Biological age is the thing that we're trying to lower with some of these interventions. When we see that an intervention revered aging by a certain amount of time, it typically means it lowered a biological-age clock reading.

title: The 12 Hallmarks of Aging
course: Slowing Aging: Everything to Fight Aging
text:
In 2013, there was a paper in the journal Cell that identified nine "hallmarks of aging" which were measurable biological processes that drive aging. In 2023, the same people published an updated version that expanded it to twelve hallmarks which are the framework for longevity research and what we will use to organize how we understand what to fight. 
 To qualify as a hallmark, it has to meet three criteria: appearing during normal aging, experimentally accelerates aging, and therapeutically targeting it slows, stops, or reverses aging. 
 There are three categories that these are grouped into. Primary hallmarks are the initial causes of cellular damage. The antagonistic hallmarks are responses to that damage that are beneficial at low levels but harmful when chronic or excessive. Integrative hallmarks are the consequences that arise when the damage goes beyond what the body can compensate for and are most directly responsible for the functional decline of aging. Damage goes from primary to antagonistic to integrative, which is why targeting the primary and antagonistic hallmarks can help to prevent the downstream decline. 
 Primary (the damage) 
 Genomic instability
 Telomere attrition
 Epigenetic alterations
 Loss of proteostasis
 Disabled macroautophagy
 Antagonistic (the responses)
 Deregulated nutrient-sensing
 Mitochondrial dysfunction
 Cellular senescence
 Integrative (the consequences)
 Stem cell exhaustion
 Altered intercellular communication
 Chronic inflammation
 Dysbiosis

title: Overview
text:
Growth hormone (GH) , which is also known as somatotropin, is a peptide hormone that is important for things like growth, metabolism, and tissue repair. It is produced by the pituitary gland in a pulsatile manner and is regulated by hypothalamic hormones. Growth hormone secretagogues are compounds that stimulate the body's own GH release. Growth hormone secretagogues include GHRH analogs (drugs that mimic Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone) and ghrelin mimetics (drugs that activate the ghrelin receptors). These growth hormone peptides have become pretty popular as alternatives to GH therapy. However, many people say that nothing truly compares to the real thing. In this course, we will break down each of these things as well as giving a true comparison between them all. 
 Visual representation overview of it all: 
 https://commons.m.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:1809_Hormonal_Regulation_of_Growth.jpg

title: Growth Hormone (Somatropin)
text:
Endogenous GH Physiology: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and typically peak during deep sleep and will reduce to low baseline levels in between those pulses. GH release is stimulated by GHRH and inhibited by somatostatin. Once it is released, growth hormone will directly effect tissues and stimulate the liver to produce IGF-1 (Insulin-like Growth Factor-1). 
 Recombinant GH (rHGH) Therapy: Exogenous GH (somatropin) is a 191-amino-acid protein that is identical to natural human GH. This is why often times you'll see growth hormone listed as HGH-191-aa . The FDA has this approved for things like GH deficiency in children and adults, certain pediatric growth disorders like Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, etc) and other conditions where muscle wasting can occur. In people with GH deficiencies, rhGH therapy can restore the normal growth and metabolic function. In children, it can help with linear growth (height) and in adults with GH deficiency, it can help with body composition, bone density, and quality of life. It also is used (which is off-label) as an anti-aging or performance-enhancing compound. 
 Body Composition Effects: Growth hormone has anabolic (tissue building) and lipolytic (breaking down fat) effects. In people who have deficiencies or those who are older, it can help to reverse some of the body composition changes that come with age. There was actually a study by Rudman et al. (1990) that showed that 6 months of GH injections in men over 60 (with low IGF-1 levels) increased lean body mass by 8.8% and decreased adipose (fat) mass by 14.4% compared to controls. Now, this seems impressive but lets remember the population that's being studied. Men over 60 with IGF-1 deficiencies. It is effective, but we can't expect this to have the same results in a young, healthy adult with higher IGF-1 levels. In that study though, GH administration took their numbers from under 350 U/L to 500-1500 U/L. Important to note here is that the unit of measurement is different than how we currently test the IGF-1 with the ng/mL measurement. So they were getting it somewhere comparable to 200-400 ng/mL. It will also be used in younger adults or athletes looking for better muscle protein synthesis and better body composition. However, they don't always see significant results that people generally tie to GH usage. It was good, but not mind-blowing. 
 Metabolic and Other Effects: GH promotes lipolysis (especially in visceral fat) and has something called a diabetogenic effect of raising blood glucose by reducing insulin sensitivity (basically you could get diabetes from it). It also can be glucose-sparing by stimulating adipocytes (fat cells) to release fatty acids for fuel. GH can also increase protein synthesis and help with the growth of bone, cartilage, and organs, which is mostly done by IGF-1 increases. Most of the people who use GH will have better recovery, skin quality, and overall well-being improvements. On the other side of the coin, inc

title: Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone Analogs
text:
GHRH analogs are peptides that are going to act like our natural growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and bind to receptors on pituitary somatotrope cells to stimulate GH release. Natural GHRH has pretty rapid degradation, but the synthetic analogs have modifications to increase their stability or half life. Ultimately what they are trying to do is boost GH in a more physiological manner by being more pulsatile. They do this by leveraging the body's own systems to do so. We recognize the GHRH analogs with things like Sermorelin, CJC-1295, Tesamorelin, etc. 
 Sermorelin - Sermorelin is a synthetic peptide that is made up of the first 29 amino acids of GHRH. It has a shorter half-life and can increase GH and IGF-1 modestly, but has really been passed by things that work a bit better. One thing to note is that it was an FDA-approved therapy at one point. 
 CJC-1295 with DAC - this is a modified GHRH analog that is designed to have a longer duration. CJC with DAC (Drug Affinity Complex) adds in a molecule that binds to albumin which gives it a half-life of about a week. This can create a more sustained elevation in GH and IGF-1 while still preserving some of the pulsatility of GH release. In a clinical trial, one injection of CJC-1295 gave a GH increase of about 2-10x over baseline for 6+ days, and raised IGF-1 by about 1.5-3x for 9-11 days. The numbers that were associated this were increases from a baseline of 123-152 ng/mL and went up to 232ng/mL at the lowest dose, all the way up to 435 ng/mL at the highest dose. Here's a link to the article , but you'll only be able to see the abstract which doesn't show the specific numbers (I had to login to do so). With multiple weekly injections, the IGF-1 levels remained elevated above the baseline for up to 28 days. One benefit of CJC-1295 w/ DAC is that it only has to be administered 1-2x weekly at a minimum due to the longer half-life, so it's a bit more convenient than doing daily GH injections. CJC-1295 no DAC is a very similar, but has a shorter half-life. In terms of data, there is no real data to support this compound that is peer-reviewed. 
 Tesamorelin - Tesamorelin is FDA-approved under the brand name of Egrifta as a treatment for HIV-associated lipodystrophy specifically to reduce excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV patients on antiretroviral therapy. It is typically given as a 2mg subcutaneous injection once daily for that purpose. Clinical trials were very effective and over the 26-week trial with HIV patients , they were able to reduce visceral adipose tissue by about 15% on average, where the placebo group actually increased 5%. That creates about a 20% relative reduction in visceral fat and was alongside of improved lipid profiles (triglycerides dropped by 50mg/dL in the Tesamorelin group where the placebo actually rose). IGF-1 levels also increased about 81% from baseline with Tesamorelin, which shows a pretty strong GH-axis activation, but with no significant changes in blood glucose

title: Ghrelin Mimetics (GHRPs)
text:
The other set of growth hormone secretagogues that work by mimicking ghrelin which is the hunger hormone that can stimulate growth hormone release. Ghrelin is going to bind to the Growth Hormone Secretagogue Receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, which is different than the GHRH receptor. The ghrelin mimetics are things like GHRPs (Ipamorelin, GHRP-2, etc) and the non-peptide analogs like MK-677. These can override somatostatin inhibition and cause strong GH pulses and work especially well when combined with GHRH signals. 
 GHRP-6 - GHRP-6 a hexapeptide that can result in GH release with sharp GH spikes and a strong stimulation on appetite. I want to reiterate the STRONG appetite stimulation. Some who use this feel incredibly hungry, so just know that can happen. GHRP-6 has been observed to have some very strong peaks that are comparable to a strong physiological GH pulse. The downside with GHRP-6 is that it can potentially raise prolactin and cortisol slightly and are generally mild at normal dosages (which all GHRPs could potentially do). 
 GHRP-2 - GHRP-2 is another GHRP that is more potent than GHRP-6, but doesn't seem to have the same strength of appetite increases that GHRP-6 has, although it can still raise it in some capacity. GHRP-2 can also raise cortisol and prolactin potentially. In animal studies, GHRP-2 showed that the potency was higher, but the maximal GH release was lower compared to GHRP-6. So it was more potent, but less effective. GHRP-2 is also called pralmorelin and has been used as a diagnostic test for GH deficiency in countries like Japan. 
 Hexarelin - Hexarelin is a GHRP that is very potent in terms of GH release and is an analog of GHRP-6. A single IV dose of hexarelin took GH levels from basically zero to 55 ng/mL within 30 minutes , which was basically the theoretical maximum of GH output for the subjects. Hexarelin is typically administered via injection, but also has been studied to have some effects in both oral and intranasal methods of administration. One thing that is interesting about hexarelin is tachyphylaxis, which means that when used continuously, the GH response is going to attenuate, or reduce, over time. After two weeks or so of daily administration of hexarelin, the GH peak is reduced which could be due to receptor desensitization or increased somatostatin tone. For this reason, cycling or pulsing hexarelin (few days on, few days off) may be a better option for using it. Outside of the normal benefits, hexarelin has been shown to be cardioprotective in animal models, outside of the benefits of GH. From the research that's out there, hexarelin improved cardiac function in post-myocardial injury models and may activate cardiac receptors related to growth hormone secretagogue receptors in the heart. Hexarelin is really best for increasing IGF-1 more acutely, but not the most ideal for long-term therapy due to the attenuating effects of this compound.

title: Pairing GHRHs with GHRPs
text:
You will often see a GHRH paired with a GHRP. For example, CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin is a very common way of doing this. Is it necessary? No. But they can be synergistic in their effects when combined together. It is going to work through two pathways - GHRH receptor and GHS receptor (ghrelin receptor) to amplify the output from the pituitary glands more than either of them could do alone. Basically, the GHRH peptides are stimulating the release and the GHRP's can allow that to be magnified by inhibiting somatostatin's suppression (the hormone that inhibits the release of GH) and acting through that ghrelin receptor pathway. In some cases, we can see that using both a GHRH and a GHRP together can give a larger GH spike than just using one of these by themselves. Their synergistic relationship can be seen across a variety of studies online, such as this one . This is the reason why people will often times combine CJC, Tesa, Sermorelin, etc with Ipamorelin or something similar. Combining them can allow for maximum benefits and increases in IGF-1 levels, while still generally remaining within the physiological ranges. 
 Note - You don't HAVE to pair a GHRH with a GHRP. As stated above, there are benefits to doing so. If you want to get the most out of them, pairing them together will give the best results. However, either can be used individually.

title: Comparison Between Exogenous GH and Secretagogues
text:
A question / statement that I get all the time is that you should just use GH and that everything else is pointless. But really, how does exogenous GH and the secretagogues really compare to each other? Based on some of the previous pages, you can probably interpret some of this for yourself, but I will break it down within this section so you can see it in a consolidated manner. 
 IGF-1 Increases : Exogenous GH can raise IGF-1 significantly, almost limitlessly, depending on the dose that is administered. Obviously, you're not going to run 40IU of exogenous GH daily. But 6IU of GH will increase IGF-1 levels more than 2IU of GH would. So using high-dose GH, you can push IGF-1 numbers well above the normal ranges. With the secretagogues, you can have some pretty noticeable IGF-1 increases, mostly to the high-normal levels, but not typically far beyond that. At some point, the secretagogues will run into a ceiling due to the body's natural feedback mechanisms (like somatostatin) or pituitary exhaustion. If your goal is maximum IGF-1 elevation (usually for people like bodybuilders), then the only thing that will really do that is going to be high-dose GH. But, if you wanted to restore IGF levels with some notable increases, both normal / lower dose exogenous GH and the secretagogues will be able to accomplish this. The other benefit of the secretagogues would be that it can increase IGF-1 with pulsatile GH and potentially contribute less to insulin resistance than constantly high GH levels. 
 Efficacy Regarding Body Composition Changes : Both exogenous GH and the secretagogues can promote lean tissue growth and fat loss, but the amount in which they do so can differ from each other. Especially in people who are deficient in growth hormone, GH therapy can be pretty effective in terms of the results and their is some pretty solid data supporting this. The secretagogues are less studied generally speaking, but as long as the pituitary gland can respond to their stimulus, there can be good results. In the growth hormone page of this course, we referenced the Rudman study to show the benefits that can be observed using exogenous GH administration. Tesamorelin is another with very significant benefits that are observed in clinical settings, especially when it comes to visceral fat reduction (which was about 15-20%) in a matter of 6 months (referenced in the Tesamorelin section) while also preserving lean mass in the patients that were observed. It's also important to remember the population it was studied in (HIV patients) and understand that the results may vary in different populations and under different circumstances. Ultimately, when it comes to the secretagogues, the amount of anabolic benefits and fat loss can depend on the compound itself as well as the population it's studied in. Exogenous GH is also a great fat-burner, especially in visceral fat, but could cause hyperglycemia whereas Tesamorelin was able to do so with less of that glycemic effect

title: IGF-1 and Cancer Risks
text:
It's been coming up a lot lately with the risks of cancer and the increase in IGF-1 from things like the growth hormone secretagogues (tesa, CJC, ipa, etc) or exogenous growth hormone. Hopefully this post can help sort out just how risky it really is when evaluating the decision to explore these compounds.
 First let's talk about the Tesamorelin studies. They had over 800 patients with HIV-related lipodystrophy and 500 some got tesamorelin and the rest had the placebo. 15 different people got cancer, 12 of them in the group who was using Tesa and 3 in the placebo group. The investigators who looked at this only found that two of the cases of cancer could even be considered to be related to the treatment they were receiving. The interesting thing? One was using Tesamorelin and one was on the placebo. Technically, the placebo group had a higher occurrence if you look at it as a percentage of the population. Here's the review that looks at the risk profile of Egrifta (tesa): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2010/022505orig1s000riskr.pdf 
 Another thing to consider is that the FDA wanted a post-marketing surveillance to continue to look at patients to see if cancer was a major concern. In the 14-15 years since it was approved, they haven't observed this to be a significant risk and have it classified essentially as a theoretical concern based on the mechanisms of IGF-1 potentially causing growth. It even says it can be considered for use if cancer is gone and treatment is completed. Also, another important thing to note is that the HIV patients are generally at a higher predisposition for some cancers anyways vs the normal population, so not seeing a significant increase in that population should provide even more assurance.
 If this is the case then why are these concerns even around? Well, because IGF-1 can cause cells to grow and survive. It helps us grow muscle, bone, tissue, etc, but can it also grow cancer?
 Well there is some data that supports IGF-1 creating higher risk of developing some cancers like colorectal, prostate, and breast cancer. Somewhere in the 5-40% increase. In acromegaly where IGF-1 levels are at extreme levels for very long periods of time, they do see the higher rates of colorectal and thyroid cancers, but those also come alongside of significantly higher levels of IGF-1 than what the secretagogues are producing. Also, they're not seeing a spike in cancer for those on growth hormone replacement therapy either, which further solidifies that it might not be so incredibly risky like it's made out to be.
 Another thing worth looking at is what that percentage increase really correlates to. Let's just assume that everything is on the high end and that there's a 40% increase in risk. It's relative to the current risk percentage. So if your lifetime risk of colorectal cancer is around 4%, a 40% increase makes it around 6%. Prostate cancer would go from 12% to 17%. title: Estrogen, AIs, and Growth Hormone
text:
There has been some discussion about aromatase inhibitors (AIs) blocking the benefits of growth hormone secretagogues. This section is going to break down the relationship between all of these and help you understand what goes on here. 
 The first question is do AIs blunt GH secretagogue effects? There is a relationship between estradiol and GH secretion / IGF-1 production. In this article , you can see that in men there is definitely a relationship between the suppression of estradiol and the blunting of GH secretion and as a result IGF-1. So if you're running an AI pretty aggressively or suppression E2 below where is necessary, then it is likely that you are also crushing your body's IGF-1 potential as well. If you're looking at a secretagogue, it would play a role into this as well since it's using your body's natural systems to secrete more and increase these levels. 
 So what is the relationship between Estradiol and IGF-1? Well estradiol can stimulate GH secretion and in return increase IGF-1 levels. A big piece of the benefits also come from the aromatization of testosterone into estrogen. Outside of just the GH and IGF-1 component, estradiol is important for men and can help with a lot of things like cognitive function, bone health, body composition, etc. Also, as an example of SERMs/AIs and their effect on IGF-1, Tamoxifen has supporting data for its use to control IGF-1 in acromegaly patients. 
 So basically, don't crash estradiol. The AI itself may not be the biggest issue in terms of AI = poor IGF response, but more so the amount of suppression that you're doing to your estradiol. Estradiol is important for more than one reason. Lower isn't always better and it shouldn't just be looked at as a number on paper.

 Pre-Workout or Intra-Workout: Best used before or during training. Helps improve blood flow, muscular endurance, and recovery between sets. This blend is ideal for anyone doing high-volume lifting, circuit work, or endurance training where fatigue usually sets in fast.

 Method of administration: Subcutaneous or intramuscular. 
 Dosage (in units): 50 - 100 units. 
 Frequency: Administered 30-45 minutes before training 3-5x per week.

text:
There are a lot of uses for peptides. Of course, because this is my passion, this may come across as biased. But, we can see that many users of peptides have had remarkable benefits from using them, but is not always the case. Sometimes when they are used in animal studies or when we hear personal testimonials, they might seem like almost miracles. But when they go through human trials, the results might be disappointing or inconclusive. 
 Why do compounds like SS-31, FOXO4-DRI, MOTS-C, etc. seem to have great anecdotal success but never results in a robust amount of evidence in clinical trials? My goal with this is to take a deep dive into that question specifically. I'll talk about why trials may fail and why negative trial results might not necessarily mean that a peptide is useless. I'm also going to discuss the evidence landscape of peptides in tiers from things that are well-proven to those that are pretty much just experimental. I'll also talk through things like pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD), minimal clinically important differences (MCID), the placebo effect, subgroup analysis, and trial design. The goal is to help you understand some of these things and interpret results as well as pitfalls that exist within this space.

title: Why Do Clinical Trials of Promising Peptides Fail?
text:
This part can be a bit frustrating. There are compounds that might show some extraordinary results in pre-clinical studies and animal models, or even a few patients or anecdotal experiences, but the formal clinical trials end up finding little to no benefit. There can be a lot of different reasons that this can happen. I think one point to note though is that potentially up to 90% of drug candidates fail at some stage before they get to approval. So why is that? 
 Lack of Efficacy in Humans: This is probably the most obvious reason a peptide would not make it through. It didn't work well enough in people. The therapy might work well in mice but then it doesn't translate to meaningful improvement in outcomes for a human disease. It might improve a biomarker but not actually help a patient feel better or live longer. Or it might have a very observable effect in animals, but the effect was much smaller in humans and a trial might not be able to detect it. 
 Differences in Pharmacokinetics/Pharmacodynamics : A really important piece of this is pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) which is basically how the drug acts in the body and the effect it has. In simple terms, pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug, and pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body. Peptides might have a short half-life (meaning it breaks down quickly in the body) or poor bioavailability (might not be absorbed or distributed properly). As an example, a lot of peptides wouldn't be given as a pill because the stomach enzymes can destroy them so they may need to be administered through an injection or other method of administration. If a trial doesn't get the dosage or the delivery right, an effective peptide might actually seem to fail because of those reasons (think AOD-9604 via oral administration). PK/PD studies are typically done pretty early to help guide dosing and will look at things like how long it stays in the system and how much and if those levels correlate with the desired effect (can see this in the 43 day observation after single ascending dose in Phase 1 of Retatrutide clinical data in the Retatrutide Deep Dive Course). Some trials might use a dose that was effective in animals but not humans (SLU-PP-332 as a potential example) or a dosing schedule that doesn't match the peptides active window. Sometimes, the design issues of a trial can lead to it failing, even if biologically the drug could work under better conditions. 
 Trial Design Flaws: This leads us to trial design flaws. Even if the peptide is potentially effective, a poorly designed trial can mask its benefits. Some design pitfalls include too few participants, improper placebo or control, or choosing the wrong endpoints to measure (SS-31 walk test maybe?).
