text:
There are a lot of times where we hear about anecdotal experiences where someone uses a peptide or compound that isn't approved for use and have fantastic results. I want to take a moment to address that as well as how subgroup responses may be indicative of actual benefits to the point where we can't dismiss them completely. 
 Is It A Placebo or Not: I think it's absolutely reasonable when looking at anecdotal benefits to account for the occurrences of the placebo effect as well as the natural fluctuations that can occur in someone's symptoms. Just the belief that someone is using something that can improve their health can actually allow them to see the benefits and see measurable improvements in different areas. A lot of conditions can also phase in and phase out in terms of severity. Think about something like an autoimmune disease where it can somewhat go into remission on their own, an injury or surgery recovery can happen regardless, and people's mood can fluctuate with the day or season. So because of those factors, if someone starts a peptide and then starts to feel better, it could have just been coincidence or psychology. Because of this, we have controlled trials that allow us to separate those types of factors from the true effects of the compound. Anecdotal reports really cannot PROVE cause and effect. However, if there are a lot of independent anecdotes that can start to tell a similar story to each other, especially in areas where you wouldn't expect random or spontaneous improvement, it's worth keeping an eye on. Think about the phases of taking SS-31. About 2-3 days in you feel extreme fatigue that lasts for 2-3 days, then energy returns and typically stays. That's not something that is documented in clinical trials as the experience, but so many people experience that same thing so it seems indicative of what the compound is doing. In practice, the best thing to do would be to utilize this data and experiences to allow for further digging, rather than definitive proof. Again, it may be difficult and expensive to get this definitive proof. 
 Analyzing Subgroups: Another thing in clinical trials that can be observed is subgroups. These are smaller population groups of participants that are grouped by different characteristics like age, gender, disease, genetics, etc. You can look at some of the Phase 2 Clinical Trial Data for Retatrutide in the deep dive course to see how data might be broken down across different subgroups within the population. Sometimes a trial that doesn't have overwhelming data for overall effectiveness is neutral, but a subgroup within that population that was studied had clear and stronger benefits. One of the downfalls of this though is that they can produce false positives and false negatives. This is an interesting discussion about subgroup results being fun to look at, but don't over-trust them.

text:
This section is going to look at different peptides by classifying them into tiers based on the evidence that exists to support their efficacy. There are three tiers we can break this down into: 
 Tier 1: Therapies that are approved and established in mainstream medicine and that are FDA-approved (or by other similar agencies) with robust data to support efficacy and safety. 
 Tier 2: Peptides with mixed evidence or promising results that only exist in specific subgroups or specific conditions where there is some clinical trial support or real-world use, but have either failed trials or aren't universally accepted worldwide. 
 Tier 3: Peptides with early human evidence or very strong rationale based on the mechanisms of action. These might be tested in a small study or are supported by the mechanism and animal data. They look promising, but don't have human evidence to support. 
 Tier 1: Established Peptide Therapies 
 These peptides are the ones that have made it through the trials and tribulations of the system and are utilized in standard medical practices. They have clear benefits in placebo-controlled trials and have regulatory approval. 
 Insulin: Insulin is the OG peptide hormone that has been used for about a century now to treat diabetes. It was so effective that it never really needed modern RCTs to be accepted since it's literally a life or death situation without it. It is really the base of diabetes management. 
 GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: These are things like liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide that are used for type 2 diabetes and have a significant amount of clinical trials evidence to support it. We have clear and statistically significant data (15% body weight loss with an outperformance over placebo) to show the efficacy of these compounds. It is FDA-approved and was a game-changer for obesity treatments. It also has other data such as the ability to reduce the risk of major cardiac events in obese people without diabetes. 
 Bremelanotide (PT-141): This is one that was originally derived from Melanotan 2, which was an experimental peptide that people use for tanning and observed the unexpected side effect of sexual arousal. This anecdotal experience led to the development of bremelanotide which is now FDA-approved for treating hypoactive sexual desire disorder in women and was approved in 2019 (brand name is Vyleesi).

 This can be where it gets to be a little more ambiguous. These peptides have shown some evidence of benefits like a positive Phase 2 trial, approval in specific countries, significant improvements in a subgroup of patients, etc. but may have failed larger trials or lack universal acceptance by regulatory groups.

title: Checklist for Interpreting Data
text:
I think it's important to understand how to appropriately evaluate the data that exists and some things you can keep in mind when assessing data and understand does something or will something potentially work and could it apply to me. 
 What is the Source? Is it a peer-reviewed clinical trial, a case report, or gymbro6969's Reddit post? Obviously we're going to give a lot more weight to the controlled trial data that is published in reputable journals vs, anecdotes or self-published data. 
 How Big and Well-Designed was the Trial? Sample size and methodology are important. This can go for both sides of the spectrum. If the sample size and methodology are wrong and the outcome seems positive, it could be skewed and actually not be effective. On the other hand, it could have been too small or improper methodology to truly find out the effectiveness of the compound. 
 What Endpoints were Measured? You have to look at the outcomes that were examined and measured. Were they clinically meaningful? Something might have changed in bloodwork, but do they feel better? Was the changes big enough that someone would actually notice them? 
 Statistical vs. Clinical Significance? Was the result statistically significant (which is usually p<0.05 )? Or, if it wasn't statistically significant, was the study too small and underpowered? If it's not statistically significant, it doesn't always mean there is no effect. Also look to see if a trial failed but there were trends or subgroups that did better (remembering that it could also have been a random chance that they did better). 
 Subgroup Analyses or Specific Population Response? If a trial has a pretty underwhelming result, look to see if they saw a subgroup that experienced different results. Like people over 60 getting significant improvements or with a certain condition. If there was, is there a potential reason why that group might have responded better? These always should have verification to confirm these results, but it can be somewhat indicative of their potential. 
 Has it been Reproduced? Usually, a single study doesn't give us a definitive answer. We want to build confidence by replicating those results. So, are there multiple independent trials that show similar results? This can allow you to aggregate data and results and lead more towards an answer. 
 Does the Studies Population Relate to the One I Care About? If you're looking at something that helps Alzheimer's patients but you're a young, healthy adult, the data might not support it's effectiveness for you. title: Overview
text:
ARA-290 is an 11-amino acid peptide that is derived from erythropoietin (EPO). There is a component of EPO that is tissue-protective and anti-inflammatory and that is the component that is isolated to make ARA-290 to avoid the risks of red blood cell production. 
 There is a component that is targeted specifically by ARA-290 to allow it to act preferentially on damaged tissue which is the innate repair receptors (IRR). This deep dive will have a special section dedicated to that so you can better understand how it works and how the benefits may be recognized from ARA because of how that works.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Innate Repair Receptor Activation 
 As mentioned in the previous graphics, the IRR is upregulated in injured and inflamed tissue so ARA-290 will have concentrated activity at those sites of damage. ARA-290 has a short half-life, but once the peptide binds to the receptor, it creates downstream signaling cascades which can give longer-term benefits. So every time you administer a dose, it's going to signal these reparative processes that are going to continue after the peptide itself can clear from your system. 
 Downstream Signaling Cascades 
 Once ARA-290 activates the IRR, it triggers several intracellular signaling pathways that are going to give the benefits that we see :
 Anti-apoptotic signaling: the IRR activates the JAK2/STAT5 and PI3K/AKT pathways, which suppress programmed cell death or apoptosis. In injured tissue many cells that would otherwise die from the stress of injury or inflammation are instead rescued. This is really the core 'cytoprotective' effect that allows these at-risk cells to stay alive long enough to go through the recovery process. 
 Anti-inflammatory modulation: ARA-290 suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine cascades and modulates NF-KB signaling, which is that same master inflammatory switch which we talk about in the immune system and other courses. This is going to dampen the activation of innate immune cells that drive chronic inflammation but it's going to do this without broad immunosuppression. What we have here is a rebalance of an overactive inflammatory response rather than just shutting the immune system down, which potentially could have negative effects. 
 TRPV1 and neuropathic pain modulation: In neuropathic states we have something called the TRPV1 ion channel, which is going to integrate pain signaling and neurogenic inflammation. This is going to become up-regulated and sensitized in peripheral nerve fibers. What ARA-290 is going to do is interact with this pathway, which is part of how it reduces that neuropathic pain alongside the structural nerve regeneration that it can promote. 
 Nerve Fiber Regeneration: Outside of just protecting the existing tissue, ARA-290 actively promotes the regrowth of small nerve fibers. This is really the most surprising and well documented effect, which is observed and measured in clinical trials, showing objective regrowth of nerve fibers, which most of the therapies out there are actually unable to achieve.

title: Benefits of ARA-290
text:
A lot of the benefits that we see with ARA-290 actually come from Phase 2 clinical trials. I'm going to break them down in order of the quality of evidence that we have for these benefits, starting with the neuropathy and nerve components. 
 Small Fiber Neuropathy and Nerve Regeneration 
 This is really the primary application for this compound and has some pretty strong data to support it.
 Small fiber neuropathy is a condition where the small nerve fibers, the unmyelinated C fibers and lightly myelinated A delta fibers that are responsible for sensing pain, temperature, and autonomic function, are going to become damaged and die back. What this ends up causing is a burning pain, numbness, tingling, and autonomic dysfunction. Most of the time these conventional treatments are really just limited to masking the symptoms because nothing is really able to regrow those lost nerve fibers. 
 The ARA-290's evidence comes from a double-blind randomized placebo trial where they looked at 64 patients with sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy . The patients got either 1 mg, 4 mg, or 8 mg of the compound or they were on a placebo and they were given it subcutaneously for 28 days.
 What they saw was that a 4 mg dose produced a significant increase in corneal nerve fiber area versus the placebo group and had about a 23% increase from baseline, which shows a pretty good measurable nerve growth. That same dosage also significantly increased skin nerve fiber length and the patients reported clinically meaningful reductions in pain, which is really a huge win because the pain is the most miserable component of this. 
 One thing that's interesting with this is that the 4 mg dose is actually what produces the strongest nerve response. In this case more doesn't really seem like it's actually better. 
 Diabetic Neuropathy and Metabolic Effects 
 They did another placebo-controlled trial where they administered 4 mg of ARA-290 daily for 28 days to patients with type 2 diabetes. Outside of just the neuropathic symptom improvement, they actually noticed that there were some improvements in HbA1c, which is a marker of long-term blood sugar control, as well as lipid profile, with really no safety signals that were associated with this. This suggests that the IRR's anti-inflammatory and tissue protective effects might actually branch out into metabolic regulation, potentially through reducing chronic inflammation that can drive insulin resistance. This is something that they found that actually is going to need some more studies to determine exactly. 
 Diabetic neuropathy is really the most common and difficult complication that's associated with diabetes and the same way with sarcoidosis-related neuropathy. The conventional treatments are really just masking and managing symptoms but the nerve regeneration component is relevant here because the metabolic improvements are also an added bonus that makes sense with the overall anti-inflammatory mechanism of this com

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Across the phase 2 trials whether it was for the sarcoidosis-associated small fiber neuropathy or type 2 diabetes, the standard protocol was 4 mg subcutaneously once per day for 28 days. They did study it at 1, 4, and 8 mg but the 4 mg dose did produce the strongest nerve fiber response even better than the higher 8 mg dose. Some of the ophthalmic trials also extended the treatment to 12 weeks at 4 mg a day without safety issues and so really the most optimal dosage for this is going to be 4 mg a day. 
 Now there are people who have benefits using smaller dosages. I've seen people have benefits around 1 mg. However some people do have to increase the dosage up to something like 2 or even 4 mg before they start to really recognize the benefit. 
 As a cost savings measure it may be reasonable to start somewhere like 1 mg and work up over time but the more effective dosages are likely going to be in that 2 to 4 mg range.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
ARA-290 has a pretty clean safety profile and is backed by human trial data. Across the Phase 2 trials there were really no significant safety issues that were observed at any of the doses that were tested, even the 8 mg dose. 
 The biggest key safety component of this is that there are no erythropoietic effects and it doesn't stimulate red blood cell production. That's really the entire reason that this compound was designed: it selectively avoids the risk of EPO while taking all of the benefits towards healing. 
 Now some of the side effects that people might experience are:
 Injection Site Reactions: as always this can occur with any compound that is being injected. 
 Hypoglycemia: this one is unlikely to happen but for somebody who's using a GLP or some other compound, it's important to understand that this may also bring down blood sugar and so it's important to track and manage that appropriately. 
 One caveat that I want to mention is that you probably should avoid it with any type of active cancer because it can help to keep alive some of those cells, like we mentioned earlier with the anti-apoptotic signaling. You would not want to protect any type of malignant cells from the cell death that they should be experiencing.

title: Overview
text:
Outside of the GLPs, BPC-157 is probably one of the most mainstream and talked about peptides for the general population. What makes it interesting starts with where it came from. It's a partial sequence pulled from a protective protein that's naturally found in your own gastric juice. So it's based on a fragment of something your stomach already makes to protect and heal itself.
 The main reason that people are interested it is for healing. In animal studies, it's been shown to speed up repair across a variety of tissues. Typically, the most common application is for tendon and ligament injuries. 
 What makes it stand out 
 What makes BPC-157 stand out from other compounds in this category?
 Breadth - BPC-157 seems to help across a variety of tissue types, as opposed to being very tissue-specific.
 Stability - Most people talk about peptides being destroyed in the gut. BPC-157 actually shows some significant stability within the gut, which makes sense considering is derived from gastric juices. 
 Safety signal - Generally speaking, BPC-157 has a strong safety profile outside of a few nuances we will discuss later.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
BPC-157's effects reach a lot of different tissues, but there are a few core mechanisms that create the effects that BPC-157 provides. Understanding these helps you to understand why the benefits created by BPC-157 exist. 
 Angiogenesis - This is the main component of how BPC-157 works. Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels. When we are healing tissues, we ultimately end up in a bottleneck of blood supply because new vessels are what deliver oxygen, nutrients, and repair cells to a damaged area and carry the waste byproducts of inflammation away from it. Growing that new blood supply is usually the rate-limiting component of repair. A tissue can have the growth signals it needs, but if it's unable to build blood supply fast enough, the healing will just stall. That's why tendons and ligaments heal slowly as they're poorly vascularized. BPC-157 seems to speed up that vascularization component which is likely why it helps those tissues that may typically struggle. 
 This occurs mostly through upregulating something called VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor), which is the signal that triggers new capillary growth. BPC-157 increases VEGF, VEGF activates a receptor, then that switches on an enzyme called Akt, and Akt activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase to product nitric oxide. That puts the blood vessel effect into the nitric oxide system which we'll talk about in the next point. 
 The nitric oxide system - BPC-157 interacts with the nitric oxide system which is a signaling network that regulates blood vessel tone, blood flow, inflammation, and cell survival. Part of the angiogenic effects that was previously discussed runs through it. But some of the research suggests that BPC-157 actually helps to regulate and stabilize the nitric oxide system, supporting healthy nitric oxide function and counteracting damage that can come from it getting dysregulated. That regulating component as opposed to just standard stimulation is important. 
 The FAK-paxillin pathway - There's also a component of healing that requires cells to physically migrate to a damaged area to rebuild it. BPC-157 activates this FAK-paxillin pathway which governs how cells spread and move. When we look at tendon and ligament healing specifically, that means it may promote the migration and proliferation of tendon fibroblasts, which are the cells that actually lay down the new tendon tissue, and support the collagen and extracellular matrix that can rebuild the structure. So not only does it improve blood flow, it can also help with the physical rebuilding itself. 
 Growth hormone receptor upregulation - This one is pretty important when it comes to the tendon aspect. BPC-157 increases the expression of growth hormone receptors on fibroblasts, which mean those healing cells become more sensitive to the growth hormone that's there, amplifying the growth and proliferation signals that can drive repair. This is another added benefit outside of the angiogenesis comp

title: Benefits of BPC-157
text:
Like we discussed in the mechanism section, there is a broad range that this target, ultimately leading to a broad range of benefits as well. 
 Tendon, ligament, and joint healing - This is the main use of BPC-157. Tendons and ligaments are slow healers because of their poor blood supply and that's where the benefits of the angiogenesis mechanism should help the most. In animal studies of tendon and ligament injuries, BPC-157 reported up to 60-80% faster healing than untreated controls, as well as better quality tissue and better recovery of function. It's been studies in tendon-to-bone healing, ligament damage, and muscle tears with pretty consistent results. This is why you see it used so commonly and the popularity of this compound in people who go to the gym and various types of athletes. 
 Gut and digestive health - Considering this is where the compound comes from, it makes sense why this could be one of the top applications for it. In animal models, it's shown strong protective and healing effects throughout the digestive tract, healing things like stomach and intestinal ulcers, protecting the gut lining from NSAID and alcohol damage, supporting gut barrier integrity, and showing benefit in inflammatory bowel disease. Because of the stability it has in stomach acid, it also makes this one pretty effective for use orally. 
 People typically use this for gut issues and inflammatory bowel conditions like Crohn's and ulcerative colitis, gut lining and leaky gut support, and recovery of digestive function. 
 Muscle and bone - The healing effects of BPC-157 can also extend here. In the animal studies, BPC-157 has sped up the recovery from muscle tears, crush injuries, and just general damage through the better blood supply and cell repair, and has shown some benefit in bone healing and fractures . In my opinion, something like Bonothyrk may be more beneficial in bone/fracture situations as opposed to BPC-157, or they could potentially pair together well when used for more complex injuries involving bone and tissue. 
 Nerve and neuroprotection - This is an interesting component of the research on BPC-157. In animal models, this actually has shown some nerve regenerative effects that support recovery after nerve injury, as well as some neuroprotective effects including TBI models and models of neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's. Some of this ultimately ties back to the gut-brain axis and the effects on neurotransmitter systems .

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Because there are no large human trials, there's no officially established human dose for BPC-157. What we have instead comes from animal studies scaled down, clinical experience at telehealth and compounding practices, and community protocols. What follows is the commonly used reference range and the reasoning behind it. This is educational, not a prescription, and given the regulatory situation covered later in this course, BPC-157 is something you want to be running under medical supervision.
 Because there are no large human trials, there is no officially established human dosage for BPC-157. However, there are common protocols that are typically ran. 
 Standard dosing - The most common protocol for injectable BPC-157 is roughly 250 to 500 mcg per day, sometimes as a single daily dose and sometimes split into morning and evening. Some try to start higher and taper down for injuries, but I don't believe it is completely necessary to do so. 
 Standard injectable: 250 to 500 mcg/day, once or twice daily subcutaneous, 4 to 6 weeks.
 Conservative start: 250 mcg/day once daily, assess, then adjust.
 Acute injury: 500 mcg/day split AM and PM through the acute phase, then taper.
 Oral, gut-focused: 250 to 500 mcg/day once daily, oral or sublingual, as needed.
 You don't have to inject at the injury 
 This is the biggest misconception about BPC-157. People come to me and say they were injecting BPC-157 in their foot to heal something there. It is NOT necessary. It just leads people to try to inject in areas around joints and tendons when there's no need to. 
 BPC-157 appears to work systemically and once it's in your system, it travels through your body and acts wherever there's damage that needs repair, because the mechanism gets triggered where the injury signals are, not where the injection went. In the animal research, it produces wide-ranges of healing effects through routine systemic administration. A standard subcutaneous injection into the stomach will help a tendon injury in your ankle just as well as an injection near the ankle would. Now, if your hip is injured could you inject in the glute? Sure. Because that's a common injection site anyways. But I'm not pinning the bottom of my foot for plantar fasciitis. 
 Injectable vs oral 
 Outside of just the injection site, there's the question on whether or not injecting or oral works/is better. The answer really depends on what you're trying to treat. 
 Oral use is logical for gut-localized conditions like IBD, ulcers, leaky gut, or other gut damage, where you want local action on the gut lining and systemic absorption matters much less. For a systemic goal like a tendon injury, injectable is likely the better supported route.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
In the animal studies, BPC-157 is very well tolerated, however there is no long-term human safety data and there's always the theoretical concern around cancer that is CONSTANTLY brought up. 
 The clean safety signal - Within the animal research, BPC-157 is very clean. They haven't found any type of toxicity issues or significant adverse effects. There was an IV pilot study in 2025 in two adults with no reported adverse effects. 
 Reported side effects - 
 Injection site reactions - mild irritation, redness or discomfort at the site, which is common to basically every subcutaneous peptide.
 The cancer question 
 This is the caveat that people typically parrot more than any other and the way that it gets brought up usually creates more fear than any science supports. Basically, what people say is: BPC-157 causes angiogenesis, cancer needs angiogenesis, therefore BPC-157 causes cancer. But let's discuss that for a minute. 
 Solid tumors really do depend on angiogenesis to grow beyond a tiny size and to spread. A cancer has to build its own blood supply and it can't grow past a couple of millimeters without recruiting new vessels. Since BPC-157's main healing mechanism is promoting angiogenesis, the theoretical concern is that taking it could feed an existing tumor. In my opinion, if you have active or prior cancer, you could practice more caution and likely avoid. 
 However, this misses a few things. 
 Cancer already drives its own angiogenesis, aggressively - A tumor isn't sitting there in your body just waiting for an outside compound to build its blood supply. Cancer cells actively push out their own angiogenic signals, massively overproducing VEGF and other factors to hijack the body into building vessels for them. The switch already gets flipped hard by the cancer itself.
 Angiogenesis is a normal process your body runs constantly - New blood vessel growth isn't inherently cancerous. This is a fundamental repair and maintenance process that happens every time you heal a wound, build muscle after training, or repair the gut lining. If normal angiogenesis caused cancer, then exercise, which is a strong driver of angiogenesis, would cause cancer. But it seems to do the opposite. Angiogenesis is a tool the body needs and uses for repair, cancer just misappropriates it. 
 BPC-157 appears to regulate angiogenesis rather than crudely amplify it - As opposed to blindly forcing maximum vessel growth everywhere, the research actually suggests that it modulates and stabilizes angiogenesis in a controlled way, promoting it where healing is needed while keeping the rest in line.

title: Overview
text:
People ask me all the time what they can take to build muscle. Before we get into any compounds, I want to explain what your body is actually doing when it builds muscle and what you can do to support that process.
 We’ll start with what happens inside a muscle fiber, then get into the things you can control: how you train, how hard your sets are, how much protein you need, and how recovery affects your progress. We’ll also cover losing fat while keeping muscle, which is especially relevant for anyone using a GLP-1.
 Later in the course we’ll look at creatine, testosterone, anabolic steroids, growth hormone, and peptides. 
 This course is educational and is not individualized medical advice. If you have a health condition, injury, or questions about medication, work with your healthcare professional.

title: Steroids, Peptides, GH, and Supplements
text:
Some compounds can substantially increase muscle. Others not so much. The most important things to actually increase muscle are the things that were mentioned prior to this section in the course. 
 Testosterone and anabolic steroids 
 Anabolic steroids can directly increase muscle size and strength. In a 10-week randomized trial, men given a high, supraphysiologic dose of testosterone increased muscle size even without lifting. The group that received testosterone and trained gained more than both. As you can see here, training and nutrition were STILL the most important pieces of this. 
 You would be surprised at the amount of people taking steroids that you would never guess. Many have underwhelming results from these as they don't do it themselves and won't outperform the basics. 
 Growth hormone 
 Growth hormone can increase lean body mass in some capacity, but lean mass includes water and other tissue. A review of studies in healthy young adults found that GH did not improve muscle strength over the weeks to months studied. This is relatively overrated for muscle growth and is better used for sleep, recovery, and moderate fat loss. 
 Peptides 
 The GH peptides are the most common that are discussed when it pertains to this. These ultimately fall into the same discussion we just had as it pertains to growth hormone. 
 Creatine and protein 
 Creatine monohydrate helps regenerate energy during short, demanding efforts. Combined with resistance training, studies suggest it can modestly improve lean-mass gains on average. A common daily amount is around 5 grams. Creatine can help, but isn't doing it all for you. Protein powder is best used to assist you in reaching your total protein intake needed each day.

title: Overview
text: Epitalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide that is derived from epithalamin, which is a peptide that is naturally produced within the pineal gland. It was originally isolated in the 1970s by Russian scientists and later derived by Professor Vladimir Khavinson to isolate the portion with the most active components.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Telomerase Activation - Epitalon can activate telomerase which is an enzyme that elongates telomeres (the protective caps on the ends of your chromosomes). 
 Each time your cell divides, your telomeres will shorten the same way that the plastic tips on your shoelace can wear down over time. That's basically what the telomeres are. They're like protective caps on the end of your chromosomes. When your body boosts telomerase, you have the potential to delay aging at the cellular level (since they typically become shorter as you age), help with tissue repair, and help fight against damage and age-related diseases. There is a POTENTIAL risk associated with telomerase increases which is that unregulated telomerase activity can exist in cancer cells. So they are essentially allowed to divide indefinitely and avoid senescence. The important aspect here is that Epitalon is going to generally be self-limiting in the sense that it is not going to results in this uncontrolled growth and unregulated telomerase activity. This article actually gives some interesting insight into the activity on telomeres in healthy and cancer cells. What they basically noticed is that the telomerase activity was increased by Epitalon in normal, healthy cells. It took a couple of weeks to have noticeable changes and wasn't significant or uncontrolled. They had a moderate level of extension and seem to have natural mechanisms that keep these types of things within range, the same that most peptides do. With cancer cells, Epitalon still raised the gene signaling for telomerase activity, but the cancer cells turned on ALT, or Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres, to basically have an uncontrolled, chaotic process to live forever. There's also some data that exists that suggests that Epitalon may even reduce tumors . 
 Pineal Gland Regulation and Circadian Rhythm - Epitalon targets the pineal gland in the brain and helps to recover some of the hormone output that has decreased over time. It can increase the secretion of melatonin , which is a hormone that regulates our sleep-wake cycles or circadian rhythm. As we get older, those levels can drop which is going to disrupt our sleep patterns and cause various aging effects. Epitalon helps to revive the function of the pineal gland and help contribute to higher nighttime melatonin levels and better circadian signals which are the cues your body gives to regulate your internal clock. One of the potential benefits of this is that it may actually help to modulate the expression of the genes that regulate circadian rhythm. In a 20-day course of Epitalon, pineal melatonin output was increased and they say the circadian gene expression improve in older adults. This means that Epitalon may actually help your body reset it's natural clock at the molecular level and help with sleep and hormonal balance. This also supports the efficacy of a 10-20 day cycle of Epitalon having continued benefits after the cycle is complete. 
 Immune System Modula

title: Benefits of Epitalon
text:
Based on the mechanisms of how Epitalon works, what are some of the benefits we can observe? 
 Longevity and Anti-Aging - This is a benefit that many look for from a variety of different peptides. Epitalon potentially can be contributed to a longer life and health span. In animal studies, they actually were able to see that treated mice lived longer, where the last 10% lived 13% longer than the control groups. Even when rats were exposed to things like constant light or extreme season light, the median lifespan still increased even though they had more circadian stress. They actually observed over a 12-year study of older adults with cardiovascular risks, that the groups that were treated with Epitalon had a 28% reduction in overall mortality and half of the cardiovascular mortality than the control group . They still need to further confirm these studies, but it shows that it can potentially have an influence on lifespan and reduce some of the age-related death rates in different populations, along with being biologically younger during the years that someone lives. 
 Telomere and Cellular Aging - This ties along into the first benefit, but through the telomerase activation of Epitalon, it can help cells continue to divide in a healthy manner and avoid premature senescence. It could potentially increase telomere length by 30-40% and allow the cells to divide longer than they normally would. So basically, it's slowing down your aging at the cellular level. 
 Enhanced Sleep and Circadian Rhythm - Many people who use Epitalon notice pretty significant sleep improvements. In a 2021 placebo-controlled trial, older adults with a low dose of Epitalon (0.5mg daily) increased their nighttime melatonin production by over 150% relative to the placebo group. With this increased, they also noticed better sleep patterns and things like improved sleep onset and sleep depth. Most of the people who use Epitalon feel like their sleep is more refreshing and they have better energy throughout the day. Epitalon is not a sedative like most sleeping medications, but it helps the body's clock regulate to help lead to better sleep and and easier time falling asleep. 
 Immune System Support - In the mechanism of action section, we covered most of the benefit here. It seems to help with immune response for many as well as reduce some of the chronic inflammation markers people may have. It also may normalize some of the immune overreactions that can occur from some and lower things like C-reactive protein.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
There is quite a lot of variance in how Epitalon can be dosed. The original Russian and Ukranian protocols did 10mg/day for 10 days, done 1-2x yearly. Some did 10mg every other day for 20 days total. Many say that this was translated improperly and that people can use lower dosages. Here's what I will say: 
 There is nothing wrong with trying to run the first 10 days of Epitalon at 1mg to see if you have noticeable effects. I know some who feel like their sleep improved pretty well with that protocol. If for some reason you have no noticeable effects, bump to 2mg for the next 10 days. 
 If that never works at those amounts, take a break, and try 5mg/day for 10 days. If that doesn't work, bump to 10mg/day for 10 days. 
 The reason that I have it broken down like this is that there are many people that I see through anecdotal evidence that still have to go to those higher dosages before they start to recognize observable benefits. It is more cost effective if you're able to get the benefits at 1mg, but just know that some do have to increase higher to achieve those. This typically only has to be ran 1-2x yearly. Most of the time, people take Epitalon in the evening and think that seems to be the best time to take it for improved sleep.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Overall, Epitalon has a pretty good safety profile. In the Mechanism of Action section, we did touch on some potential concerns from telomerase activity, but it seems that the data could go either way there. Outside of that, here are some potential side effects: 
 Injection Site Reactions - This is true for basically everything. Usually not that bad for most, but may be a little spicy for some. 
 Vivid Dreams - Some people do feel like their sleep improves but it comes with more vivid dreams which they may not like. 
 Fatigue - Some may feel fatigued as their body's internal clock begins to regulate and typically will go away as the body adjusts to the compound.

title: Overview
text: GHK-Cu is a peptide that is already naturally produced by the body and typically is utilized for benefits like skin, wound healing, hair, and anti-aging. It is a regulator of thousands of genes within the body and has a lot of potential benefits. As we age, our levels start to decline significantly, which puts GHK-Cu as potentially one of the most beneficial anti-aging peptides out there.

text:
There are really a couple of distinct mechanisms that are benefits of GHK-Cu.

This is what drives a lot of downstream consequences because copper is an essential cofactor for dozens of enzyme systems (basically things that fuel other processes) throughout the body. If copper is low within specific tissues, then those downstream processes can start to degrade. This occurs as we age. Some of those processes include: 
 Collagen cross-linking - this is where collagen fibers are woven together and connected to things within skin, tendons, organs, etc. There is an enzyme that helps with this, lysyl oxidase, which NEEDS coper to function. If it doesn't then the collagen that is produced isn't woven together as well. This means you will have weaker, less elastic tissue which leads to things like aging skin and slow healing wounds. When GHK-Cu helps improve this copper supply, the collagen structure is stronger. Think about it like a tightly woven net and how strong that can be vs. one more open. 
 Antioxidant Defense - There's an antioxidant enzyme called superoxide dismutase which helps get rid of damaging free radicals produced by the mitochondria. This again requires copper to work well, so if copper drops, then oxidative stress increases, and your cells will ultimately age faster. If you remember from the mitochondria course, we talked about needing to clean up the ROS within the cells, but this basically helps to mitigate the amount of cleanup you'll have to do. 
 Wound Healing - There are multiple enzymes that are going to be at the site of a tissue injury that need copper to function such as the ones that help with new extracellular matrix, regulating inflammatory signaling, and replacing scar tissue with healthy tissue. GHK-Cu is supporting the processes that will ultimately make an injury heal faster, cleaner, and better. 
 The important thing to understand here with all of these is that as we age, our GHK-Cu levels will decline, and so will our ability to deliver copper to all of those processes above (and more). Our collagen quality will degrease, our antioxidant abilities will decrease, our wounds will heal slower, etc. They don't just stop one day. Over time, they will just continue to decrease, which is exactly how we age. You don't wake up one day with wrinkles. 
 Gene Modulation - GHK-Cu can modulate the expression of over 4,000 human gees within the body. It basically can help to do the opposite of what we see happening with genes as we age.  Wound Healing / Tissue Repair

You have a few different ways in which all of this occurs which is the delivery of copper to the wound-site enzymes, collagen production signaling, and MMP-mediated clearance of the scar-forming fibrous tissue. GHK-Cu is basically targeting all of the pieces of the healing process at once resulting in faster closure, less scarring, and better quality tissue at the wound site.

It can help to enlarge hair follicles and extend the anagen (active growth) phase and increase the thickness of the hair. They actually have done a study with GHK-Cu applied topically and daily for 6 months with significant hair growth improvement.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
GHK-Cu is primarily administered in two main forms: topical (creams, serums) and injectable. Topical works well for localized benefits for skin and hair, where injectable can be used for systemic benefits throughout the body. 
 Topical: 
 1% for facial use,
 2% for body application,
 3% for promoting hair growth .
 One important thing here is you don't HAVE to make it any more concentrated for these other applications. 300mg in 1oz of Hyaluronic Acid is generally sufficient for all applications. 
 Injectable, oral, intranasal (injectable is going to be the most effective here): 
 1 - 2 mg daily for 4 - 12 weeks on, followed by 4 - 8 weeks off. My preferred protocol is 2 mg daily for 4 - 8 weeks.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
GHK-Cu seems to have a pretty good safety profile overall, especially for the topical applications. 
 Potential Side Effects Include: 
 Injection site reactions - GHK-Cu can be quite painful at the injection site. There are a few main ways to mitigate this. 
 Go deeper. Use a 1/2" needle instead of 5/16"
 Dilute with more BAC water
 Inject in the glutes instead of stomach
 Use a massage gun on the site after injecting
 Copper uglies - This is VERY rare, but basically people are reporting that their skin looks worse before it gets better. This may be from using too much for the individual and dialing it back some can potentially help so using a smaller dosage or less concentrated serum can help. But in some cases, it could be that the MMP component is causing a breakdown of collagen faster than it can be replaced. Another potential cause of this is "purge" before the improvement, similar to how Accutane works. 
 Copper accumulation - This is quite unlikely to occur based on the amount of copper that is actually within GHK-Cu, but if someone used high amounts for long periods of time, potentially this could be a concern. But like I said, it is very unlikely.

title: Overview
text:
This is a tough course. Why? Because GLP-1 maintenance looks different for everyone. There is no set answer on what is 100% guaranteed to be the right answer that works for you. You will have to figure it out through trial and error. It might not be incredibly difficult, but it might take some effort. 
 Once you reach your goal weight, how to you stay there? How do you keep the weight off that you've lost over the period of time since you started a GLP-1? The goal of this course is to discuss that and the strategies that can help you do this successfully.

title: Why is Maintenance Important?
text:
You've probably tried to diet before in your life. You lost some amount of weight and then gained it back again. That is incredibly common. Ultimately, without a continuance of the lifestyle and habits, that is almost bound to happen. GLP-1 medications can be incredibly beneficial for making this process easier. They help you with appetite control, they help your body release insulin more effectively and efficiently, and they support the effort that you put in to reach those goals. 
 If you don't have a plan for maintenance, you could gain it all back when you lose those "boosts" that you get from the GLP-1s. People can successfully stop taking them (that's one of the options for maintenance), but it does take more work to do so. You've probably seen all of the information out there about people gaining the weight back after stopping a GLP-1. This is because they did not have a maintenance plan / strategy to keep their results, especially when hunger and cravings go back to where they were before.

title: What Maintenance Options Are There?
text:
One thing that is important to understand is that this is going to be very individualized. In my opinion, nobody can tell you 100% which of these options is going to work for you with full certainty, or if you are going to be able to use the same approach forever. The reality is that you may start off with one of these options and change 6 months later. That is what makes maintenance a little bit more difficult. But, this is also what happens when starting the medication too. Some people respond very well at the lowest (or sometimes, lower than the typical lowest) dosages, and some have to work their way a little higher. Ultimately, we just need to understand how to look at these options conceptually, look at indicators of effectiveness, and understand how to approach this successfully. 
 Continue to use the GLP-1 at the same dosage. This one doesn't seem like it's a "maintenance" option, but there are some who ultimately end up staying on 15mg of Tirzepatide because that's what works for them to maintain. Just know that it is an option although most people's goal seems to be to reduce their amount once they reach maintenance. 
 Reduce the dosage and / or frequency. With this, you either reduce down the dosage you take or you reduce the frequency in which you take it. Sometimes, you might even reduce both where you're taking a lower dose at a lesser frequency than you were before. 
 Discontinue the GLP-1 completely. Truthfully, this is probably the most difficult of all of the options as you no longer have the benefits of the medication within your system. Understand that this is not always an option for everyone to do depending on their own personal situation. If you choose to do this, it is the same as any other diet or lifestyle change. You HAVE to maintain the lifestyle and habits. The kicker is you no longer have the GLP supporting you in doing so, which makes it just a bit more difficult, but not impossible.

title: Option 1: Stay Where You're At
text:
This one may just fall into place naturally for you. We all know that while using these your body may begin to adapt to how you feel in terms of appetite suppression and other effects. We also know that over time, the rate of weight loss may slow. And for those who have gotten to, or are at this point, we know that the last 10 lbs always seem to be the most stubborn. So, this option may almost "fall into place" for you. 
 As you start to near your goal weight, you might realize that the dose you're on almost turns into maintenance. This is why I say that this option may almost seem to fall into place for you. Once you reach that point, you may realize that the dosage that you're using keeps everything in check the way that it needs to be, whether it's appetite, A1C, etc. 
 What are some of the reasons we might look at to decide if staying on the same dosage is the right answer outside of it "falling into place?" 
 You've had issues regaining before. Maybe you lowered your dose, maybe you hit a stall and started gaining, etc. These could be indicators that staying at the same dosage might be the best option. There's also a component of this that plays into the second reason which is health conditions that cause reason number 1 to be more likely. 
 You have other medical conditions that benefit from the higher dosages. This could be anything from diabetes, PCOS, fatty liver disease, blood pressure issues, cholesterol, etc. If there is a medical condition that is being controlled by using a higher dosage, then typically it makes more sense to stay there as opposed to titrating back down or coming off. Now, in certain scenarios, these issues may be fixed and allow for a dosage reduction once maintenance is reached. 
 Everything feels good where you're at. Sometimes, you are tolerating a dosage well and everything about where you are just feels right. You have just the right amount of control over appetite and food noise and there's really no reason to change. You may be able to test the waters and see what reducing dosage or frequency might feel like, but where you're at just seems to feel right. In this case, there's really not a need to change things up. 
 In any of these scenarios, staying where you are might be the right answer. Maybe you're not ready to titrate down. That's okay. But, eventually, maybe you will be. These are the things that I would evaluate to determine if staying at the same dosage is the right move.

title: Option 2: Reduce Dosage and / or Frequency
text:
This is probably the most common option that people choose when they reach maintenance. Typically, people will continue to lose (regardless of how slow those last 10lbs might seem to be!) until they reach the point where they reach their goal. Once they reach that goal, they typically will continue to lose unless they make some type of adjustment. This is where it become a bit tricky. What is the adjustment we need to make, and how big of an adjustment do we need to make? There's really 3 ways to go about this, considering we can reduce dose, frequency, or both. Let's look at the ways that might make sense for this to be done:
 Reducing frequency. This may be the easiest thing to start with. The reason being is that you can almost immediately gauge how you are going to respond to is as you can track things like hunger, satiety, food noise, etc. as the days go on. The easiest way to approach this in a gentle manner is going to be to increase the time between injections by one day each week until you find the sweet spot for it. At some point you will likely reach the point where you say "yep, this is the frequency that works for me." Now, it might be every 10 days, every 14 days, etc. The reality is that the frequency of time between dosages doesn't really matter much, as long as it's the frequency that works for you. Some people may choose to go straight to every 10 days vs. every 7, but I like the slow and steady approach to it just in case that seems to be too big of a jump to start with. It saves some headache of trying to figure out where the sweet spot might actually be. Here's a good study that talks about the efficacy of using a reduced frequency dosing with GLP-1 RAs https://dom-pubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/dom.16229 . 
 Reducing the dosage. I said that reducing the frequency is probably the easiest thing to start with. This can be pretty easy too in all reality. Now, the same way that we went with a gentler approach to reducing frequency by going slowly can also apply here. Typically, a dosage schedule is a set range that jumps by the same amount each week as we increase dosages. For tirzepatide, it's 2.5mg typically. So, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15. That doesn't HAVE to be that way on the way up, and it doesn't HAVE to be that way on the way down. There's nothing to say that the dosage can't be reduced by a half-dosage on the way down just to make it a little less significant of a jump in case it's too much. So, it could be reduced by 1.25mg at first to make sure it's not too much. There's nothing wrong with reducing by a full-dose either though. But, if you're nervous about it not being sufficient for appetite control, etc, then the half-dose reduction is a little "safer" of a bet. Ultimately, you continue to reduce down the dosage until you finally reach the one that ends up being the amount that works best assist you in staying at your goal weight. Here's an article on tapering that talks about some observations that we

title: Option 3: Stop Completely
text:
This is probably the most daunting of all of the options when people think about maintenance. When people think about coming off of GLP-1s, they think about all of the times where they tried to lose weight before without success. They think about all of the food noise they had before. They think about everything that they have experienced over the past years of their life where they feel like they failed and the only thing that finally allowed them to success was the support of the GLP-1s. 
 But here's the thing - the GLPs weren't the only thing that got you to this point! Every step that you took on a treadmill, every time you walked in the gym, every time you chose a healthier meal option, those were all things that YOU did to get you to where you are. The only difference is that you had the support of a GLP-1. Now, this is also the part that can make this option more difficult. You've been using something that aids your body in many ways to support this process and ultimately make it a little easier. You might not have had to exercise as much discipline in your eating because these compounds took the food noise away. It changed the way your body handled and responded to the food that you ate. So the reality is, you do lose that when you come off of the compounds. 
 However, you may have also created a new set point for your body as long as the weight was lost gradually and not a 2-month loss and then try to quit type of thing. You've changed your relationship with food and your relationship with exercise. You understand all of these things a little more because you've spent time learning about these things as well as your body and understanding yourself a little more. All of this plays into it. It isn't impossible to quit GLP-1s, it's just a little tougher sometimes. 
 GLP-1s have a long half-life. Which means they do take quite a while to get out of your system. So, even if you quit cold-turkey, you still have some level of them in your system for potentially a month or longer depending on the dosage you were on. So, if you completely come off, those cravings and feelings might not come back in full swing for a month or so. 
 But, the reality is, that you might have to do Option 1 or Option 2 before getting to the point that you can come off completely. This may be the best option to coming off completely. Again, not everyone will want to or be able to do this for various reasons. But if you continue to reduce your dosage and frequency over time, you may find that you can come off completely and no longer need them. 
 The most important piece here is remaining committed to lifestyle changes. There will be a level of personal discipline where you have to tell yourself that you don't need the cookies before bed and instead opt for Greek Yogurt with some berries. You have to tell yourself you will remain committed to physical activity. If you come off of the medications completely and lose all discipline, it's the exact same scenario as every ot

title: Importance of Lifestyle
text:
No matter which of the previous options you end up choosing, maintaining a healthy lifestyle that is committed to the right practices is the most important thing you are going to do. This doesn't mean you have to eat chicken and rice 4x a day for the rest of your life. But diet, physical activity, sleep, and managing your stress is going to support your weight goals for the rest of your life. I touch on some of this stuff in the nutrition and exercise courses, but let's go over some important things you can do to help maintain your results. 
 Nutrition: 
 Focus on getting in your protein. This is going to be just as important in maintenance as it was in your weight loss journey. It helps support lean muscle tissue and for a lot of people, eating higher protein can help with appetite control. Also, maintaining muscle tissue can help you burn more calories which will also help keep the weight off. 
 Get fiber-rich foods. Fiber-rich foods can also help with a fullness feeling and allow you to have that fullness with fewer calories and can also help with stabilizing blood sugar (so great for those who had issues with this prior to GLPs). They also can help to slow digestion, which is a benefit that you were getting from the GLPs. So in a way, you're naturally adding something that gives you a similar (albeit maybe a less significant) ability to slow gastric emptying. You'll also want to ensure you're getting in plenty of water along with your fiber intake. 
 Focus on portion control. An important thing here is to NOT overly restrict yourself thinking that it is needed when you come off of a GLP. There's some more details about this in the nutrition course, but eat your meals slowly. Focus on eating the meal when you sit down to eat and avoid distractions. This can help your body focus on the process of eating and help cue fullness. Also, if you're someone who eats when bored or stress eats, find a way to shift your mindset in those situations, or choose a higher volume, lower calorie snack. And if you have to, have you a piece of dark chocolate at night to help the sweet tooth. There's nothing wrong with that if it helps you not binge out on sweets. 
 Exercise: 
 Continue to do cardio and resistance training. As mentioned before, a higher level of muscle mass will also help your body continuously burn more calories. This can help mitigate a decrease in metabolism that may contribute to weight gain. Continue to do cardio and really try to walk 10-minutes after every meal. This helps with insulin sensitivity, digestion, and allows you to easily add in some extra calorie expenditure to your day. 
 If you look in the training and exercise course, there's also a section that discusses NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). This is another CRITICAL piece of increasing caloric expenditure throughout the day. This is ways that you burn calories through various movement throughout the day. title: Overview
text: Glutathione is a tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. It is commonly referred to as the master antioxidant of the body, and is produced within every cell of the body, especially the liver.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
So what does glutathione do in the body? 
 Glutathione basically helps to main a reducing environment within the cells, which means that it keeps the balance within them away from oxidation and more towards protection and repair. 
 Antioxidant Buffer - Glutathione is really the main redox regulator within the cells of the body . When it's in the reduced form, it's able to donate electrons to unstable molecules like reactive oxygen species (ROS) which allows those molecules to be neutralized before they are really able to damage the DNA or mitochondria. Then, once GSH (the reduced for of Glutathione) donates that electron, it turns into oxidized glutathione which your body will then try to recycle that back into it's reduced form to restart that entire process. By going back and forth between those two versions, your cells are protected vs being inflamed or oxidized. 
 Detoxification - Glutathione also plays a large role in Phase 2 liver detoxification, which is basically where your liver is neutralizing and getting the toxins and everything together so your body can excrete them safely. To do this, your liver is going to use enzymes called glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) to bind Glutathione directly to the toxic molecules . At that point, they become water soluble, so your body is able to excrete them through the bile or urine. If you start to become deficient in glutathione stores, your detoxification processes are gong to slow down and the toxic intermediaries start to build up in your system, creating more oxidative stress and negative effects associated with that. 
 Immune Modulation - Glutathione helps to balance your immune system's activity. When Glutathione levels are high, it can help with Th1 immune responses which can help the body fight off viruses, bacteria, and cancer cells. If levels drop, the balance is going more towards a Th2 state, which can cause allergic or autoimmune issues. Glutathione also helps T cells and natural killer (NK) cells (see TA-1 Deep Dive for more info on these) and allow them to release cytokines like interferon-gamma more effectively, which is an antiviral and antitumor defense signal for the body.

title: Benefits of Glutathione
text:
Liver Health and Detox - As mentioned previously, the liver has the highest concentration of glutathione within the body. It's basically your body's filtering mechanism that helps your body process the toxic byproducts. This is really the biggest and most noticeable benefit of glutathione. One interesting thing to note is that N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which is a precursor to glutathione, is used medically as a treatment for Tylenol overdose. It helps to break down many things like estrogen metabolites, alcohol derivatives, and heavy metals. Even outside of significant toxin exposure, people with lower GSH levels can be more prone to fatty liver and oxidative issues. In a trial of patients with NAFLD, they supplemented with 300mg/day of oral glutathione for 4 months and saw an improvement of about 37% in liver fat and also saw improved ALT and AST compared to the placebo group . 
 Immune Function and Inflammation - Glutathione will help to regulate the immunes system's function and by managing the redox environment within the immune cells, it will determine which pathways are getting activated. When the body is keeping GSH higher, the T helper 1 (Th1) activity is going to be higher which is what allows the immune system to target viruses and abnormal cells. When the Th2 is higher due to depleted GSH, allergic and autoimmune issues can occur. Ultimately, the person's immune system and function will be increased through Glutathione usage / supplementation. They actually see low glutathione in monocytes and T cells of HIV-infected patients with aligns with suppressed immune function. It will also likely lower some of the inflammation that can occur and allows the body to have a necessary immune response, but prevent the chronic, low grade inflammation that can cause a variety of other issues in the body. 
 Mitochondrial Function - In some of the other courses we talk about the function of the mitochondria to generate ATP, but that comes along with leakage of reactive oxygen species in the process. Without some type of antioxidant defense mechanisms, the ROS can start to damage mitochondrial membranes and DNA and result in other potential issues. The defense system that is in place is mitochondrial glutathione, or mGSH, which can help to neutralize the ROS within the mitochondria right as it can become an issue. By maintaining those levels, it can preserve mitochondrial integrity and allow the body to continue to produce more energy day to day. One interesting study on this and glutathione restoration is with GlyNAC which is a Glycine and NAC combination which are precursors. What they saw was a 200% rise in intracellular GSH, 20-25% improvement in insulin sensitivity, and reduced oxidative stress markers. 
 Skin Health - Glutathione can help with the skin, especially with lightening or brightness. What Glutathione does is interferes with the tyrosine to dopaquinone conversion which helps with pigment synthesis by inhibiting tyrosinase and moving the m

title: Dosage and Protocols
text:
Glutathione can be taken a few different ways. I'm going to touch on all of these (to include precursors) just to cover all of the bases here. 
 Precursors: 
 N-acetylcysteine (NAC): Typical dosages of NAC are 600-1,200 mg/day and in certain cases can go up to 1,800 mg/day . 
 GlyNAC: The studied amounts are quite high. You don't find the supplements in as high of a dosage. I think it's reasonable to start around 600mg of each and increase as needed. The studied dosage was up to 7-10g daily though, which is 10x what the starting amount listed is. 
 Direct Supplementation: 
 Oral Reduced GSH: 250-1000mg/day. Used for at least 8-12 weeks consistently. 
 Liposomal GSH: 250-500mg/day. 
 Injectable: 200-1200 mg/week, divided into multiple dosages typically. I like sitting in the 600-800 mg/week range. 
 Intravenous: You'll really only get this in a medspa. They might run anywhere between 600-1200 mg per infusion.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Glutathione is pretty well tolerated (across all forms). There are some things that can occur. 
 Injection Site Reactions - Glutathione injections can be a bit spicy. It may be sore afterwards for a couple of days. Over time, may become more well tolerated. 
 Fatigue - As the body starts through detoxification, you may notice headaches, fatigue, or other similar symptoms. These are typically transient and go away over time.

text: Here is my method- 275F until color is good and bark is set. This could be an hour or two. Depending on humidity. Wrap them in double foil, meat side up, with whatever mix you want to use. title: The Great Hambino’s Pulled Pork
text:
Preheat smoker to 225
 Season with your favorite seasoning. I prefer Kinders seasonings but anything works! Pork pairs well with BBQ, sweet, or savory flavors.
 I prefer smoking with Apple pellets but any pellet will do, its just personal preference
 Place the shoulder on the smoker at 225 til it hits 160-170 internal. 
 ***Not necessary but you can spritz every hour with apple juice. It keeps the top layer moist and will help build the bark and give it good flavor. You can also add a light coat of seasoning when you do this.***
 Once it hits 165, take it off and wrap it in butcher paper. If you don’t have butcher paper, tinfoil is fine but it will just soften the bark. I do 2 layers and I wrap it tight.
 After you wrap it, put it back on the smoker at 225 til it hits 202 internal 
 Once it hits 202 take it off and let it rest for at least 30 minutes to an hour then unwrap it and shred away! 
 ***If it finishes earlier than you were expecting DON’T WORRY! You can pull it off the smoker, keeping it wrapped in the butcher paper, wrap it in a large towel and place it in a cooler. It will stay hot for a couple hours! The longer it sits the better it gets!
 Expect cook times to be long – an average of 1.5 hours per pound.

title: Hair Biology and Growth Cycle Basics
text:
Hair Structure : Your hair grows from follicles in the skin and each follicle is producing the hair shaft which is made of the protein keratin. At the base of the follicle is the bulb and dermal papilla which supply nutrients and signals for growth. On average, we have about 100,000 hair follicles on the scalp, and hair will grow about 0.5 inches (1.25cm) per month. 
 Growth Cycle : It is important to note that hair growth isn't continuous. Each follicle cycles through different phases. Anagen is the active growth phase, which for scalp hair will last for about 2-8 years (this is why the head on your hair can grow so long). Around 95-90% of the hairs on a normal scalp are in anagen at any time. The next phase is Catagen and is a short 2-3 week transition where growth stops and the follicle shrinks. Then hair goes through Telogen, which is a period of about 2-4 months where the hair is resting. The last phase, Exogen, is the shedding phase when the resting hair falls out to make room for new growth. When the body is in healthy conditions, the cycle keeps a balance where you shed some hair each day but new hairs are also growing in. It's normal to shed somewhere between 50-100 hairs per day from this cycle. So when you're seeing hairs in the shower, on your pillow, in your brush, etc, they were probably already at the end of their life cycle and ready to fall, you just assisted this process. 
 At any given moment you have new hairs coming in, long hairs growing, and old hairs that are resting. That's why losing some hair every day doesn't ultimately result in thinning by itself. The problem really comes when the cycle is disrupted and too many hairs are shedding at once or the growth phase is shortened.

title: Causes of Hair Loss
text:
Hair loss (known as alopecia) has many possible causes and typically, multiple factors are going to play a role. The main categories are: 
 Genetics / Hormonal Causes (Androgenic Alopecia): This is the most common cause of hair loss in both men and women. In men, it's usually called male pattern baldness (MPB) and is linked to hair follicle sensitivity to the androgen hormone DHT (dihydrotestosterone). The follicles that are genetically prone to balding shrink under the influence of DHT which produces thinner hairs and eventually none. This typically results in a receding hairline and thinning at the crown for men. Generally, about 50% of men by age 50 have some level of male pattern hair loss. Women can also have female pattern hair loss which is usually thinning on the crown/top instead of a receding hair line. About 40% of women by age 50 will have noticeable pattern hair loss. Also, genetics from either side can contribute to this (it's not just your grandpa on your mom's side). Hormonal shifts modulate this and many women will see an increase in thinning after menopause since estrogen, which was protecting your hair, decreases. Things like PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) can raise androgen levels and can cause pattern hair thinning in younger women. Ultimately, DHT + genetic susceptibility = follicle miniaturization which is the main culprit in pattern baldness. 
 Inflammatory / Autoimmune Causes: Sometimes hair loss occurs outside of genetic reasons. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks your hair follicles which can cause to sudden hair loss. It can happen at any age and both men and women and typically causes you to have bare patches around the size of a coin and can sometimes turn into full hair loss, even on the body. The immune attack forces hair to go into the telogen (shedding) phase prematurely. You also can have scalp inflammation as a contributor to hair loss like severe seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis. You can also have scarring alopecia where inflammation can permanently destroy the hair follicles, but is pretty rare. For someone with redness, scaling, or pain in the areas where there is hair loss, then they may potentially be experiencing inflammation driven hair loss. Basically, if the immune system or inflammation targets hair follicles, the hair can fall out. 
 Nutritional Causes: Deficiencies in certain vitamins and minerals can cause hair to shed or grow poorly. Iron deficiency (especially in women) is a well-known trigger for hair thinning. Vitamin D deficiencies, insufficient protein intake, over restricted calorie intake can all result in hair loss because hair growth is one of the first things the body will shut down if is malnourished. The good thing about this cause of hair loss is that it's usually reversible. Once you fix the deficiency or diet, the hair cycles will normalize themselves over the next few months. title: Hair Loss Diagnostics
text:
How do you determine what type of hair loss you have? This is critically important and is half the battle in treating it since they can differ. Here's how this can be approached: 
 Assess the Pattern and History : The first thing that should be done is to look at where and how you're losing hair. Pattern hair loss (androgenetic) in men usually presents with a receding hairline and/or thinning at the grown. In women it's more of a general thinning on the top with an intact hairline. If you start to notice a patterned distribution that matches male or female pattern baldness, then it very strongly indicates potential androgenic alopecia. Doctors will typically use the Hamilton-Norwood Scale for men or the Ludwig scale for women to classify the severity of hair loss. Patchy hair loss (like coin-sized patches) can suggest alopecia areata. Diffuse shedding all over suggests telogen effluvium (stress or systemic causes). Another thing to consider is the timing of the loss. Did it come on rapidly over a few weeks (potentially telogen effluvium of alopecia areata), or slowly over years (pattern baldness). Family history can also help to indicate which type as a family pattern of early baldness supports the likelihood of genetic alopecia. Essentially, the pattern + the pace of loss + personal history (like stress events, health, etc) will form a story that can lead to diagnosis. 
 Examining the Scalp and Hair: A dermatologist will typically do a close examination on your scalp with something like a dermatoscope or densitometer to look for miniaturized hairs since in pattern hair loss, some follicles shrink and produce fine, wispy hairs before they actually disappear. Seeing variation in hair thickness is a hallmark of androgenetic alopecia. In alopecia areata, you might see short, broken hairs at the patch edges. If there is redness, scaling, or scabs then it could be indicative of an inflammatory or fungal cause. Doctors also might perform a "hair pull test" by gently pulling some bunches of hairs to see how many come out. If someone is shedding more than 5-6 hairs per pull (from multiple spots) then it could suggest active telogen effluvium (excess shedding). They will also check for signs of scarring to see if it's cicatrical alopecia. 
 Medical Analysis: Depending on what the suspected cause is, a doctor might have certain tests be done. For something like diffuse hair loss in women, doctors might look at thyroid function, iron levels (ferritin), vitamin D, and hormone levels to rule out deficiencies or thyroid disease since treating those aspects can reverse the hair loss. If the doctor thinks something like an autoimmune disease like lupus is the cause, then they might run labs specific to that. If they aren't completely sure, then a scalp biopsy, where they take a small piece of scalp skin and examine it under a microscope, is the gold standard in determining the cause. title: Treatments for Hair Loss
text:
There are numerous potential treatments and interventions when it comes to addressing hair loss. We'll look at FDA-approved treatments first, experimental or supplemental therapies second, and also have some regimens in the next section. 
 FDA-Approved and Mainstream Treatments
 Right now, there are only two medications officially FDA-approved for treating androgenic alopecia (pattern hair loss) which are Minoxidil and Finasteride. 
 Minoxidil: Minoxidil is most commonly used as a topical treatment that you can apply to the scalp. Interestingly, it was first used as an oral blood pressure treatment but people noticed that their hair was growing, so now it's used for that. Minoxidil is a vasodilator , meaning that it widens blood vessels. When applied to the scalp, it's supposed to help increase blood flow to hair follicles and extend the anagen (growth) phase of the hair cycle. It may also directly stimulate the follicle cells and promote thicker hairs. It is pretty effective and slows hair loss for many people who use it and can stimulate new hair growth in some. The clinical trials showed vertex (crown) hair count increases and improvement in density in many users after 4-6 months. It typically works better on smaller, recently thinned follicles than on completely bald areas. Not everyone responds well, but 60+% will see some stabilization or hair regrowth. For men, a 5% solution or foam is typically applied once or twice a day and for women, the 2% twice daily was originally approved, but most women now also use the 5% concentration. Minoxidil has to be used consistently. Think about it like fertilizer for your hair. If you stop, the plant can still wilt away. The same thing happens with minoxidil where the benefits you gained from it might go away. Minoxidil is generally safe and the main side effect is scalp irritation. One important thing to note is that you will shed at the start, typically in the first couple of months, as the old airs are pushed out to make way for new growth. This is the worst / scariest part but is usually a sign that the treatment is working. The studies show that minoxidil can give better results when combined with other therapies. 
 Finasteride : Finasteride is an oral prescription medication that is a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor. Basically, it blocks the enzyme that converts testosterone to DHT. By cutting DHT levels (about 60-70% reduction in scalp and blood DHT with the standard 1mg/day dosage), it can remove the hormone that is shrinking the follicles in androgenic alopecia. It has been shown in multiple trials to stop the progression of hair loss in the majority of men, and to even give some regrowth to some. In a 5-year study, about 90% of men on finasteride had no further hair loss and about 65% had moderate regrowth. This is typically dosed at 1mg daily (FDA-approved dose, also achieves near-maximum DHT suppression) and typically takes 6-12 months to see results. Like minoxidil, if you stop using finasteride

title: Sample Protocols
text:
Here are some ideas of what a protocol might look like, but these can absolutely be changed based on an individuals needs. 
 Beginner Protocol (Early or Prevention Focus, Low Risk):
 GHK/AHK-Cu: This can be used topically and/or subcutaneously. Subcutaneous administration (GHK-Cu) is typically 1-2.5mg daily. The GHK-Cu or AHK-Cu serum can be applied topically once per day.
