 General Health: Ensure you're getting in enough protein, iron, vitamins, etc. Consider a hair supplement or multivitamin to meet any nutritional gaps. 
 Monitoring: Start taking photos of your hair every 3 months in the same lighting / setup so you can track changes. 
 Who is this for? Someone who just started noticing a little shedding or thinning or has a family history and doesn't want to move into medications. 
 Intermediate Protocol (Moderate Loss or More Aggressive Early Treatment):
 Everything in the Beginner Protocol, plus: 
 Finasteride: For adult males with pattern hair loss, oral Finasteride at 1mg daily. For post-menopausal women, it would be worth discussing with a doctor for off-label use. 
 Minoxidil: Apply once per day to the scalp with a 5% minoxidil solution. Apply this at a separate time of the day from when you apply the GHK-Cu topical. 
 Microneedling: At this point, you could introduce something like microneedling with a dermaroller or dermastamp (around 1.5mm depth) on thinning areas once a week. The tiny needles can create micro-injuries that release growth factors and promote hair stem cell activation. 
 Who is this for? Someone who has noticeable thinning/balding starting and is trying to halt and try to reverse it. 
 Advanced Protocol (Aggressive or Stubborn Hair Loss, Max Regrowth)
 All of the above, plus: 
 Topical Anti-androgens: Adding in something like RU-58841 can add some localized action on top of these other compounds. Applying a 5% solution once per day (just separate from the other topical compounds) is generally what most users do. 
 Low-Level Laser Therapy (LLLT): Adding in a red light therapy cap or comb 3x per week can increase hair density and growth. This will typically be done in 15-30 minute sessions. 
 Who is this for? People with significant hair loss who want to use every method that is scientifically supported to maintain and regrow hair. Understand that the more aggressive the protocol, the more potential for side effects. 
 As stated in the beginning, these are examples of what can be done. You may want to avoid finasteride and instead use RU-58841 or PP-405. The ultimate goal is to combine therapies that will compliment each other: an anti-androgen + a growth stimulator + something for scalp health. 
 Just remember that any hair regimen requires patience. Hair cycles are slow and you should expect 3 months before seeing less shedding, 6+ months before seeing visible growth, and up to 12-18 months for the most improv

title: Scalp Optimzation
text:
Think about your scalp like soil where your hair grows. Optimizing the environment of your scalp can improve results from other treatments or even help on its own. 
 Microneedling: This is a very popular tool in the hair loss toolkit. Basically, you're using a device with a bunch of tiny needles to create micro-punctures in the scalp. I know it sounds counterintuitive, but doing this causes your body to generate a healing response that releases growth factors which can turn the dormant hair follicles into growth mode. It can also help with the absorption of topical products, so applying something like minoxidil after needling it can penetrate deeper. People will gently roll or stamp (to the point of slight redness) and then apply minoxidil about 24 hours later. This only needs to be done about once per week. It is also important to make sure your tool is sterilized and your scalp is clean so you don't get an infection. 
 Red Light Therapy (Low-Level Laser Therapy - LLLT) : Red or near-infrared light at specific wavelengths can stimulate hair follicles. Things like laser combs, LED helmets/caps are designed to emit light onto the scalp that penetrates a few millimeters into the skin and is absorbed in cellular mitochondria. This can boost ATP production in the cells and release nitric oxide which leads to improved cell function and vasodilation (blood vessel widening). In hair, this can help to prolong the anagen phase and wake up some telogen follicles to re-enter growth. Multiple studies and a meta-analysis found that these devices increased hair counts significantly vs. placebo in both men and women without serious side effects. This is also incredibly easy to integrate into your schedule as you can put it on your head virtually any time of the day. 
 Reduce Traction and Damage: Even outside of traction alopecia, the things you do day-to-day can help your hair. Don't wear extremely tight ponytails or buns frequently. If you start to notice thinning around where you part your hair, try alternating the part line to reduce the stress in one specific area. Doing things like this aren't going to prevent hair loss, but can help control the things that you can control that may cause more issues.

title: Overview
text:
Energy is the thing people ask me about more than almost anything else. 
 The problem is that "I'm tired" isn't one thing. It has about twenty different causes, and the right fix depends entirely on which one is actually yours. That's why most people never fix it. They grab another coffee or an energy drink and treat the symptom without ever finding out what's driving it.
 This course is going to fix that.
 We're going to start with what energy actually is, all the way down to the molecule your body runs on (ATP). Then the nine systems that produce and regulate it, because when you're tired, one or more of those systems is the reason. Then everything that drains you, which is the diagnostic part of this. Then we're going to go through everything that actually fixes it.
 One idea runs through this whole course:
 There's a difference between BORROWING energy and BUILDING it. 
 Caffeine and stimulants borrow. They take energy from later today and hand it to you now, and you pay it back with interest. Fixing your sleep, your mitochondria, your hormones, or a deficiency builds energy that you actually own.
 Both have a place. But confusing the two is exactly why so many people are wired and exhausted at the same time.
 How this course is laid out Part 1 - What energy is: the biology, ATP, and how food and oxygen become power.
 Part 2 - The systems: mitochondria, thyroid, adrenals, blood sugar, oxygen delivery, breathing, the gut, circadian rhythm, and the nervous system.
 Part 3 - What drains you: the deficiencies, the medical causes, and the everyday stuff that's quietly wrecking you.
 Part 4 - The fix catalog: sleep, food, movement, light, breathing, caffeine, supplements, hormones, peptides, and the mental side of energy.
 Part 5 - Putting it together: figuring out which one is YOUR problem and building a plan around it.
 The evidence tiers Everything in here has an evidence tier that correlates to the data we have to support it. 
 Tier 1 - Proven. The basics that unquestionably drive energy.
 Tier 2 - Strong. Good evidence for real benefit. Worth doing for most people.
 Tier 3 - Promising. Real mechanism and encouraging data, but not fully proven.
 Tier 4 - Experimental or situational. Thin data or niche use.
 Put your effort into the low numbers first. 
 Before we start This course is educational. It's not medical advice. Being tired all the time can be the first sign of something real, like anemia, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, or diabetes. Those need to be monitored and evaluated appropriately. 
 If your fatigue is significant, new, or getting worse, skip ahead to Part 3 first. I list the labs to ask for and the red flags that mean go see somebody now.
 The most important thing I can tell you is this: chronic tiredness almost always has a cause you can find and fix. Don't just caffeinate over it.

text:
Fertility is complex and has an underlying emotional component associated with it, as well as a lot of confusion. Couples trying to conceive get buried in advice, supplements, and expensive interventions, usually without a lot of understanding of what's actually happening in their bodies or what can truly make an impact. This course is meant to fix that and be a full map of the fertility for both men and women.
 The approach is the same one that runs through the rest of the courses within the classroom, which is understanding the biology first and the interventions will start to make sense on their own. 
 Fertility is a two-person equation and male factors contribute to roughly half of all infertility cases. Fertility still gets treated culturally as a woman's issue and men typically get skipped in the analysis of what might be wrong. That's why this course gives both sides a full discussion, a full men's section, and a full women's section, because optimizing fertility means optimizing both partners. The biology, the causes, and the treatments can be different for each. 
 How this course is structured Part 1 - The biology. How conception actually works, and the foundations both partners share.
 Part 2 - Men's fertility. Sperm biology, causes, hCG/hMG/FSH and the medical therapies.
 Part 3 - Women's fertility. The cycle and egg biology, causes, the workup, and the medical treatments including IVF.
 Part 4 - The cross-cutting toolkit. Diet and lifestyle, supplements, and the peptides and bioregulators.
 Part 5 - Putting it together. A couple's game plan and when to get help.
 Fertility optimization is mostly about creating the healthiest possible environment for eggs and sperm. Both take about three months to develop, so the work you do now shows up in roughly three months, not overnight. Understanding that can help you get into the right mindset when you know that this process will take time.
 Read this part before anything else This course is educational. It's a map, not a treatment plan and not medical advice. Infertility needs proper evaluation of both partners, because it can have a lot of different causes. Some are easily fixed, some are serious, and some are time-sensitive. The right treatment depends entirely on what's actually going on, and you can't know that without getting evaluated.

title: The Basics
course: How Much is Needed for a Cycle
text:
Before you try to figure out how much to buy, you have to understand the dosing schedule and frequency. Some peptides are taken daily, some might be 5 days a week, and some are taken once a week. This is important to understand, because it changes how much you will use each week as well as over the course of the cycle. 
 Here's the information you need to figure out: 
 How much do you need for each dose? 
 How many times per week are you taking that dose? 
 How many weeks are you running the cycle? 
 Will you increase the dosage over the course of the cycle? 
 How many vials will that add up to based on the total amount of mg in the vial? 
 Peptides are typically labeled by milligrams (mg) vs mL, which can throw some people off. You are getting a certain number of mg (typically in a 3mL vial) and then you are adding the liquid. What is really important is how much of the compound is actually in the vial. 
 Let's say that you're dosing BPC-157 at 250mcg daily. A 5mg vial would be 5000mcg. If you take it daily, then that vial will last you 20 days. If you are doing it 5 days per week, that will last you 4 weeks. This is the type of logic that you have to apply to this and I will try to teach you in this course.

title: Daily Dosing Example
course: How Much is Needed for a Cycle
text:
This section is going to break down BPC-157 used daily as an example for how to calculate based off of the length of time you want to use it. 
 Assumptions: 
 250mcg per day dosage
 Taken daily (7 days per week)
 6 week length of cycle
 Step 1: Figure out weekly dose
 250mcg per day x 7 days = 1,750mcg per week
 Step 2: Multiply by the number of weeks
 1,750mcg/week x 6 weeks = 10,500mcg total
 10,500mcg is equal to 10.5mg
 Step 3: Determine the vial size you're going to get
 Let's assume BPC-157 vials are 5mg each
 You'll need at least 3 vials of 5mg to cover that 10.5mg, or adjust your cycle length a couple of days short to give an even 10mg amount. 
 If you got 3x 5mg vials, you would have 15 total mg, which is enough to cover the 10.5 mg. Or you could extend the cycle to be longer to use the entire 15mg.

title: x Weekly Dosing Example
course: How Much is Needed for a Cycle
text:
This next example will cover a peptide that is being used 5 days per week, like CJC-1295/Ipamorelin since those are typically 5 days a week as opposed to 7. 
 Assumptions: 
 300mcg per dose (of each)
 Dosed 5 days per week
 Cycle length is 8 weeks
 Step 1: Determine weekly dose
 300mcg x 5 days = 1,500mcg per week
 Step 2: Determine total cycle dose
 1,500mcg x 8 weeks = 12,000mcg total
 12,000mcg is 12mg for the entire 8 week cycle
 Step 3: How many vials are needed? 
 If the vials are 5mg each, you will need 3 vials to cover the 12mg which would give you 15mg total. You could extend the length of the cycle to use the entirety of this, or you will have some left over unused.

title: Once Per Week Dosing Example

 Assumptions: 
 Tirzepatide dosed at 7.5mg per week
 Dosed 1x weekly
 Need enough for 2 months
 Step 1: Determine total amount needed: 
 7.5mg x 8 weeks is 60mg total. Therefore, you will need 60mg total to last you for 2 months. 
 Step 2: Determine how many vials are needed: 
 For the purposes of calculating, we'll use a 20mg vial of Tirzepatide. 
 You will need at least 3x 20mg vials to cover those 2 months. Or, you could get 1x 60mg vial.

title: Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

 Daily (7x weekly)

title: Overview / Introduction
text:
I wanted to develop this course as a way for people to understand systems of the body so they can better understand how things may be utilized to assist as well understanding how things play into each other and drive different things within the body. 
 The immune system is basically your body's defense network against things that can come in and create harm. It's composed of various organs, white blood cells, and chemical signals that all work together to protect our body against things that may cause harm. Some of those things that can cause harm are things like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, as well as abnormal cells within the body like cancer cells. Basically what the immune system's job is to recognize what ISN'T supposed to be in the body and eliminate it while keeping the healthy cells of the body around. 
 The immune system can prevent bad things from coming in to your system, get rid of those that do make it in, and minimize the damage that can be caused by various infections. One thing about the immune system that is incredibly interesting and unique is the ability for it to learn and adapt and essentially "remember" things so it can respond more effectively in the future. 
 There are two components to consider when thinking about the immune system which is the innate immune system and the adaptive immune system. The innate immune system is really the first line of defense for the body and will give non-specific protection against a variety of things. This piece of the immune system includes things like skin and mucous membranes, enzymes and acids, and various types of cells. The adaptive immune system is basically like it sounds where it develops immunological memory and helps the body to respond better and faster to future issues with the same pathogens.

title: Immune Organs and Tissues
text:
Various organs within the body play a role in the immune system's function. The primary lymphoid organs are where immune cells (lymphocytes) are produced and include the bone marrow and the thymus. The bone marrow is a spongy tissue that is found inside the bones and is where most immune system cells are made and multiply. The thymus is a small organ in the upper chest where T cells mature and essentially learn to distinguish the body's proteins from foreign ones. Interesting fact - the thymus will gradually shrink as we go into adulthood and turn to fatty tissue. 
 Secondary lymphoid organs are tissues where immune cells are going to do the job of fighting off the bad things that are coming into the body. These organs are the lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, and some mucous membrane layers in the body like in the bowel. The lymph nodes are little bean-shaped groups of tissue that are along the lymphatic vessels and essentially act like filters in the body. Different cells are going to trap germs within the lymph nodes and help produce special antibodies within the blood. So when you're going to the doctor and they check something like your lymph nodes for swelling or pain, they're checking to see that the immune system is active fighting something off essentially. The spleen is going to be within the abdomen and does thing like storing immune system cells to respond via the bloodstream when needed as well as filter germs within the bloodstream, bread down red blood cells, and store and break down platelets. Tonsils are located in the mouth and can help prevent germs coming into the body through the mouth or nose. They have many white blood cells within them to help kill off germs. It's very common for tonsils to be removed so, if that were to happen, the lymphoid tissue on the side of your throat will take over those duties of the palatine tonsils. The last secondary lymphoid organ is going to be the mucous membranes. These are within the intestines, respiratory and urinary tracts, and the lining of the vagina. The gut is probably going to be one of the biggest components of this as more than half of the antibody producing cells are found within the intestine. You also have gut flora which is very important to prevent issues. This is part of why the gut is such an important thing to keep healthy within the body. Immune system cells are going to be located beneath the mucous membranes and help to prevent bacteria and virus growth in those areas.

title: Immune Cells
text:
Just like there are multiple organs and tissues that make up the immune system, there are also multiple different types of cells that make up the immune system. The ones that run around and fight the battles and seek out the enemy so to speak are the white blood cells (WBCs) or leukocytes. These are going to originate in the bone marrow and move throughout the body ready to fight against whatever they need to. There are a lot of different types and each of them serve their own purpose where they can recognize issues, communicate with others, and accomplish the mission. There are a few different types of immune cells that respond differently to those bad things that make their way into the body: 
 Phagocytes - These cells are going to essentially eat and digest the pathogens or debris that get into the body. You could picture them as sucker fish that move around the fish tank eating all of the bad things that get in. The phagocytes include neutrophils, macrophages, and dendritic cells. The neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs within the blood and are very fast to respond to infection or injury sites and eat the bacteria and other bad things that try to make their way in. Macrophages are going to be in tissues throughout the body and come from monocytes that enter the tissues and mature. They also are going to eat pathogens and get rid of bad cells, but also release signaling molecules to bring in other immune cells to the defense lines. Dendritic cells are phagocytes that are going to break down the pathogens that they ingest and then take parts of it (antigens) to the lymph notes. Once they get those antigens to the lymph nodes, they'll show the other immune cells (T cells) what the bad things look like and allow the adaptive immune system to understand what kind of threat they're dealing with. So these are going to be very important in their role as a messenger between the innate and adaptive immune responses within the body. 
 Lymphocytes - These cells are going to be central to the adaptive immune system and basically work as commanders coordinating targeted attacks against different pathogens. There are two primary versions of lymphocytes which are B cells and T cells. The B cells are going to mature within the bone marrow (which is why they're called "B" cells) and they are primarily going to produce antibodies. When a B cells recognizes antigens, it can differentiate into a plasma cell that is going to let off a lot of antibodies to either neutralize or mark the pathogens to be destroyed. The T cells are going to mature in the thymus ("T" cells) and come in various forms. There are helper T cells which are going to act like managers within the body and can be activated by an antigen-presenting cells (like dendritic cells) and release cytokines and direct other cells on what to do (like telling B cells to produce antibodies, recruiting phagocytes, etc). Cytotoxic T cells are going to be the killers. They are going to find virus-infected ce

title: Immune Molecules
text:
Immune cells also rely on various immune molecules to help identify their targets, talk to each other, and get rid of the bad. There are various types that include:
 Antibodies - Antibodies (which are also known as immunoglobulins) are Y-shaped proteins that are produced by B cells. They are going to seek out antigens within the body. When B cells turn into plasma cells, they begin to secrete antibodies into the bloodstream and lymphs. An antibody will tightly bind to specific antigens and can directly neutralize a threat or they can mark it for destruction by other immune components. You have different classes of antibodies and each have slightly different roles and locations within the body, but all of them are going to assist with recognizing and helping to eliminate foreign substances within the body. They're going to be very specific in what they do where each antibody is going to fit into one antigen. They'll bind to the antigens and then mark pathogens so phagocytes can more easily ingest them. 
 Cytokines - Cytokines are essentially communication signals for the immune system. They are small proteins that immune cells release to influence the behavior of other cells. When your body initiates an immune response, cells start to secrete cytokines to say who should do what and where. Different cytokines are going to have different messages that they send. Cytokines like interleukins are going to mediate communications between white blood cells (leukocytes) to promote activation or growth, interferons help defend against viral infections, chemokines create chemical gradients to attract cells to an infection site. Cytokines ultimately instruct the immune cells to increase or decrease a response, move to a certain spot, produce certain enzymes, and more. 
 Complement system - The complement system is a group of proteins in the blood and tissue fluids that work together to fight against invasions and facilitate inflammation when they are activated. They get triggered in a cascade, where each one activates the next when there are pathogens or antibodies bound to pathogens. Once they're activated, they can punch holes in the membranes of bacteria, coat microbes to make them easier to be eat3n by phagocytes, and release different factors that attract immune cells to the area. These are a bridge between the innate and adaptive immune systems and can be activated by pathogen surfaces directly or antibodies that attach to a pathogen. Regardless of how they are activated, they complement the action of the antibodies and cells resulting in a set of membrane attack complexes and tag microbes for cleanup. It also helps to trigger inflammation by causing mast cells to release histamine and recruiting phagocytes. These basically amplify the immune response to help clear infections.

title: Innate Immunity
text:
The innate immune system is basically the rapid response immune system that exists within the body. It's considered "innate" because it's something you are born with and do not require prior exposure to pathogens in order to be effective. Innate immunity includes the physical barriers that were mentioned previously, as well as various cells and molecules that can respond quickly to common features that invaders have. Innate responses are not specific and don't target a certain pathogen by its identity, but instead are going to attack any invader that gets through the walls. Even though it isn't specific, it's important to help control the early stages of an infection and activate the adaptive immune system when it's needed. As an example, this is how your innate immune response is going to look:
 The barrier is breached . Let's say you get a cut that gets past your "first line of defense" which is the skin. Once that happens, it allows for bacteria to enter. As soon as that happens, mast cells in the area are going to sense tissue damage and potentially that there are bacteria within the area. Once they happens, they will respond by releasing histamine and other inflammatory responses. Other cells that are close by are going to help to release different signals as well to "sound the alarm" that something is happening. 
 Inflammation response occurs . Once histamine is released, the blood vessels within that area start to dilate (get bigger) and start to leak. This is what causes those common signs of inflammation like redness (more blood flow to the area), warmth, swelling (fluids and proteins start to leak into the tissue), and pain (pressure exists on nerves and chemical signals). Even though this type of response is generally uncomfortable, it's helpful as it is going to bring in more immune cells and nutrients and allow for immune proteins and cells to move into the tissue.

The neutrophils and monocytes that are nearby in blood vessels are going to sense these signals and stick to the vessel walls, move out of the vessel and into the infected tissue (called recruitment or extravasation). 
 Attack the bacterial invasion . Neutrophils and macrophages will start to phagocytose the bacteria (engulf it) and ingest them. This is going to destroy the pathogens as well as clean up the debris. While they're fighting, the phagocytes can release more cytokines to amplify the response and bring in more backup. title: Adaptive Immunity
text:
The adaptive immune system is going to act as the next line of defense and takes a little longer to start working, but also works very specifically and has a memory. Innate immunity is going to broadly attack where adaptive immunity is going to tailor that attack to the specific invasion after learning its characteristics. Adaptive responses get executed by lymphocytes (mostly B and T cells) and the antibodies and other molecules that they produce. The system is known as the adaptive system because it adapts to the invaders and each time a new pathogen is encountered, they conduct a specialized response and remember the pathogen in the future in case they ever encounter it again. 
 The important pieces of the adaptive immune system are that they are antigen-specific, they are systemic and can mobilize all defenses, and it has memory. But with this, it is slower to start working and usually doesn't really kick in and become effective until a few days after the initial infection starts as it takes some time for the appropriate lymphocytes to be active and expand. This is how adaptive immunity works: 
 Antigen recognition - An antigen is a molecule or piece of a pathogen that the immune cells can recognize which is the cornerstone of the adaptive immune system as it has to be able to recognize these. Each B and T cell have receptors that can bind to specific antigen shapes. Before exposure, the body is going to hold a lot of B and T cells with random specificities that are generated in their development. Once an infection occurs, the antigen-presenting cells are going to take some pieces of the pathogen to the lymph nodes or spleen and present the antigen to T cells that haven't yet encountered their specific antigen. This will activate a matching T cell to respond. They can also be recognized by B cells and typically use the help of a T cell to do so. 
 Clonal expansion - Once a B or T cell is activated by a specific antigen, it going to undergo a process called clonal expansion where it proliferates and makes thousands of clones of itself that target the same antigen. Once they've cloned themselves, they differentiate into effector cells (ones that carry out an immune response) and memory cells that stay long-term. 
 Getting rid of the pathogen - Effector T cells are going to move from the lymph node to the infection site where helper T cells are going to secrete cytokines to boost local immune response. Cytotoxic T cells are going to look for cells that display the antigen they are looking for, bind to them, and kill those cells, typically through apoptosis.

title: Overview
text: KPV is a tripeptide composed of three amino acids (lysine, proline, valine) which is where it gets its name (lysine is denoted as K). It is primarily used for it's anti-inflammatory action that it gets from being a small sequence of a-MSH.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Anti-Inflammatory (NF-kB Inhibition) - KPV is an incredible anti-inflammatory compound that drives this by suppressing nuclear factor kB (NF-kB) pathway which is a regulator of inflammation. Basically, NF-kB is a protein complex that can move to cells and turn on the pro-inflammatory cytokines and enzymes. It has also been observed to reduce the inflammatory things like TNF-a as a response to the NF-kB inhibition. It will reduce the levels of these inflammatory cytokines in cells and tissues that are exposed to inflammation as well, driving down inflammation that is already present. 
 Cytokine Suppression and Immune Modulation - As mentioned, it helps to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines . They have observed decreases in TNF-a, IL1b, IL-6, and IL-8 levels, but interestingly things like IL-10 were even increased to some extent, showing that it has a specific effect on pro-inflammatory cytokine activity but does not have a suppressive effect on anti-inflammatory cytokine activity. 
 Antimicrobial Effects - One very interesting characteristic of KPV is its ability to act as an antimicrobial that can fight against both inflammation and infection. In some invitro studies, they observed KPV's ability to kill certain microbes and that levels of a-MSH peptides (KPV) were able to kill Staphylococcus aureus bacteria and Candida albicans yeast. In one assay, about 90% of the S. aureus cells were dead within 15 minutes of exposure. KPV by itself has an ability to act against Candida albicans, but a specific analog of KPV was able to inhibit C. albicans growth by about 90%. The beauty of KPV is that it is able to get rid of some of these pathogens with suppressing immunity and can be great to fight against things where both infection and inflammation exist (things like IBS and gut dysbiosis).

title: Benefits of KPV
text:
Gut Inflammation Issues (IBD, Colitis, Chron's) - KPV has been studied in preclinical trials where it had protective effects on the intestinal lining and oral administration of KPV in mouse models alleviated colon inflammation and promoted mucosal healing quite significantly. In something like colitis, the colon can express something called PepT1 which is the peptide transporter that KPV uses to enter those cells. This link also shows how it may be able to be used for something like colorectal cancer. Alongside of this, KPV seems to also have an effect on restoring the gut barrier and was even tested with hyaluronic-acid coated nanoparticles to reduce inflammation by binding to CD44 receptors . 
 Skin Disorders (Psoriasis, Eczema, Acne) - KPV can be incredibly effective for skin issues such as psoriasis, eczema, acne, and rosacea where things like excessive inflammation and immune activity can contribute to redness, itching, and tissue damage. Since KPV has the ability to reduce cytokine release and inflammation, it works well through a variety of methods of administration to target these issues. They studies KPV's effect on skin cells that were exposed to urban fine dust which can cause oxidative stress and inflammation on the skin and observed that KPV treatment was able to protect against reactive oxygen species and blunt the downstream inflammatory effects that result from this exposure. There are some studies contributing further to how this may be used for various skin issues, but the results that people have for these in anecdotal experiences is incredible. 
 Wound Healing - KPV also shows some promise for wound healing and tissue repair. Especially with issues where there are chronic wounds like sores or ulcers, typically they come along with excess inflammation or infection which is exactly what KPV can target. They have actually done a study on rabbits where they had abraded corneas and were given KPV eye drops 4x daily and within 60 hours, they had completely re-epithelialized and none of the untreated ones had healed within that time. In a lot of cases for wound treatment, they may attempt to use it topically, but KPV also seems to exhibit similar benefits when used as an injection as well.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
The dosage for KPV is pretty straight forward and can really be varied as desired. However, I think there is a general effective range and going higher doesn't necessarily yield more results. 
 The most common dosages for KPV is going to be 250-500mcg daily whether it's via capsules or injectable. Some may choose to go up to 1-2mg per day and, in my opinion, that can be fine but may not always provide you with more relief or results. Because of this, I think 500mcg is generally the most effective amount to use for most applications. 
 The length of time that this can be ran can vary as well. I think that the best approach is 4-8 weeks on and then take a break to assess how the issues that you are targeting are doing. Do you feel joint pain relief? Has inflammation gone down? Have stomach issues resolved? During that break, look to see how long things can stay better. Maybe they stay better for long terms. Maybe only for a few days. But you can at least see how the body is without it before continuing.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text: Overall, the tolerability and side effect/safety profile for KPV is very favorable. There have really been no observed issues with KPV usage outside of the potential for maybe injection site reactions (rare with KPV, but can occur with any injection). The only consideration here is there is not a lot of strong human data, so if studied extensively, may show something otherwise. But based on its mechanism and what has been observed anecdotally, it seems to be pretty safe and well tolerated.

title: Overview
text:
Almost everybody who has lost a decent amount of weight describes the same experience where the first bit comes off pretty easily and predictably. Then it might slow down or fluctuate throughout the middle. Near the end the whole thing basically stops and that last 5, 10, or even 15 lbs. is completely different than everything that came before. Everything that has been working for you now doesn't and your scale is basically stalled for weeks. You start to get frustrated with actually being able to successfully get that weight off. 
 This course is meant to be a troubleshooting guide but with a very specific focus. You could look at it as a companion course to the Breaking a Stall course within the community not necessarily a replacement. If your weight has stalled and you want the full general-purpose step-by-step protocol through any plateau at any point in the journey then that course would be the primary resource. 
 What the goal of this course is adding is the specificity about the end of the journey. The last 10 lbs. are really a different physiological and psychological situation. Your body is going to defend its weight the hardest when you're already lean and your margin of error gets significantly smaller. There's honestly a question that may come up here, which is: is this last bit even worth chasing?

title: Is this even worth it?
text:
I think that this page is one of the most important sections and most people probably won't tell you that this is the reality. Sometimes the healthiest wisest thing to do when you're trying to answer the question of "How do I lose the last 10 lbs?" is you don't. You just shift to maintaining and you call that success. Knowing when to stop is important and it may be a healthier decision for you in the long run. 
 There is a meaningful difference between losing weight for health and chasing a number for aesthetics or because that was a number that you set in your head in the beginning. If you're already at a healthy body weight and body fat level, the last 10 lbs. might represent something arbitrary more so than an actual need to reach it. It may cost more in your well-being than the result is worth. 
 As covered throughout this course, the final little bits require progressively more precision, restriction, and management of hunger and stress for progressively smaller and slower results. This is exactly the part where disorder patterns start to take root, where you have this obsessive tracking and extreme restriction and over-exercising and anxiety around food. This is more of a negative relationship that can damage the quality of life that you're living.
 For many people grinding towards that last 10 lbs., it costs them sleep, social life, mental peace, and sometimes physical health in exchange for a marginal cosmetic change. That's honestly a bad trade and recognizing that isn't bad. 
 So how do you know what situation you're in here? 
 Are you already in a healthy weight and body fat range? If the answer is yes then that last 10 may not be something that you actually need to lose. 
 Is the pursuit of that last 10 lbs. costing you your sleep, mood, social life, or your relationship with your food? If yes that cost may actually exceed the benefit. 
 Are you showing any signs of disordered patterns like obsessive tracking or food anxiety or extreme restriction? If the answer is yes then stop and try to build a healthy relationship with food. 
 Would maintaining where I am and being strong and healthy actually be a good outcome? For a lot of people the answer to this is probably yes.

title: Overview
text:
Melanotan 1 and Melanotan 2 are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (a-MSH) which is a naturally occurring peptide that your body produces in the pituitary gland and can help regulate skin pigmentation, sexual function, appetite, and pain responses. They were originally developed at the University of Arizona in the 80s and 90s for photoprotection by creating something that could stimulate tanning without the need for UV exposure which would theoretically reduce skin cancer risk. 
 One thing that is important to understand is that there is a whole system of melanocortin receptors within the body that can be activated. They're found throughout the body and have pretty diverse functions like skin pigmentation, sexual arousal, appetite suppression, inflammation, and compulsive behavior.

title: The Melanocortin Receptors (Mechanism)
text:
Melanotan 1 and Melanotan 2 have some pretty distinct differences. Melanotan 1 is more selective than Melanotan 2 and primarily targets the MC1R (melanocortin 1 receptor) which is the receptor that is responsible for melanin production in your skin. MT-2 is less selective and hits all of the melanocortin receptors which is why you have the changes in libido and appetite changes, as well as worse side effects that come alongside of it. MT-1 also targets the MC1R receptor the same as afemelanotide (which is FDA approved for specific uses under the name Scenesse) and has the same chemical structure, but with different dosages and methods of administration (afemelanotide is an implant). Melanotan 2 is not approved in any capacity, but the sexual benefits of it were isolated and approved as the compound bremelanotide (PT-141) and is sold under the name Vyleesi. 
 Now there are technically 5 melanocortin receptors, but I'm going to give you an overview of 1-4. 
 MC1R - This is primarily located in skin melanocytes and immune cells and is responsible for melanin production (tanning) and some anti-inflammatory signaling. 
 MC2R - This is located in the adrenal glands and is responsible for cortisol production. 
 MC3R - This is located in the hypothalamus and the gut and is responsible for energy balance, appetite, and inflammation regulation. 
 MC4R - This is located in the hypothalamus and the brainstem and is responsible for appetite suppression, sexual function, and cardiovascular regulation. 
 Melanotan 2 activates all of the receptors except for MC2R as it responds to ACTH instead of a-MSH analogues (which melanotan is), where as Melanotan 1 primarily is selective towards MC1R. Below I will discuss how each of these receptors are activated and ultimately dictate specific outcomes: 
 Tanning and MC1R Activation - When the MC1R is activated on melanocytes (the cells that produce pigment) it signals the body to increase the production of something called eumelanin which is the dark brown-black pigment that is responsible for the protective, darkening tanning response. This is different than the reddening you may have when you're strictly exposed solely to UV. The melanocortin pathway actually produces a constitutive tan which is basically your "base tan" or skin color that gives you photoprotection from eumelanin's ability to absorb UV radiation. Once you understand this, you realize why these were developed for photoprotective properties and can be used for EPP which is a severe sensitivity to sun exposure. 
 Sexual Function and MC4R Activation - The MC4R in the hypothalamus are involved in sexual arousal in both men and women. When MT-2 activates this receptor, it produces pro-erectile signaling through the central nervous system. This increases nitric oxide production in penile tissue and activates the autonomic pathways to increase sexual arousal which is also what causes the libido-enhancing effects in men and women outside of MC4R receptor activa

title: Benefits of Melanotan
text:
Tanning and Photoprotection (Both) - The tanning effect was the original goal of both of these peptides. Both of them will produce a deep tan through eumelanin production that is more photoprotective than a tan that comes strictly from UV as eumelanin is produced with these compounds instead of phaeomelanin which is less protective. The tan will typically start to develop over 1-2 weeks (sometimes within 1-2 days) and can last for months after stopping. The melanin pigment is retained within the skin cells until they turn over. Now, this is able to do this in some capacity without UV, which is why it is used for conditions like EPP where people have extreme UV sensitivity. However, if you want to get the best results out of it, some sun exposure is going to give more tanning benefits. These compounds don't completely eliminate DNA damage, but can help protect against it in some capacity with the eumelanin absorbing some of the UV before it reaches your DNA. 
 Sexual Function (MT-2) - The sexual benefit of MT-2 is pretty well-known and reliable. For men, it will cause spontaneous erections and increases sexual desire. For women, it will results in increased arousal and libido more so than a physical response. This component of MT-2 is where PT-141 came from to treat hypoactive sexual desire disorder. It basically took MT-2 and modified it to be more specific into MC4R and reduce the tanning and other effects. But generally speaking, for most people, you will get the sexual function enhancements from MT-2. 
 Appetite Suppression (MT-2) - The appetite suppression of MT-2 can be pretty strong after using it. It usually can last for a few hours or more and can often be coupled by nausea. So, I guess if you were going to use MT-2 and weren't already having enough suppression to be in a calorie deficit, this could be an additional benefit. But if you want to avoid that issue disrupting your ability to intake calories, then I would eat and hydrate prior to using it. 
 Anti-Inflammatory (Both) - MC1R can suppress NF-kB inflammatory signaling in immune cells (see the Immune System course for more info), but is not the primary reason that I would try to use this compound. I would say it's more of a potential added benefit that you may experience over a primary use case. 
 Vitiligo (MT-1) - Now I want to preface by saying that MT-1 can either help or worsen vitiligo as I have seen people report both. But there is some data to suggest that MC1R agonists may help. I would say that this would only make sense to try if you are willing to accept that it may get worse.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Melanotan-1: 
 For Melanotan 1, I do think a loading phase can be more appropriate as it is milder. For the loading phase, I like to do 100-250mcg daily for one week. 
 After the loading phase, that same dosage is only needed 1-3x weekly. Using it once weekly is honestly sufficient in most cases. 
 Melanotan 2: 
 For Melanotan 2, it is so strong that you really don't need a loading phase as much. If desired, 100mcg daily for the first week could work. But I prefer the entire protocol of melanotan 2 to be done no more than 3x weekly at the 100-250mcg dosage range. 
 The cycle of melanotan only needs to be a maximum of 4-6 weeks. As outlined earlier, the effects will last for months. 
 You may see people online pushing .5-1mg dosages for melanotan. For either of these, it is NOT NECESSARY to go that high. People have started to realize that those dosages are higher than needed. 
 Both of these two can work well as nasal sprays and is my preferred way to use them. 
 If nausea occurs, grab some Zofran from AlgoRX and eat some food prior to taking the Melanotan.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Melanotan 1 and 2 both may cause darkening or changes in moles. You also may notice more moles appearing. 
 There are only case studies that report melanoma during or after use of melanotan, but there is no definitive causation. In certain scenarios, the people were chronic tanning bed users. So what was the reason for the melanoma? 
 However, I do think the responsible thing is to be aware of that and monitor for any potential issues and if you see anything changing, go get it checked out. 
 Nausea and Flushing - This happens for probably 50% of people, more so with MT-2 than with MT-1 (maybe 5-10% of people report it with that one). Typically this will go away after a few hours and may diminish over time as you continue to use the compound. 
 Priapism - With MT-2, you will likely have spontaneous erections. There is a small potential for priapism which is where an erection lasts for longer than 4 hours and would more likely happen at higher dosages.

title: Reconstituting Nasal peptides
text:

 How much liquid you add (usually 10ml)
 How much liquid is dispersed per spray

 Transfer the reconstituted peptide into the air dispersal unit (spray bottle)
 Add the remainder 7-9ml of deionized water into the air dispersal unit so a total of 10ml of liquid was added.

title: Overview
text: P21, also referred to as P021, is a synthetic peptide that was designed to support neuron growth and protection in the brain. Most of the research behind it has focused on Alzheimer's disease and age-related cognitive decline but it is also typically used as a general cognitive enhancer and a neuroprotective compound by people who don't have Alzheimer's.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Neurogenesis: One thing that your brain is going to do throughout your life is grow new neurons. Most of the time it occurs in the hippocampus, which is the part of your brain that is most involved in memory formation and learning. 
 Your body regulates the rate of new neuron production and one of the signals that your body uses to suppress it is a molecule called LIF (Leukemia Inhibitory Factor). LIF activates this signaling pathway called JAK-STAT3, which basically tells your brain's neural stem cells to slow down, so it's like an engine governor on your brain's neurons. P21 blocks that suppression signal and showed that it could reduce the STAT3 activation by about 30% in animals. 
 Basically what P21 is doing is taking off the governor and letting your brain proliferate (dividing) and differentiate (transforming) into new neurons at a higher rate. So instead of increasing neurogenesis, it's basically removing the restraint that prevents it, which ultimately results in a better safety profile. 
 BDNF Increases: This component of P21 is where it really gets interesting when it comes to Alzheimer's and neuroprotection. P21 increases the production of BDNF, or brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is basically a growth and maintenance signal for neurons in the brain. It helps with neuron survival, promotes the formation of new synaptic connections, and plays a very important role in learning and memory. Low BDNF is associated with things like depression, cognitive decline, and Alzheimer's. Higher BDNF is one of the main things that you are trying to optimize when you are looking at overall brain health. 
 When BDNF increases, it creates a reaction inside of your neurons, which turns down this enzyme called GSK-3beta. Here's why that is important. Your neurons have a support structure inside of them that contains a protein called tau that helps hold it together and keep everything running how it should. When things go wrong like aging or disease, this GSK enzyme becomes overactive and starts to attack that structure, which puts too many signals onto tau and causes it to clump and tangle up instead of doing what it's supposed to. Those clumps are one of the major things that go wrong when it comes to Alzheimer's disease. When the neurons are full of tangles, they will stop functioning and eventually die off. 
 P21 through BDNF basically puts the brakes on that enzyme. Less activity means that you will have less damage to that structural support system, which means that you will ultimately have less tangle formation and your neurons will be healthier. The animal study showed about a 50% reduction in this type of damage in the treated animals, which is a pretty large number. It also was able to reduce amyloid beta, which is the other major component of Alzheimer's, but that was less consistent than the tau improvement. 
 So all of this basically means that you will have:
 new neuronal growth
 less tangle build-up in the brain
 stronger synaptic co

title: Benefits of P-21
text:
Cognitive Enhancement and Memory: The most consistently documented benefit is improved learning and memory performance and they were able to observe that in both diseased and healthy animals so it's not just fixing things when you're sick. They were able to look at normal healthy mice and see a significant improvement in object recognition and spatial memory after treatment with P-21. In aged rats after 88 days, they saw improved spatial memory but it wasn't brought back to the level it was for the young animals. It also shows how it may be able to bring things back, but not perfectly, within humans as they age. 
 In Alzheimer's models that started treatment early, cognitive performance was basically maintained at normal levels over the course of nine to 15 months. That's a pretty long time especially to see consistency of the effects through different methods of testing. That's really the most promising component of the preclinical data. 
 Now over the course of a few weeks, what people are noticing is that they start to have:
 clearer thinking
 better word retrieval
 improved recall
 better focus under cognitive load
 The mechanism really explains why it happens over that timeline. You were growing new neurons and waiting for them to basically mature and integrate into the functional circuits in your brain so it's not going to be an overnight process.
 Neuroprotection and Brain Aging: The tau damage reduction is one of the most significant components of the preclinical data and those problems aren't exclusive just to Alzheimer's. The same processes that will turn into that neurodegeneration and disease are also happening in a healthy aging brain but at a slower rate. By targeting this, P-21 is addressing something that is relevant way before somebody is even concerned about Alzheimer's. 
 Synapse loss is also a strong predictor of cognitive decline compared to things like amyloid plaques or tau tangles in a lot of analyses. When P-21 helps to preserve and enhance the synaptic proteins, it is basically protecting the molecular components of cognition most directly connected to real-world cognitive function. For someone who is not dealing with any neurodegeneration but wants to preserve the sharp functions as they age (which is most people), the things that P-21 is targeting are where you really want to focus. 
 Neurogenesis: The hippocampus will continue to generate new neurons throughout your adult life and those neurons are important for memory and learning capacity. P-21 created about a 4x increase in hippocampal neurogenesis in animal studies that were in diseased animals with severely suppressed baseline neurogenesis. For healthy users the effect would likely be smaller but the same mechanism can still apply. Taking that governor off of the LIF/STAT3 pathway and increasing BDNF will push neurogenesis above what the brain would otherwise be producing. 
 Retinal Health: This one isn't as common for P-21 but is an extra benefit that is worth k

title: Dosage and Protocols
text:
P-21 is typically used either subcutaneously or as an intranasal spray. My preferred way of using it is intranasal, which is similar for all of the cognitive compounds. As you are able to leverage the olfactory and trigeminal nerve pathways that run through the nasal cavity. 
 The common dosage ranges are below: 
 Intranasal: The lower end would be 500mcg - 1mg daily. Some will go higher, like 1 - 2mg daily. I prefer using 1mg personally. 
 Subcutaneous: The same dosage ranges apply for subcutaneous administration. 
 Cycle length: Minimum of 4 weeks, but ideally 8 - 12 weeks is more optimal as we are focusing on sustained neurogenesis over time. 
 Frequency: Daily is preferred, but 5 on 2 off could also work.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text: The biggest thing with P-21 is that there are no human studies that we can reference for the safety profile but with the animal studies things seem to be relatively safe overall. From what I have seen there has been nothing that is a major concern but if we had to assume the biggest risk will be something that we just don't know of.

This is a blend that is commonly growth hormone support to increase muscle and decrease body fat. CJC-1295 will help growth hormone, and Ipamorelin can amplify this by providing a fast-acting pulse. When combined together they can work synergistically to improve sleep, recovery, and fat loss.

title: How to Read Peptide Blend Labels
text:
When you look at a peptide blend, the label will usually list each compound and how many mg there are of each one in the vial. For example, BPC-157 5mg / TB-500 (TB-4) 5mg. What messes most people up is knowing how to read those numbers and use them to calculate the concentration of the peptide for the appropriate dosing.
 Understanding Ratios Some labels will show the amounts like this:
 BPC-157 5mg/TB-500 5mg 
 GHK-Cu 50mg/BPC-157 10mg/TB-500 10mg 
 Usually, it will be written out the way it is above with slashes in between the individual compounds. Regardless of how it's written, those numbers are typically telling you the total amount of mg of each that are in the vial, not the dosage of each.
 If you see BPC-157 5mg/TB-500 (TB-4) 5mg, that doesn’t mean each injection is 5mg of each. What this is telling you is that the vial contains 5mg of BPC and 5mg of TB-500 total, and you will need to divide that based on the concentration and how many doses you’re taking.
 Don’t Add Them Together The most common mistake that people make when looking at peptide blends is that they add all of the mg amounts of the individual peptides together and try to calculate based on the total number of mg in the vial. This is incorrect. So a 5/5 blend is not going to be calculated as 10mg for the purposes of reconstitution, it would be calculated as 5mg. 
 The next section will walk you through how they would be calculated and dosed through the reconstitution process.

title: How to Dose Peptide Blends
text:
When it comes to blends, you're not adding the amount of each individual peptide in the vial to determine the math. You will pick one peptide in the vial to determine dosage, usually the one with the highest milligram amount, and then figuring out how much of the others you're getting based on those calculations.
 Everything else is determined based on how many doses you’re taking from the vial.
 You can also watch my TikTok for an explanation on a 50/10/10/10 KLOW blend: https://www.tiktok.com/t/ZTjuJRWtM/ 
 Example: GLOW Blend Amount of each peptide within this blend:
 GHK-Cu 50mg 
 BPC-157 10mg 
 TB-500 10mg 
 You reconstitute it with 3mL of bac water
 Typically, people choose to dose 1-2.5mg of GHK-Cu per day. For this example, we are going to use 2mg of GHK-Cu per day. This is how the process of calculating the blend is determined: 
 Step 1: Total number of doses in the vial 
You've got 50mg of GHK-Cu total.
If you’re taking 2mg per injection:
 50 ÷ 2 = 25 doses (total amount of mg divided by the amount of mg in each dose) 
 That vial gives you 25 total doses. Since this is daily, that means it gives you 25 total days worth.
 Step 2: Determine the number of units on an insulin syringe for the amount of mg per dose 
 For this example, we added 3mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial.
That means that the 50mg of GHK-Cu is divided across 3mL.
 50mg ÷ 3mL = 16.67mg per mL 
 Now we have to determine how many units give us our desired mg amount (you can use a peptide calculator to determine this as opposed to doing the math, but here is the concept behind it).
1mL = 100 units, so:
 16.67mg ÷ 100 units = 166.7mcg per unit 
 To get a 2mg (2000mcg) dose:
 2000 ÷ 166.7 = ~12 units 
 So you would have to draw 12 units on an insulin syringe to get 2mg of GHK-Cu.
 Step 3: What you’re getting from the other compounds 
 You’ve got 10mg of BPC-157 and 10mg of TB-500 (TB-4) in the vial.
You’re taking 25 total injections as we already calculated that it would give you 25 doses.
 10 ÷ 25 = 0.4mg per injection (10mg of BPC divided by 25 days/doses) 
 Based on these calculations, each 12 unit injection gives you:
 2mg GHK-Cu 
 400mcg BPC-157 
 400mcg TB-500 
 Final Dosing (per 12-unit injection): 2mg GHK-Cu 
 400mcg BPC-157 
 400mcg TB-500 
 This is the concept and process behind understanding blends. Don't look at it in terms of total milligrams. Instead use the highest mg peptide in the blend and figure out how many doses that gives you, then divide the others across that number. Use your reconstitution volume to figure out how many units that equals on the syringe.

title: Overview
text: This course will go over different peptides and their common cycle lengths. I will also try to explain some of why they are used for that amount of time and why it may be important to come off.

title: What is Peptide Cycling?
text:
A peptide cycle is talking about the length of time that you are using a peptide (or multiple peptides) followed by a scheduled break from those compounds. 
 Why Cycling Matters: 
 Prevent Diminishing Returns - In some cases, different peptides may lose their effectiveness overtime due to receptor downregulation. By cycling, you can keep those fresh and mitigate this issue. 
 Safety - Cycling can help mitigate the risk of long-term side effects depending on the compound. Things like blood pressure issues, insulin resistance, or immune suppression. 
 System Reset - This can be viewed similarly to the diminishing returns, but sometimes you just have to give your body a break. Often times, you will feel like you have better results again once you start back. 
 Cost Effectiveness - In my opinion, this is an important one. Often times, in an off-cycle, you can keep or retain a lot of the benefits you had before. Why not save a few bucks during that time? 
 Cycle Terms: 
 On-Cycle: The time that you are using a peptide (ranges from days to months)
 Off-Cycle: The time that you are taking a break from using a peptide. Many will be within the 2-8 week range. 
 Tapering: This doesn't have to happen, but it can refer to gradually lowering the dose when you're coming off instead of quitting cold turkey.

title: Overview
text: This course will break down what half-lives are, why they are important, and the half-lives for different peptides.

title: What is a half-life?
text:
A half-life is the amount of time it takes for half of a compound to break down and clear from your system. The active concentration of the compound is being cut in half, hence half-life. 
 This is important, because the half-life can play into the following: 
 How often it needs to be dosed
 Stability of the compound in your body (levels in the blood, etc)
 How long the compound will stay in your body
 If you're dosing something with a really short half-life once per week, it's basically pointless. If you're dosing a full dose of something with a long half-life, you may increase the risk of side effects. 
 This is also important to understand when looking at something like Tirzepatide, and can explain why around days 4, 5, and 6, people start to feel the hunger return as you are getting to half of the active level in your system.

title: Half-Life Example (Retatrutide)
text:
For this example, we're going to assume a dose of 8mg per week. 
 The half-life of Retatrutide is 6 days, meaning every 6 days you will half 50% less of the active compound in your system. 
 The example below shows how that 8mg of Retatrutide will break down in your system over time and how long it would take for it to be completely out of your system based on the half-life period. 
 Day 0 (Injection Day) - 8mg
 Day 6 - 4mg
 Day 12 - 2mg
 Day 18 - 1mg
 Day 24 - .5mg
 Day 30 - .25mg 
 Day 36 - .125mg
 Day 42 - .0625mg
 So, looking at this, after 6 days half of the amount you were at will be left in your system. After 12 days, 75% of the amount in your system will have gone away, and after 24 days, 93% of the original 8mg will be out of your system. All of this is if you do not administer another dose.

title: My Thoughts
text:
One thing I think is critically important when understanding half-lives, is understanding what might make the most sense when determining injection frequency for something like a GLOW blend vs. 5 on 2 off, as well as how long you might need to take a break from something like a GLP to reset your system. 
 If you are using the GLOW blend, everything in that blend typically has a short half-life, and would likely be best administered 2x daily to maintain inflammation reduction benefits, etc. Doing a 5 on 2 off method for this would limit the amount of healing that you are doing because of those 2 days off, and you're not doing anything to mitigate receptor sensitivity with that 2 day break. Therefore, it makes the most sense to use something like that at a higher and more continuous frequency to maximize the benefits that you are receiving from it. 
 For something like a GLP, if you're pushing almost week-long half-lives, then it is taking an incredibly long amount of time to process out of your system. Coming from something like 5mg of Tirzepatide, it will take quite a while to get down to low amounts in your system. Because of this, a 2-week break might not be long enough. Especially in a transition to something like Retatrutide. Coming off for 4-weeks, in my opinion, is even better to really let your body get closer to resetting and "feel" the effects of the Retatrutide. 
 The other thing that is important to take into consideration is how something may build up in your system over time. I am going to put a picture below of Retatrutide dosed 2mg weekly to show how they will build up over the first 4-weeks. Therefore, you might not really feel the effects / benefits of Retatrutide "hit" until you get to that Week 4, 5, 6 point. That is why I always preach patience for any GLPs until that point has been reached to allow it to fully saturate in the system and get to maximum levels before trying to jump higher in dosing.

title: Painful Pins Guide
text:
Some peptides just… hurt more than others.
 Sometimes it’s during injection.
Sometimes it’s hours later.
 Here’s what to expect.
 🔥 Most Common “Spicy” Injections 🧬 GHK-Cu / GLOW / KLOW Usually not painful immediately.
 A few hours later:
• Feels like a charlie horse
• Deep muscle soreness
• Possible welt
 What helps:
• Massage gun after injection
• Go deeper (½” needle)
• Inject in glute instead of stomach
• Add extra BAC water to dilute
 🧪 Tesamorelin • Mild burn during injection
• More noticeable early in cycle
 Usually tolerable.
 🧊 AOD-9604 • May sting slightly
• Worse if reconstituted with acetic acid
 Not severe — just noticeable.
 💪 Amino Blends These are commonly sore.
 Why?
• Thicker solutions
• Higher concentrations
• Often larger injection volume
 Can:
• Leave welts
• Feel tender for a day or two
 Anything containing L-Carnitine falls in this category.
 🥩 L-Carnitine Very common to cause:
• Soreness
• Hard lump
• Temporary welt
 Helpful tips:
• Warm the area first (heating pad)
• Inject slowly
• Massage after
 ⚡ NAD+ • Can burn during injection
• May feel sore afterward
 Injection speed matters.
 🧄 Glutathione • Can sting
• May leave site sore
 Also:
Yes — it smells like rotten eggs. That’s normal.
 🧠 MOTS-C In my opinion:
 The most painful.
 • Hurts going in
• Stays sore
• Can itch later
• May cause a mild local reaction
 This one just tends to be “spicy.”
 🧬 FOXO4-DRI • Mild burn
• More noticeable later than during injection
 Not terrible — just present.
 🌙 Epitalon • Can sting slightly
• Usually mild
 🔬 SS-31 • Slight sting
• Mild soreness afterward
 Short-lived.
 🛠 General Tips to Reduce Injection Pain • Dilute with more BAC water
• Inject slowly
• Rotate sites
• Use glutes for deeper injections
• Warm the area before
• Massage after
• Stay hydrated
 Important Reminder Pain does NOT mean:
• It’s bad
• It’s contaminated
• It’s harming you
 Some compounds are simply more irritating to tissue.
 If you notice:
• Severe swelling
• Fever
• Spreading redness
• Signs of infection
 That’s different — address that immediately.

title: Does Shaking Damage Peptides?
text:
Source study: Does Shaking Damage Reconstituted Peptides?
 https://peptidecrafters.com/does-shaking-damage-reconstituted-peptides/ 
 “Don’t shake it, it’s fragile” is one of the most common rules repeated in peptide research especially after reconstitution. With larger, more complex peptides, the concern is that agitation might cause degradation, reduce purity, or damage the molecule in ways that compromise downstream experimental reproducibility.
 This study isolates a single question and tests it under controlled conditions: Does aggressive shaking damage reconstituted peptides? Specifically, we evaluated GLP-3 R because it represents a complex peptide where handling myths are most likely to surface, and where real degradation would be easiest to detect analytically.
 To answer this decisively, we paired HPLC (purity + degradation profile) with LC-MS (molecular integrity confirmation). We intentionally created a “worst-case handling” condition by aggressively shaking one reconstituted sample and comparing it to normally handled controls.
 Study Summary 
 Purpose: Determine whether aggressive shaking during/after reconstitution causes measurable degradation or molecular damage.
 Peptide: GLP-3 R Complex peptide containing 39 amino acids (single batch, multi-vial controlled handling conditions).
 Design: Two controls (normal handling) vs one intentionally shaken sample (~60 seconds aggressive agitation).
 Analytics: HPLC to detect purity/impurity changes; LC-MS to confirm intact molecular mass and screen for structural damage.
 Conclusion: Shaken and unshaken samples were analytically indistinguishable under the conditions tested.
 In practical terms: agitation alone did not produce measurable degradation in this GLP-3 R study. The data supports that accidental or brief shaking is not inherently catastrophic under controlled lab conditions.
 Methods 
 Controlled Reconstitution
 Samples were reconstituted under standard laboratory preparation conditions using ultra-filtered laboratory water. Handling was kept consistent across samples, with the only variable being the intentional agitation applied to the experimental vial.
 Sample Groups 
 Sample A (Control): Normal laboratory preparation and handling.
 Sample B (Experimental): Aggressively shaken for approximately ~60 seconds to simulate a worst-case handling event.
 Sample C (Control Repeat): Normal laboratory preparation and handling.
 Analytical Approach 
 HPLC was used to quantify purity and detect changes in chromatographic profile (new impurity peaks, peak broadening, retention time shifts, and/or loss of main peak area).
 LC-MS was performed to confirm molecular integrity — i.e., to verify that the molecule itself remained intact and to screen for evidence of truncation, fragmentation, or major chemical modification.
 Why LC-MS? HPLC can show purity remaining stable, but LC-MS confirms that the molecule’s mass/structure is still correct. In short: LC-MS validates molecular integrity post-a

Knowing the difference can save your data and your investment in research.
 Expanded Dataset Update: Additional third-party COAs were added following the initial study. The expanded dataset further reinforces the observation that pH nonconformity was a more common failure mode than benzyl alcohol concentration deficiency among tested products.
 Reminder: Never let a $10 solvent compromise a $100 or $1,000 experiment. Verify the solvent before investing in the research. Poor solvents can compromise even the highest-quality research chemicals.

 The selection of an appropriate solvent is a foundational aspect of in-vitro experimentation, yet it remains one of the most frequently overlooked variables impacting data reliability. This report investigates the impact of bacteriostatic water (BAC water) quality on peptide integrity, solubility, and visual appearance. Through third-party testing of five commercially available BAC waters, significant deviations in benzyl alcohol content and pH were found.  Adamax: Memory, focus, neuroprotection, mood stabilization. A nasal spray in the same family as Semax, and reported to be stronger. It works through BDNF, which is a signal that helps neurons grow and survive.
 AICAR: Endurance, fatty acid oxidation. It switches on AMPK, the enzyme your cells use to sense that energy is running low, which pushes the body to burn fuel instead of storing it. Cycles are deliberately short here. The most common complaint is fatigue, which catches people off guard for an endurance compound.
 AOD-9604: Fat loss. It is the fragment of growth hormone that handles fat metabolism, without the rest of what GH does. That means no IGF-1 rise and no blood sugar effects, which is the safety advantage.

title: Overview
text:
PNC-27 is a peptide that has some potential anti-cancer benefits and is derived from the p53 protein that can be tumor suppressive . If you have looked into FOXO4-DRI, you'll also see that the p53 protein is also what the FOXO4 relationship relies on to help senescent cells survive. Since PNC-27 is so niche, I want to dive a little extra into this here in the overview to give a better understanding. 
 So p53 is sometimes known as the "guardian of the genome" as it helps to maintain genomic stability and prevent mutations which can help to protect cells from becoming cancerous . They can also use portions of p53 to target different cancer cells. With PNC-27 (there's also PNC-28 which is a shorter analog of this) they selectively lyse ( breaking down a cell by damaging its plasma (outer) membrane ) the membranes of cancer cells which results in the necrosis of the cancer cell lines and primary human tumors, but seems to leave the untransformed cells in tact . The way it does this is by binding to the HDM-2 membrane on cancer cells, inserts itself into the membrane, and then creates holes within the cells that cause them to rupture and die. HDM-2 is typically overproduced and is displayed externally on the cancer cells surfaces (which normal cells typically don't have) which is what makes this super interesting as a cancer treatment as it would kill tumors / cells without the typical collateral damage that comes to healthy cells too.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
HDM-2/MDM2 Targeting - PNC-27's main mechanism of action revolves around this HDM-2 (MDM2) protein. Basically what this protein does is keeps p53 in check and keeps it from turning on different genes that can cause cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. In some cancers, they overexpress this HDM2 which would keep p53 from being able to do it's anti-cancer job. By exploiting this in cancer therapies, they're basically able to let p53 do it's job since it's no longer being inhibited by HDM2. Those cancer cells are going to display HDM2 on the plasma membrane (or the outer barrier of the cell) which is typically found internally to the cell, which becomes an abnormal flag that can be seen on cancer cells but not on normal cells. The way that they looked at PNC-27 for this was to take advantage of that HDM2 expression and take a small piece of p53 that fits into the structure of HDM2 to bind to it. 
 Pore Formation - Once the PNC-27 binds to the HDM-2, they gather together and go through a process called oligomerization which is where they join together to create a complex. Think of it like ants gathering on the food you dropped on the ground during a picnic. Once it does that, it seems to form a hole that breaks open the cell. This pore that it creates basically allows molecules to go in and out of the cell and destroys the cell's permeability layer. 
 Once this happens, the cell will very quickly start to lose it's balance and is unable to maintain proper functions. Water can flow into the cell and basically makes it swell up like a water balloon that you forgot to take off the spigot. Eventually, this causes it to tear and explode (like a balloon). When this happens, it causes necrosis which is more of a violent destruction of the cell, where apoptosis is more of a programmed death of the cell where it takes itself apart neatly. Instead of disassembling, the cell basically blows itself up when the intracellular components break out into the surroundings. Necrosis is the primary cell death that is caused by PNC-27 and really relies on this pore formation as it's means of doing so. It's also important to note that the ability for PNC-27 to bind to HDM-2 is crucial and is the way that it will ultimately work to get rid of these cells. Another important thing to note is that it doesn't seem to be reliant on p53 which would normally help regulate this as it skips that and uses the HDM-2 binding affinity to create this necrosis as opposed to using the normal apoptosis pathways.

title: Benefits of PNC-27
text:
The primary benefit of PNC-27 is the ability to target and eliminate cancer cells. This section won't look the same as most benefits sections of deep dives since this is really the benefit that is being had. Instead, we'll talk about how PNC-27 as a whole creates this benefits as well as the benefits of this as a potential cancer therapy based on the mechanism of action. 
 The biggest benefit to PNC-27 is its ability to be selective on various cancer cell types (but not all) and basically leaving alone the non-cancerous cells. This is due to the targeting of the HDM-2 that is bound to externally on the cell membranes. Typically, this is going to exist inside the cell in the nucleus or cytoplasm and be pretty tightly regulated. It will not normally be displayed on the outer membrane in normal cells. Because of this, when PNC-27 is around those normal cells, there is no HDM-2 for it to grab onto when it encounters them. Without this ability to bind, there's really no ability for it to insert itself into the membrane and form those pores within normal cells which is the component that is responsible for the cell destruction. They were able to observe this where non-tumor cells that were treated were not seen to be harmed by PNC-27 . 
 Numerous different cancers have this overexpression of HDM-2 , but not all of them. So which ones are commonly going to have this ? 
 56% of breast cancers
 65% of colon cancers
 41% of prostate cancers
 39% of lung cancers
 80% of lymphomas
 70% of leukemias
 Some of these include things like pancreatic adenocarcinoma, chronic myelogenous leukemia, mantle cell lymphoma, merkel cell carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, certain ER-positive breast cancer subtypes, more advanced, androgen independent prostate cancers, among others. 
 If PNC-27 is used for cancers that don't have the overexpression of HDM-2 on the outside of the cells, then they would likely be ineffective since there is nothing for them to target. Since they are looking for that HDM-2 on the membrane, they're not going to see that and instead look at them as normal cells and, as stated earlier, not target them to create the pores that cause cell death.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
It is important to understand that there have only been cell models and animal models that have been studied with PNC-27, which makes this difficult in terms of what would work for humans. 
 There is also very limited data that exists in any sort of "biohacker" protocols online. The most commonly discussed is 500mcg/day. In animal models and testing, it seems like they did go higher than that in terms of how the animal models may translate to human models. This creates the question on whether something like 1-2mg/day may be more effective than 500mcg. It's hard to gauge and this is something that will need to have a better understanding to fully know what the dosage protocols might look like for this. 
 The positive aspect of this is that it seems to leave healthy cells untouched, so likely not creating an issue of targeting the wrong cells if using the wrong amount, but potentially having other concerns that will be discussed in the next section.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text: Just like dosage protocols, there is really nothing out there to support side effects and safety of PNC-27. On the FDA website, they state that they have not received any reports of illnesses or serious adverse effects related to PNC-27. Could there be issues with immunogenicity where the body has an immune reaction or antibodies? Maybe. Nothing in animal models shows any major concerns, but it's always a consideration. Unfortunately, I don't have much more information to provide here due to the limited data and usage of PNC-27.
