title: Overview
text:
The racetams are a family of compounds that all share a similar structure. They are actually the original Nootropics and where they word Nootropic was coined. 
 In 1964, there was a Russian chemist named Dr. Cornelius Giurgea that synthesized paracetamol. Originally, his goal was to calm motion sickness by pulling a structurally similar compound similar to GABA which is the primary calming neurotransmitter in the brain. What he instead found was a compound that enhanced learning and memory without sedation, stimulation, or toxicity that may be found in psychoactive drugs. Alongside of this, he defined what nootropics should be which is: 
 enhances memory and learning
 protects the brain
 works with few side effects
 low toxicity
 And that's how racetams were built. 
 This course is going to look a little different than the single compound deep dives because the racetams are a family of compounds. The easiest way to understand them is to learn what they share once by looking at the core mechanisms and the relationship with choline, and then go compound by compound to understand how each one varies from the baseline. Some are significantly more potent or stimulating, or can have some completely different mechanisms.

title: Shared Mechanisms
text:
Before we get into each compound, we need to discuss the shared mechanisms between each of these. These are really the things that make a racetam a racetam, even though not all of these share each of these mechanisms. 
 AMPA Receptor Positive Allosteric Modulation - This is the effect that is most commonly associated with the cognitive effects of this class of compounds. AMPA receptors are glutamate receptors that are crucial to synaptic plasticity, specifically long term potentiation which is the process by which synapses strengthen with repeated activation. LTP is really the foundation of learning and memory at the cellular level. Many racetams act as positive Allosteric modulators of AMPA receptors which means that they don't bind to the receptor directly, but instead make it respond more effectively when glutamate binds. The result of this is enhanced synaptic plasticity meaning the brain forms and strengthens connections more readily and therefore results in improved learning and memory. 
 Cholinergic System Modulation - This is the mechanism that explains the need to supplement choline. Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter of learning, memory, and attention. Racetams enhance cholinergic function, but most of them do it by not adding any acetylcholine. They do it by increasing the brains utilization of acetylcholine, increasing the turnover rate, and in some cases they upregulate high-affinity choline intake which is the process that pulls choline into neurons to make acetylcholine. 
 What this means is that racetams increase the demand for acetylcholine. So if the supply of choline doesn't keep up with that demands, you'll have issues. You'll likely feel WORSE with racetams if you reach that point. 
 Not all racetams increase cholinergic demand or interact with acetylcholine signaling the same way, so it may not be universally required for everyone using them. In certain cases, someone may actually feel worse if they use too much choline. 
 Cerebral Blood Flow and Membrane - Several racetams can help to improve cerebral Blood Flow and have effects on cell membrane fluidity. Piracetam interacts with the phospholipid head groups in cell membranes which can improve membrane fluidity which affects how receptors function and how cells communicate. This could potentially help with issues involving compromised blood flow and aging where membrane fluidity declines. Improved cerebral function also contributes to neuroprotective benefits as well. 
 Safety Profile - The foundational 1994 review covering piracetam, oxiracetam, prammiracetam, aniracetam, nefiracetam, and more showed that they have very low toxicity and no real major side effects. They show negligible affinity for major receptor systems you would worry about like adrenergic, serotonergic, dopaminergic, benzodiazepines, or opioid receptor impacts. This is also why they don't produce dependence, withdrawal, or acute toxicity like many psychoactive drugs.

title: Choline Connection
text:
This is the most important thing within this course. Bottom line is that you should not run a racetams protocol without a choline sources. This section will explain why. 
 Why There is a Choline Demand 
 As covered in the mechanisms section, racetams increase cholinergic transmission. They can increase acetylcholine turnover and upregulate high-affinity choline uptake which is the mechanism that pulls choline into neurons that synthesize acetylcholine. The brain basically makes that whole system work harder. Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline which your brain typically gets from your diet and your body's stores. But if a racetams cranks up that acetylcholine demand and your choline supply can't keep up, you deplete available acetylcholine. 
 They actually did a study on this in 1981 where they say that combining piracetam with choline created better memory improvements in aged rats than either of those compounds by themselves. The racetams drives demand, choline supplies the substrate, and together they get more done through a synergistic relationship than either can do by themselves. 
 Racetams Headaches 
 The most common and recognizable side effect of inadequate choline on a racetams is the "racetam headache." People consistently describe it as a distinct, typically localized headache that might feel like a dull pressure in a specific part of the head. Alongside of that headache, it can also create brain fog, irritability, and feeling like cognition is worse. If you start to experience any of those symptoms, the first guess would be a choline issue that can be resolved through supplementation.

title: Choline Sources
text:
There are a few different types of common choline sources, with the best options typically being either CDP-Choline or Alpha-GPC. 
 CDP-Choline (Citicoline) 
 CDP-Choline is my primary choice for racetam pairing. It has high bioavailability, crosses the blood-brain barrier efficiently, and also provides cytidine which converts to uridine which has additional cognitive and neuroprotective benefits like supporting the synthesis of something called phosphatidylcholine which is a brain cell membrane component. CDP-choline is also pretty well tolerated. Typically people will supplement anywhere between 250-500mg per day when using racetams. 
 Alpha-GPC
 This is another good option overall and can help deliver choline efficiently to the brain and is highly concentrated. It is beneficial for acute cognitive and even physical performance uses with some potential power output benefits. There may be some potential cardiovascular risk associated with Alpha-GPC but isn't fully established as a significant risk overall. This one is typically supplemented at around 300-600mg per day when using racetams. 
 Choline Bitartrate
 This is the cheapest and least effective version of choline as it doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier quite as effectively. It would be better than no choline at all, but you might as well supplement one of the other two alongside of it as the costs aren't so different that it justifies using this one as the cheaper alternative.

title: Piracetam
text:
Piracetam is really where this all started. This was the original and has six decades of research and meta-analysis to support it. The major benefits are age-related cognitive decline, post-stroke recovery, dyslexia, and dementia. 
 Piracetam is going to be relatively subtle. It's not going to have dramatic or stimulating effects when you take it and they will generally build over time as opposed to being an immediate hit. Typically when someone starts taking piracetam, they don't really feel anything at first. But after a couple of week, you may start to notice things like better verbal fluency, some better recall, and some clearer thinking. Again, it's not going to be incredibly strong, but those effects along with the pretty established safety profile makes it a pretty good overall compound, especially when someone is getting into racetams. 
 Piracetam has a higher dosage range comparatively to the other racetams. It's the least "potent" of the group. Common dosage ranges are 1.6-4.8g/day, sometimes divided into 2-3 doses.

title: Aniracetam
text:
Aniracetam is one that can give cognitive benefits with the potential for reduction in anxiety. The standout with aniracetam is the anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) effects which comes from AMPA modulation and it's downstream effects on dopamine and serotonin signaling. This one is a good fit for social situations, public speaking, and work where anxiety can be a limiting factor vs. strictly raw processing power. 
 With aniracetam, people typically report having better creativity, better verbal fluency, and the ability to flow with their thoughts vs. a locked in focus. This one can pair well in a situation where you're writing, making music, or doing more open-ended creative type tasks instead of something like math or logic. 
 Aniracetam is fat-soluble so taking it with a meal containing fats allows for best absorption. It also has a short half-life so is sometimes split multiple times throughout the day. The common dosage range for this one is 750-1,500mg/day.

title: Oxiracetam
text:
We already discussed aniracetam being the more creative, holistic racetam option and oxiracetam is going to basically be the complete opposite. This one is going to be the "logic" racetam as people typically experience better attention to detail, better logical reasoning, better technical thinking, and a clean mental state with just a slight amount of stimulation. This is the racetam someone typically uses for studying more technical things like programming or math and work that requires sequential thinking. 
 Oxiracetam increases acetylcholine utilization in the cortex and hippocampus and increases choline uptake similarly to piracetam but with more potent and longer-lasting with its effect on acetylcholine turnover. Oxiracetam doesn't seem to have any major effects on GABA, serotonin, or dopamine so it typically doesn't bring about any mood changes. So you're getting all of the cognitive benefit without the emotional components that can sometimes be attached to it. 
 The mild stimulation you might get from oxiracetam is less than what phenylpiracetam might give and you're not going to have tolerance issues with it like you will with phenylpiracetam. The common dosage range for oxiracetam is 800-1600mg/day and is sometimes split 2x daily.

title: Pramiracetam
text:
Pramiracetam is going to be the most potent of the racetams by weight and is primarily geared towards memory and learning. There are minimal mood effects compared to aniracetam and loss noticeable stimulation than oxiracetam. It is going to give a very intense, narrow focus that has strong benefits toward memory formation and retention. When people use it, typically they say it gives a strong and sustained ability to concentrate that just makes it easier to learn new material. 
 The mechanism for pramiracetam is strong for high-affinity choline uptake (HACU) in the hippocampus. It significantly increases the rate at which choline is pulled into the neurons to make acetylcholine. This is why pramiracetam is the most choline-dependent of the group is its entire mechanism revolves around the acceleration of choline utilization so if supply isn't where it needs to be, then it won't work and will likely cause the strong headaches. This is the one out of all the others in the course that has the highest likelihood to cause issues because of this. 
 Pramiracetam can have potential benefits to support cognitive deficits after a TBI but has less data to support it than something like piracetam. This one is also fat-soluble so is best taken with food. The common dosage ranges for pramiracetam is around 300-600mg up to two times per day.

title: Phenylpiracetam
text:
Phenylpiracetam is piracetam with a phenyl group added to the molecule which is a modification that is going to significantly increase the potency as well as add a stimulant component that piracetam doesn't have. This phenyl group also allows it to cross the blood-brain barrier more readily and gives some psychostimulant properties like effects on dopamine, noradrenaline, and serotonin. The result of these effects is something that gives physical stamina, motivation, focus, and a stimulant push that puts it almost into a class of its own compared to the other racetams. 
 This stimulant component makes phenylpiracetam the main choice when there are demanding, high-output days like heavy workloads, athletic performance, or things that need sustained energy and drive. It actually has some data supporting performance under physically demanding conditions like cold tolerance and physical stamina (which is why athletes love it and also why it's banned by WADA). 
 One important thing to understand with this one is that tolerance builds incredibly fast. If you're using it daily, the effects will diminish quickly. This is best used on demanding days where it's needed to avoid this developing. The common dosage of phenylpiracetam is 100-200mg up to two times per day.

title: Nefiracetam
text:
Nefiracetam is somewhat similar to aniracetam in it's ability to help with calming and mood. It was developed in Japan for the treatment of cerebrovascular disease and has been studied for cognitive and mood uses. The differentiator between this one is the ability to widely target different receptor effects. 
 Nefiracetam actually has documented GABA-A activity and can potentiate presynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the hippocampus which can help with glutamate release and long-term potentiation. Combining the cholinergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, and calcium channel effects give nefiracetam a broader and more complex pharmacological profile. This allows it to help support memory and recall alongside of some anti-anxiety and antidepressant-like benefits. 
 The common dosage range for nefiracetam is 100-300mg/day with food as it is fat soluble.

title: Egg White Omelette
text:
Egg White Omelette (Base Recipe with Variations) 
 Ingredients (1 serving): 
 6 egg whites
 Optional: 1 whole egg
 Optional mix-ins: 1/4 cup sautéed onions and bell peppers, OR onions and mushrooms
 Optional: 1/4 cup shredded mozzarella (part-skim)
 Instructions: 
Heat a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Add your preferred sautéed vegetables. Pour in egg whites (and whole egg if using). Cook until set, folding gently. Top with mozzarella if using and let melt before serving.
 Macros (base with 6 egg whites): 
Calories: ~102
Protein: ~21g
Carbs: ~1g
Fat: ~0g
(Add ~70 cal / 6g fat / 6g protein for whole egg, and ~80 cal / 6g fat / 7g protein for cheese)

title: Protein Oat and Berry Bowl
text:
Protein Oat & Berry Yogurt Bowl 
Quick high-protein breakfast with balanced carbs and antioxidants.
 Ingredients (1 serving): 
 170g Oikos Pro Vanilla Greek Yogurt (2% or Triple Zero)
 40g raw old-fashioned oats
 110g frozen blueberries
 Instructions: 
 In a bowl, combine yogurt and oats. Stir until evenly mixed.
 Add frozen blueberries directly or thaw slightly for easier mixing.
 Optional: Let sit for 5–10 minutes to soften oats or refrigerate overnight for a cold “overnight oats” style texture.
 Enjoy cold!
 Estimated Macros (1 serving): 
Calories: ~360
Protein: ~28g
Carbs: ~42g
Fiber: ~6g
Net Carbs: ~36g
Fat: ~5g
 Macros may vary slightly depending on the exact Oikos variety used (Triple Zero vs Pro vs regular). Triple Zero has no added sugar and keeps fat low.

title: Egg White Veggie Bake
text:
Egg White Veggie Bake with Cottage Cheese (Easy breakfast prep)
 Ingredients: 
 2 cups egg whites
 1/2 cup low-fat cottage cheese
 1/2 cup shredded zucchini
 1/2 cup chopped peppers
 1/4 cup diced onion
 Seasonings: salt, pepper, garlic powder, Italian herbs
 Instructions: 
Mix everything in a bowl. Pour into a greased 8x8 baking dish. Bake at 375°F for 30–35 minutes until firm. Slice into squares.
 Macros (1 of 4): 
~110 cal / 16g protein / 4g carbs / 3g fat

title: Sweet Potato Hash with Turkey and Eggs
text:
Sweet Potato Hash with Turkey & Eggs (Savory meal-prep breakfast)
 Ingredients: 
 1 lb lean ground turkey
 2 cups diced sweet potatoes
 1/2 cup diced onion
 1/2 cup chopped spinach
 4 eggs (or 1 egg + 4 egg whites for leaner version)
 Olive oil, salt, pepper, paprika
 Instructions: 
Roast sweet potatoes at 400°F for 20 minutes. Brown turkey and onions in a skillet. Add spinach and cooked potatoes. Crack eggs over the hash, cover, and cook until yolks set.
 Macros (1 of 4 servings): 
~350 cal / 28g protein / 20g carbs / 16g fat

 Batch bake, fridge-stable, breakfast on the go 
 1 cup egg whites

 Bake in muffin tins at 375°F for 20–25 mins

title: Protein French Toast

Protein French Toast 
 Comfort food without the crash 
 3 slices low-calorie bread (Dave’s Thin-Sliced or Ezekiel)

 Dash cinnamon & vanilla
 Dip bread in egg mix and pan-fry

title: Cottage Cheese Banana Oat Protein Pancake Bites 🥞
text:
🛒 Ingredients:
 1 ripe banana, mashed
 1/2 cup cottage cheese
 1/2 cup rolled oats
 2 large eggs
 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
 1/2 teaspoon cinnamon
 1/2 teaspoon baking powder
 1/4 teaspoon salt
 1/4 cup mini chocolate chips (optional)
 Cooking spray or butter (for greasing the muffin tin)
 👩‍🍳 Directions:
 Preheat the Oven:
 Preheat your oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a mini muffin tin with cooking spray or butter.
 Blend the Ingredients:
 In a blender, combine the mashed banana, cottage cheese, oats, eggs, vanilla extract, cinnamon, baking powder, and salt. Blend until smooth.
 Fold in Chocolate Chips (Optional):
 If using, stir in the mini chocolate chips by hand.
 Fill the Muffin Tin:
 Pour the batter into the greased mini muffin tin, filling each cup about 3/4 full.
 Bake:
 Bake for 12-15 minutes, or until the pancake bites are puffed up and golden around the edges.
 Cool and Serve:
 Let the pancake bites cool in the pan for 5 minutes before removing them. Serve warm with maple syrup, fresh fruit, or enjoy them on their own!
 🍽 Serves: 12-14 pancake bites

title: Overview
text:
The purpose of this category is to outline different peptides, common vial size amounts, and the simplest ways to reconstitute based on the dosage and vial size. 
 The goal with each of these is to make the dosage AT LEAST 5 units on the low side to make it easier to draw and administer. This takes out the issues with a peptide calculator where it might tell you the dosage needed is 2 units and it becomes difficult to draw and/or administer. Each page will be broken down by peptide. 
 DISCLAIMER: This should be used as a general guide. This is not medical advice and you should always consult with your doctor or provider. This is not meant to replace anything from your medical provider and is meant to serve as a reference guide to help with easier understanding.

title: What is Retatrutide?
text:
Retatrutide (LY-3437943) is a triple receptor agonist peptide. What this means is that it targets three different receptors to assist in metabolic regulation: 
 GLP-1 Receptor (Glucagon-like-peptide-1)
 GIP Receptor (Glucose-Dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide)
 Glucagon Receptor
 Retatrutide will target all three pathways to help control appetite, insulin sensitivity, fat storage, and glucose metabolism. Because it is targeting all three of these at once, it can give stronger and more comprehensive benefits than previous GLP-1s that are targeting only one or two different receptors. 
 The Glucagon Receptor 
 The biggest piece of Retatrutide that makes it stand out is its targeting of the glucagon receptor. What this piece will do in the body is: 
 Increased energy expenditure: Glucagon can activate brown adipose tissue (brown fat) and burn calories to produce heat (thermogenesis). 
 Enhanced fat oxidation: Glucagon will help your body utilize stored fats for fuel, leading to more fat loss. 
 Lean mass preservation: A major issue with the other GLP-1s is the amount of muscle that is lost in the weight loss process. By promoting more fat breakdown, Retatrutide can reduce the amount of muscle loss that may occur. 
 What does the clinical data say? 
 In clinical trial data, Retatrutide showed: 
 Up to 24.2% of body weight loss after 48 weeks at the highest dose. 
 Compare this to Semaglutide (15%) and Tirzepatide (20%) in 72 weeks.
 Trial participants also saw insulin sensitivity improvements, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure, and liver fat.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Retatrutide is going to work by targeting three different pathways that will help with metabolism, appetite and hunger, and body composition. 
 GLP-1 Receptor Activation: 
 The GLP-1 receptor (glucagon-like-peptide-1 receptor) is also targeted by Semaglutide and Tirzepatide. 
 Reduces appetite by targeting appetite-regulating centers in the brain (hypothalamus). 
 Slows gastric emptying (food is going to leave the stomach slower), which will make you feel fuller longer. 
 Increases insulin secretion
 Improves HbA1c and blood sugar control. 
 This will reduce hunger and stabilize blood sugar so people will eat less calories, contributing to weight loss. This pathway is the primary reason for appetite suppression with GLP-1 compounds. 
 GIP Receptor Activation: 
 The GIP receptor (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor) is the second piece that was added with Tirzepatide, and still is targeted with Retatrutide. 
 Improves insulin sensitivity
 Improves insulin secretion
 Can support better lipid metabolism
 GIP activation can help the body partition nutrients more effectively and can help improve insulin sensitivity more than GLP-1 receptor activation by itself. 
 Glucagon Receptor Activation 
 This is the biggest piece that Retatrutide adds that separates itself from the pack of the other GLPs. 
 Increasing energy expenditure through brown fat activity
 Increase fat oxidation
 Increase resting metabolic rate
 Preserve lean muscle mass
 Glucagon activation is important because when you're losing weight in a caloric deficit, your metabolism can often slow down with it. Through the glucagon receptor activity, this can allow fat loss to continue even as the calorie intake is decreased. 
 By activating all of these receptors together, you accomplish this: 
 Appetite suppression
 Insulin sensitivity improvement
 Glucose control stabilization
 Increased fat oxidation
 Increased energy expenditure

title: Retatrutide Benefits
text:
Retatrutide is primarily being recognized as a weight loss / fat loss compound, but has far more benefits outside of this. It can have benefits on metabolic health, inflammation, insulin sensitivity, and liver function. Others even report benefits for things like ADHD and cognitive function. 
 Weight Loss / Fat Loss
 In the Phase 2 clinical trials, Retatrutide produced significant results for weight loss, especially compared to Semaglutide or Tirzepatide. 
 The trial was conducted over a 48-week period. 
 Patients who received the highest dose (12mg weekly, titrated to that point over time) lost 24.2% of their body weight on average. 
 At the 48-week point, patients were still losing weight. 
 Everyone on the trial lost at least 5% of bodyweight and 85% of trial participants lost 15% or more of their body weight in that 48-week period. 
 Compared against Semaglutide (15% loss) and Tirzepatide (20% loss), Retatrutide significantly outperformed. 
 Fat Loss
 Retatrutide adds in the glucagon activation which helps prevent muscle loss as it's primarily targeting fat. 
 In animal studies, the glucagon receptor activation stimulates fat oxidation but is sparing to lean muscle tissue. 
 When looking at this in human trials, results suggested that some lean muscle loss still occurred (as this happens when losing weight or being in caloric deficits), but the amount that was lost was better than other GLP-1 medications. 
 Improved Insulin Sensitivity
 Retatrutide can have a strong effect on insulin secretion and sensitivity. 
 HbA1c was reduced by up to 1.4% in Phase 2 trials, even in those without diabetes. 
 Fasting glucose was increased and patients with prediabetes had normalized glucose tolerance in most cases. 
 Based on this data, Retatrutide can likely benefit or even reverse Type 2 diabetes. 
 Liver Function and NAFLD
 Many people who are overweight or obese have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). 
 In studies, they observed about an 86% reduction in NAFLD in patients. 
 Hepatic fat content was significantly reduced (accumulation of fat in the liver). 
 Cardiovascular Benefits
 Retatrutide, like other GLP-1s, shows improvement in cardiovascular risk markers. 
 Many people observed a reduction in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. 
 Lipid profiles significantly improved (LDL decreased, triglycerides, improved HDL).

title: Side Effects and Risks
text:
Retatrutide, like the other GLPs, can have some risk factors that are associated with it. A lot of times they are dose dependent, and often times when people start low and increase slowly over time, these are mitigated significantly. 
 Gastrointestinal Issues
 Nausea
 Vomiting
 Diarrhea
 Constipation
 Abdominal Discomfort
 Bloating
 These can all occur due to the GLP-1 receptor activation that slows down gastric emptying and can change gut motility. Over time, the body typically adapts to these changes and symptoms can be reduced. When dosages are increased, symptoms can reappear temporarily. 
 Importance of Titration
 Slower titration schedules (going up after 2-3 months vs going up after 1 month) can significantly reduce side effects. 
 Most of the trial participants in Phase 2 tolerated the higher doses as they increased to them slowly over time. 
 Heart Rate Increases
 Heart rate increases were observed in patients. The majority of heart rate increases occurred in patients who were starting at higher dosages. One interesting piece about this is that the ones who started low and increased over time had almost no occurrences of cardiac arrhythmias. 
 Most of the GLP-1 compounds were also raising heart rate. This is not uncommon, but is something that skeptics try to hyper-focus on with Retatrutide.

title: Dosing, Titration, and Protocols
text:
Retatrutide is still in clinical trials so there is no defined dosing protocol yet. But, based on how it was dosed in Phase 2 clinical trials, as well as how other GLP-1s are usually titrated, this can be evaluated and determined. The most important thing with this is a slow, steady titration schedule and never going higher than needed or going up too quickly. 
 Clinical Trial Dosages
 In clinical trials, patients started at .5, 1, 2, and 4mg to assess tolerance. 
 They gradually increased dosages over time (4-8 weeks). 
 At 12mg weekly, patients were still losing weight at 48 weeks. 
 General Titration Schedule (low and slow)
 Weeks 1-4: .5mg weekly
 Weeks 5-8: 1mg weekly
 Weeks 9-12: 2mg weekly
 Weeks 13-16: 4mg weekly
 Weeks 17-20: 8mg weekly
 Weeks 21+: 12mg weekly
 This can go significantly slower than this. There really is no need to increase at the 4 week mark. 
 Minimal Increase Schedule: 
 Weeks 1-8: 2mg weekly
 Weeks 9-16: 4mg weekly
 Weeks 17+: Increase as needed. If in a stall for over 4 weeks when nutrition, sleep, and exercise have all been kept consistent, increase dose by 2mg as needed. 
 Individualization of Dosing Schedules:
 One thing that is important to remember, is that everyone's schedule is going to look different based on individual response. 
 The majority of patients got the best results per mg between 4-8mg per week. Trial. participants only lost about another 1% over the 48-weeks when they increased to the 12mg per week point. 
 Ultimately when looking at the individualization of the dosages, the goal is to find the point that gives maximum results, at the minimum dosage, with the least amount of negative side effects. 
 Labwork on Retatrutide: 
 When on Retatrutide, labs that could/should be monitored are: 
 HbA1c
 Liver enzymes (AST, ALT)
 DEXA scans to analyze body composition
 Timing of Injections: 
 Retatrutide is typically administered once per week. 
 Some may choose to split the dosages to 2x weekly or even more frequently. When the dosages are split, it can mitigate side effects by keeping the levels more stable in the system as seen by the images below (once weekly, twice weekly, daily):

title: Retatrutide Glucagon Receptor Activation Myth
text:
You may have heard that the Glucagon benefits of Retatrutide don't work until you've hit at least 4mg weekly. This one has always stumped me. Someone commented on my Instagram post and shared the link for why this is what people are saying, and I think I've finally cracked the nut on it!
 So, it still stands that I believe this is not true. But why are people saying this and why do people think this is the case?
 There is an article titled "LY3437943: a novel triple glucagon, GIP, and GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic control and weight loss: from delivery to proof of concept" (Cell Metabolism, 2022) that reviews the data from Phase 1 of the clinical trials. The dosages that were tested in Phase 1 are .1, .3, 1, 3, 4.5, and 6mg. What they noticed is that the largest glucagon reductions were noted at 4.5-6mg, but that's because those were the highest dosages tested, not because the GCGR activity starts to "kick in" when you get to that point. Looking at the data, they observed dose-dependent effects (meaning that the results were dependent on dosage essentially), and that the most significant reductions in fasting glucagon and the largest weight loss was at those dosages. Again, that's because they are the highest dosages tested during that phase of the trial. It stated "Following dosing at the highest 2 LY dose levels of 4.5 and 6.0 mg, a decrease in mean fasting glucagon was observed from 24 h post-dose to day 15 (Figure 4H). The observed decreases ranged approximately 50%–75% from the pre-dose levels in these cohorts, consistent with GLP-1R and GCGR target engagement."
 They also conducted Phase 1b trials and tested them at six dosage levels - .5, 1.5, 3, 6, 9, and 12mg. They never reported receptor-level biomarker changes at these dosages, so again the only data we have to go on is that limited observation in the previous piece of the study. They only looked at things like body weight, HbA1C, triglycerides, etc.
 Then, Phase 2 of the trials was conducted and the dosages were 1, 4, 8, and 12mg weekly. They also only measured the same things as the Phase 1b. So again, we have no data on receptor-level biomarker changes where we could infer the effectiveness or what level is needed to see impacts of the glucagon receptor agonist.
 Until they publish data that shows that you really get no benefits until a certain dose, the assumption should be that you are getting glucagon receptor benefits across the entire range of dosages, not just the 4mg and above range.
 Thankfully, someone commented this on my IG and told me the study that says the 4mg requirement for it (misinterpreted from the original article data) and I was able to do some digging and get to the bottom of where this information is likely stemming from.
 Hope this helps!

title: Desire, Arousal, and the Brain
text:
Sexual health is something that many people struggle with and it is also one of the most misunderstood. The usual approach to sexual dysfunction, the PDE5 inhibitors like Viagra and Cialis, works on the plumbing. They improve blood flow to the genitals so an erection is physically possible (works for women too!). But blood flow is only a small piece of it, and for many, not even the true underlying issue. For a lot of people, the limiting factor is not the plumbing at all. It is desire itself, the wanting, the spark, the mental and emotional readiness that has to come before physical arousal even matters.
 This is the gap the libido peptides address, and it is why they have generated so much interest. Compounds like PT-141 and kisspeptin work upstream, in the brain, on the actual circuits that generate desire and arousal in the first place. That is a different and complementary approach to the blood-flow drugs. Oxytocin works on connection, intimacy, and the quality of the experience. Understanding which compound targets which part of the sexual response is the key to using any of them well, because they solve different problems, and using the wrong one for your situation is a common and avoidable mistake.
 This course covers the major compounds in this space: PT-141 (the strongest-evidence libido peptide), oxytocin (the most asked about and most misunderstood), the PDE5 inhibitors like tadalafil, kisspeptin (for hormonal regulation, and the troche delivery format that combines several of these. It also covers something that deserves its own attention, which is how libido changes through menopause and the hormonal transitions, because that is a huge part of the real-world picture and it connects directly to the HRT material in the Hormone Course .

title: How Sexual Response Works
text:
The Components of Sexual Response 
 Human sexual response is not a single switch. It is a sequence of distinct processes, each of which can work well or poorly somewhat independently of the others.
 Desire (libido): the psychological wanting, meaning interest in sex, sexual thoughts and fantasies, the motivation to seek intimacy. This starts in the brain, driven by neurotransmitters (especially dopamine) and hormones (testosterone and estrogen in both sexes). When desire is the problem, no amount of blood-flow help does anything, because the wanting is not there to begin with. No matter how good YOU might think something is, if I don't want it, then it won't happen. Without fixing the desire component of this, nothing else can really occur. 
 Arousal (the physical response): the body's physical readiness, meaning erection in men, lubrication and genital engorgement in women. This is largely a vascular, blood-flow process, driven by nitric oxide and the relaxation of blood vessels. This is what the PDE5 inhibitors target. 
 Orgasm and resolution: the peak of the experience and what follows. Oxytocin surges at orgasm and is involved in its intensity and in the bonding and contentment afterward.
 Connection and intimacy: the emotional and relational side that wraps around all of it, meaning trust, closeness, bonding. This is heavily oxytocin-driven and is a real part of sexual satisfaction. 
 The Brain vs the Body 
 Here is the distinction that reframes this whole area. Traditional erectile dysfunction drugs work peripherally, on the body, specifically the blood vessels of the genitals. They do nothing for desire. They simply make the physical response possible if desire and arousal are already there. This is why so many people are let down by them. A man with low libido who takes Viagra may get the physical capacity for an erection but still have no interest in using it, because the drug never touched the actual problem. This is also why Tadalafil can be used as a FANTASTIC pre-workout type of compound, because without the desire and arousal, this compound isn't really doing much "down there."
 The libido peptides work centrally, on the brain, on the circuits that generate desire and arousal in the first place. That is a different mechanism, and it is why they can help people the blood-flow drugs cannot, people whose limiting factor is the wanting, not the plumbing. Working out whether your limiting factor is central (desire) or peripheral (blood flow), or both, is the most useful piece of self-assessment in this whole area, and it decides which compound actually makes sense for you.

title: PT-141 (Bremelanotide)
text:
What it targets: Desire and arousal (central, brain).
 Mechanism: Melanocortin (MC4) receptor agonist in the hypothalamus.
 Evidence level: Strongest in this class. FDA-approved (Vyleesi) for women.
 Best for: Low libido and HSDD in women; low desire and PDE5 partial-response in men.
 Typical dosing: 1.75mg subcutaneous (approved dose) about 45 minutes before activity, as needed. HOWEVER, if you look at the Consolidated Dosage, Reconstitution, and Cycle Lengths Course , you will see that my opinion is that you should start SIGNIFICANTLY lower to assess tolerance and effects. 
 Route: Subcutaneous injection or nasal spray
 Side effects: Nausea, flushing, headache; a transient rise in blood pressure. These are the reasons why I think starting lower is best. Many take this and get these side effects and never want to try again. 
 PT-141, also called bremelanotide, is the main libido peptide and the one with by far the strongest evidence behind it. Its story connects directly to the Melanotan course . PT-141 came out of Melanotan II, the tanning peptide, when researchers noticed that male volunteers in the early tanning studies had an unexpected side effect, spontaneous sexual arousal. That observation redirected a whole drug development program toward sexual function, and the sexual effect was isolated and refined into bremelanotide.
 How It Works 
 PT-141 is a melanocortin receptor agonist. It activates melanocortin receptors, most importantly the MC4 receptor, in the hypothalamus and central nervous system. These are the brain circuits that regulate sexual motivation and arousal. Importantly, this is not a blood-flow mechanism. PT-141 acts upstream in the brain, generating desire and arousal at their source rather than helping the physical plumbing. Downstream, melanocortin activation boosts dopamine signaling in the brain's reward pathway and increases oxytocin release, both of which feed into sexual desire and arousal.
 Someone whose problem is genuinely low desire, where the wanting itself is missing, is not helped by a blood-flow drug, but may be helped by PT-141 because it works on desire directly. It is also why PT-141 can produce desire and arousal somewhat independently of physical stimulation, which is useful precisely when lack of libido is the barrier.
 The Evidence 
 PT-141 is FDA-approved as Vyleesi, granted in 2019 for hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) in premenopausal women, one of only two FDA-approved treatments for low sexual desire in women. The approval rested on Phase 3 trials showing statistically significant improvements in sexual desire and reductions in the distress that comes with low desire, measured on validated scales. Effects are usually felt within 30 to 60 minutes of injection and last several hours. It is used when wanted, not taken daily. 
 For men, PT-141 is used off-label. An older randomized controlled trial found bremelanotide could rescue erectile response in men who had not responded well to sildenafi

title: Oxytocin
text:
What it targets: Intimacy, connection, orgasm quality (not primarily desire).
 Mechanism: Oxytocin receptor activation; bonding and orgasm pathways.
 Evidence level: Mixed. Stronger for orgasm and intimacy than for desire.
 Best for: Emotional closeness, orgasm intensity, intimacy quality, as an adjunct.
 Typical dosing: 10 to 40 IU intranasal, 30 to 60 minutes before activity, as needed.
 Route: Intranasal spray (for the CNS effect); also troches and sublingual.
 Main side effects: Generally mild; well tolerated short-term.
 Oxytocin is popularly known as the love hormone or bonding hormone, released during hugging, touch, childbirth, breastfeeding, and orgasm. That reputation leads a lot of people to assume it is a straightforward libido booster. The reality is more nuanced and more interesting, and getting this right is the main reason to read this section carefully.
 What Oxytocin Actually Is 
 Oxytocin is a natural hormone and neuropeptide made in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary. It plays a central role in social bonding, trust, empathy, and attachment, and it is involved in sexual function. It is released during arousal, peaks at orgasm, and supports the emotional bonding that goes with intimate contact. In the body, oxytocin also triggers nitric oxide production in a way that supports erection in men and engorgement in women. So it is a real part of the sexual response. The question is what supplementing it from outside actually does.
 The Evidence 
 Animal studies consistently support a role for oxytocin in sexual behavior. But human clinical trials, particularly the ones looking at libido and sexual initiation with intranasal oxytocin, have produced genuinely mixed results. The largest randomized controlled trial in women showed no improvement in sexual function versus placebo. The evidence that oxytocin boosts desire or starts arousal is weak and inconsistent. 
 Where the evidence is stronger is orgasm and intimacy quality, not desire. Controlled trials of intranasal oxytocin have shown greater orgasm intensity in both sexes and increased sexual satiety and contentment after intercourse in men. A well-known couples study found that oxytocin did not change classical parameters like sexual drive, arousal, or erection, but it did increase the intensity of orgasm, the contentment afterward, and aspects of partner interaction, with women feeling more relaxed and better able to share sexual desires. The effects were small to moderate and centered on the experience and connection, not on generating raw desire.
 Oxytocin is best understood as an adjunct for emotional intimacy, connection, and the quality of the sexual experience, including orgasm intensity and post-orgasm closeness, rather than as a standalone libido booster. If the main problem is low desire, PT-141 has far stronger evidence, and oxytocin is the wrong tool. title: Tadalafil and the PDE5 Inhibitors
text:
What it targets: Arousal and erection (peripheral, blood flow).
 Mechanism: PDE5 inhibition, which sustains nitric oxide and vasodilation.
 Evidence level: Very strong. Decades of RCTs, FDA-approved.
 Best for: Erectile dysfunction (the physical, vascular component).
 Tadalafil dosing: As-needed (10 to 20mg) or low-dose daily (2.5 to 5mg).
 Route: Oral.
 Main side effects: Headache, flushing, nasal congestion, indigestion.
 The PDE5 inhibitors are the well-known erectile dysfunction drugs: sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil (Levitra), and others. They are in this course not because they are peptides (they are not) but because they are fantastic additions to y our toolkit. Tadalafil gets specific attention because its long duration and daily-dosing option make it especially versatile for both sexual health and exercise performance. 
 How They Work 
 An erection is fundamentally a blood-flow event. Sexual stimulation triggers the release of nitric oxide in the genitals, which relaxes the smooth muscle of the blood vessels, letting blood flow in and produce an erection. An enzyme called PDE5 breaks down the signaling molecule (cGMP) that keeps this relaxation going, ending the erection. PDE5 inhibitors block that enzyme, so the relaxation and blood flow are sustained. Importantly, they do not create an erection out of nothing. They need sexual stimulation and the nitric oxide it triggers to work. They amplify and sustain the physical response. They do not generate desire.
 This is also the main limitation with them. PDE5 inhibitors are purely peripheral. They work on the plumbing. If the problem is a vascular erection issue, they are highly effective. If the problem is low desire, they do nothing for the actual issue. They can make an erection physically possible, but they cannot make you want sex. A lot of people who are let down by Viagra are let down precisely because their limiting factor was desire, not blood flow, and the drug was never going to address that.
 Tadalafil for Women (yes it works!) 
 Female genital arousal, like a male erection, is partly a blood-flow event. Arousal in women depends on increased blood flow to the clitoris and vaginal tissue, which produces engorgement, more sensitivity, and lubrication. The clitoris and the penis come from the same tissue in development and share the same nitric-oxide-driven engorgement mechanism. So the same PDE5 inhibition that improves penile blood flow should, in theory, improve clitoral and vaginal blood flow. 
 The strongest single piece of evidence is a study of premenopausal women with type 1 diabetes who had female sexual genital arousal disorder. Daily tadalafil at 5mg was measured two ways, subjectively through a validated sexual experiences questionnaire, and objectively through color Doppler ultrasound of clitoral blood flow. title: Kisspeptin
text:
What it targets: Desire and arousal (central), plus the reproductive hormone axis.
 Mechanism: Stimulates GnRH, which sits upstream of the entire sex-hormone system.
 Evidence level: Promising, but investigational.
 Best for: Low desire and HSDD.
 Route: Injection (IV or SC) in trials.
 How It Works 
 Kisspeptin is a naturally occurring hormone that sits at the top of the reproductive control system. It stimulates the release of GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) from the hypothalamus, which in turn drives the whole downstream cascade of reproductive hormones, LH, FSH, and ultimately testosterone and estrogen. This is the same HPG axis described in the hormone course, and kisspeptin is essentially the master switch that sits above it. But beyond its hormonal role, kisspeptin also appears to act directly on brain regions involved in sexual desire and attraction, and that is what makes it interesting for libido specifically.
 The Evidence 
 The best data comes from Imperial College London. Two clinical trials published in JAMA Network Open studied kisspeptin in 32 premenopausal women and 32 men, all with hypoactive sexual desire disorder. Using functional MRI while participants viewed erotic material, the researchers found that kisspeptin improved sexual brain processing in both women and men, with positive effects on sexual behavior compared to placebo, and women reported feeling more sexy after receiving it. Importantly, the team had previously shown that kisspeptin boosts responses to sexual stimuli and attraction-related brain pathways independent of testosterone, meaning the desire effect is not just a downstream consequence of raising hormones.
 A particularly notable practical finding: in women with HSDD, kisspeptin activated brain regions tied to sexual arousal and increased self-reported arousal without the nausea that limits PT-141. If that advantage holds up in larger trials, it could make kisspeptin a better-tolerated option than the current melanocortin approach. The researchers have described kisspeptin as potentially a safe and effective therapy for both women and men with distressing low desire, laying the foundation for kisspeptin-based HSDD treatments.
 In my opinion, Kisspeptin is likely still best utilized when the issue is hormonally-driven issues with sexual desire and function. The one thing you want to avoid is using kisspeptin outside of that situation, and potentially altering your current hormonal situation in a way that you'll need to adjust for in the future.

title: Troches and Combination Formats
text:
A troche (pronounced troh-kee) is not a compound. It is a delivery format and one that you can commonly find a combination of these compounds in. This is another one that you can find easily with AlgoRX . 
 What a Troche Is 
 A troche is a small, dissolvable lozenge meant to be held in the mouth, usually against the cheek or under the tongue, where it dissolves slowly and the active ingredients absorb directly through the tissues of the mouth (the oral mucosa) into the bloodstream. This sublingual or buccal absorption bypasses the digestive system and the liver's first-pass metabolism. For peptides and hormones used in sexual health, this direct absorption can mean faster onset and better bioavailability than swallowing a pill. 
 Why They Are Popular for Sexual Health 
 Troches have become a favored format in sexual health for a few practical reasons. They are needle-free, which is a major appeal for compounds that would otherwise need injection (like PT-141 or oxytocin because the last thing you want to do is have to inject something every time you want to engage in these activities). A compounding pharmacy can also put several complementary compounds into a single troche, like PT-141, Oxytocin, and tadalafil all in one. And the onset is reasonably quick because of the direct mucosal absorption, which suits the as-needed, before-activity use pattern that most of these compounds follow.
 Because sexual response has multiple components, combining compounds that target different components in a single troche is potentially even more beneficial. A common example is combining PT-141 (for desire) with oxytocin (for intimacy and orgasm quality), and sometimes a PDE5 inhibitor like tadalafil (for the blood-flow and erection component), a single troche that addresses desire, connection, and physical arousal at once. This is allowing you to hit multiple potential issues, or provide boosts in multiple different areas, all at once.

title: Libido Through Menopause
text:
One important thing we need to address is libido during menopause as that is a MAJOR time where women may experience these issues. We have to acknowledge how libido changes through menopause and the broader hormonal transitions, because it is one of the most common real-world drivers of low desire, and it connects directly to the HRT course. For a huge number of women, the low libido they are trying to address is not going to be solved with peptides.
 Why Libido Changes at Menopause 
 As covered in the hormone course, menopause involves the decline of estrogen and progesterone, and, often overlooked, a decline in testosterone, which women produce and which contributes meaningfully to their libido, energy, and sense of wellbeing. These hormonal shifts affect sexual desire through several channels at once. Declining testosterone directly reduces libido, since testosterone is a key driver of desire in women just as in men. Declining estrogen causes genitourinary changes, like vaginal dryness, thinning of tissues, and discomfort or pain during sex, that make sex less comfortable and so less wanted. And the broader symptoms of the transition, like disrupted sleep, mood changes, hot flashes, and fatigue, all indirectly suppress desire. Low libido at menopause is generally caused by the combination of all of these things rather than something specific. 
 Why This Matters 
 If low desire is being driven by menopausal hormonal decline, the most logical first-line approach is often to address the hormones, not to reach immediately for a libido peptide. You're just trying to fix symptoms in that case vs fixing the root cause. 
 Estrogen therapy (covered in the HRT course) addresses the genitourinary symptoms. Local vaginal estrogen is highly effective for the dryness and discomfort that make sex painful, and systemic estrogen helps the broader symptom picture. Removing pain and discomfort often restores desire that was being suppressed by them.
 Testosterone therapy for women (also covered in the HRT course) directly targets the desire component. The strongest evidence for testosterone in women is specifically for low libido and HSDD in postmenopausal women, dosed to female physiologic levels. For many women, restoring testosterone is the single most effective intervention for menopausal low desire.
 PT-141 can then be a complementary option. It works on desire centrally and independently of hormones, so it can be layered in for women whose desire stays low even after hormonal optimization, or used as an on-demand tool alongside hormonal therapy.
 So the best approach for menopausal low libido is usually to address the hormonal foundation first (estrogen for comfort, testosterone for desire), and consider the libido peptides as complementary or for residual low desire, rather than jumping straight to a peptide while completely ignoring the underlying hormonal drivers.

title: Dapoxetine
text:
What it targets: Ejaculatory control (premature ejaculation).
 Mechanism: Short-acting SSRI. Raises serotonin at the synapse to delay ejaculation.
 Best for: Premature ejaculation (PE) in men aged 18 to 64.
 Typical dosing: 30mg or 60mg on demand, 1 to 3 hours before activity.
 Route: Oral.
 PT-141 handles desire, the PDE5 inhibitors handle erection, oxytocin handles intimacy and orgasm quality, but none of them touch ejaculatory control. And premature ejaculation is actually the single most common male sexual complaint, with global prevalence estimated somewhere between 20 and 40 percent. Dapoxetine is specifically targeting this and helps with something none of these other compounds do, which is the timing of ejaculation.
 What It Is 
 Dapoxetine (brand name Priligy) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, an SSRI. The difference is that it was designed for on-demand treatment of premature ejaculation instead of for depression. What makes it work for this is the pharmacokinetics. It is absorbed fast, with peak levels within 1 to 2 hours, and it has a very short half-life, around 1 to 1.5 hours. So unlike the usual SSRIs that you take daily and build up over weeks, dapoxetine gets taken only when needed, a few hours before sex, and then it clears out quickly.
 How It Works 
 The mechanism ties back to a side effect everyone already knows about with SSRIs. Serotonin plays an inhibitory role in ejaculation, so more serotonin signaling in the relevant nerve pathways delays it. That is why the SSRIs used for depression can cause delayed ejaculation and trouble reaching orgasm as a side effect. Dapoxetine takes advantage of that side effect and intentionally tries to target it to get results. By blocking serotonin reuptake, it raises serotonin at the synapses of the neurons that control ejaculation, which raises the threshold and delays the reflex.
 Dosing 
 Start at 30mg, taken 1 to 3 hours before anticipated activity.
 Move up to 60mg if 30mg is not enough and is well tolerated. 60mg works better but comes with somewhat more side effects.
 On-demand only, not daily.
 Can be taken with or without food.
 Side Effects 
 Dapoxetine's side effects are generally mild, and because of the on-demand short-acting use they tend to be more short-lived than with daily SSRIs.
 Nausea: the most common one, dose-related, more common at 60mg.
 Dizziness and headache: common.
 Other SSRI effects: diarrhea, insomnia or drowsiness, and dry mouth can happen.
 Safety: 
 Do not combine it with MAOI antidepressants, other SSRIs, or certain other serotonergic drugs..

title: Skincare Basics
text:
This section will give you an overview of how peptides might interact with the skin and why certain peptides can be important for your skincare routine. 
 First, let's address what the skin does for you outside of just looking pretty. 
 Temperature regulation
 Pathogen Defense
 Nutrient Exchange
 Immune System and Nervous System Communication
 When your skin has issues, it can cause issues across your body. 
 There are 3 layers of the skin that play into all of this. 
 Epidermis- This is the outer layer of the skin. It's what we see when we look in the mirror. It helps with protection, cell turnover, and pigmentation. Most of the topical peptides are going to target this layer of the skin (think SNAP-8, topical GHK-Cu, etc). 
 Dermis- This layer is just below the epidermis and is where collagen and elastin are located. You also have things like blood vessels, hair follicles, and nerve endings in this layer. It helps with your skin's structure and firmness. When targeting skin remodeling, such as wrinkles and elasticity, this is really the layer that needs to be targeted for maximum results. Microneedling and injectables can target this layer more than topicals alone will. 
 Hypodermis- this is the deepest layer and is mostly fatty and connective tissue. Think of it more like an insulation / cushioning layer of the skin. This may play a role when you look at deep scars and stretch marks. 
 When we think about all of this, what does our skin truly need to be resilient? 
 Collagen and elastin- these help give your skin firmness and structure. Over time, these will decline with age and peptides can help stimulate their production and repair. 
 Inflammation control- This is super important as too much inflammation can lead to faster aging, redness, and irritation. 
 Hydration- This is critically underrated when it comes to skin health. This is super important to maintaining a strong skin barrier and mitigating issues like inflammation or premature wrinkles. 
 Cell turnover- This helps to keep the surface of your skin smoother, brighter, and functioning how it's supposed to. If cells are able to build up, then it can begin to dull your appearance. 
 Peptides, when used correctly, can help support all of these issues in some capacity alongside of a dedicated routine. 
 So, what can peptides help to improve? 
 Wrinkles and fine lines
 Hyperpigmentation and unevenness
 Acne and acne scarring
 Stretch marks
 Rosacea and redness
 UV damage and oxidative stress
 Poor skin recovery and wound healing
 This sounds great! Seems like peptides can basically fix all of our skin issues! Well, not exactly. What can't they do? 
 Cleanse your skin. You still have to do this. 
 Hydrate. You need to drink plenty of water and fluids and eat nutrient-dense foods. 
 Sleep good and manage stress.

title: What Peptides Do for Skin
text:
So, we discussed some of the basics of skincare, but how can peptides actually do things to help with our skin? 
 We already know that peptides are small chains of amino acids. They're going to tell your body to do specific things. When it comes to skincare, they can tell your body to produce more collagen, reduce inflammation, and speed up healing. With skincare, we can use them to target specific skin issues, often times with fewer side effects than more aggressive treatments (think KPV for acne vs. accutane). 
 How are these going to interact with your skin in order to provide benefits? 
 Tell your skin to produce more collagen or elastin
 Reduce the release of pro-inflammatory molecules
 Improve Skin barrier function
 Assist with tissue repair
 Inhibit muscle contraction
 You can use them in different ways depending on how you need them to work. 
 Topical peptides will mostly stay in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and can help with surface-level issues like texture, tone, and signs of aging. 
 Injectable or microneedling can go deeper into the dermis and can stimulate collagen production, rebuild structure, and fix some deeper issues like wrinkles and scarring. 
 When injected, they can also work systemically so they will help the skin overall by promoting healing and reducing inflammation.

title: What Does Each Peptide Do for Your Skin?
text:
Here we will discuss what each peptide actually does for your skin. Not all of them are necessary, but understanding what and how each of them work can help you understand which may be best. 
 GHK-Cu GHK-Cu is a copper peptide that can help stimulate collagen and elastin and help with skin firmness, skin repair, and reduce inflammation. It can also help even out issues with pigmentation like dark spots. 
 Best for: Anti-aging, wrinkles, dark spots, pigmentation, firmness, hair growth
 How to use: Topical, microneedling, injectable
 GHK Base (no Cu) This is the same as GHK-Cu, just without the copper. It will still give most of the same benefits, but is a bit more mild and may be better for people who are sensitive to copper. 
 Best for: Anti-aging, wrinkles, dark spots, pigmentation, firmness, hair growth
 How to use: Topical, microneedling, injectable
 GHK-Biotin This is a type of GHK that is bound to biotin and can have extra benefits for hair and nails. This is commonly used for things like hair growth, but may also help benefit skin. 
 Best for: Hair growth, skin regeneration
 How to use: Topical, microneedling
 SNAP-8 SNAP-8 is a Botox alternative that can reduce muscle contraction to soften wrinkles. It doesn't completely paralyze the muscle the way that Botox does, but can tone them down pretty significantly. 
 Best for: Wrinkles, expression lines
 How to use: Topical
 Argireline Argireline works similarly to SNAP-8 and can help facial muscles relax to help reduce fine lines and wrinkles. 
 Best for: Wrinkles, expression lines
 How to use: Topical
 Leuphasyl This works similarly on wrinkle pathways as Argireline, but slightly differently. It may enhance the muscle relaxing effect that is recognized by Argireline. 
 Best for: Deep wrinkles
 How to use: Topical
 Syn-Ake Syn-Ake is an interesting compound as it mimics the activity of a snake venom, Waglerin-1, to help relax facial muscles and reduce the appearance of wrinkles. 
 Best for: Expression lines, wrinkles, smoothing
 How to use: Topical
 Matrixyl Matrixyl can help stimulate collagen production and strengthen the skins extracellular matrix. It can help with hydration, elasticity, and firmness and may be good for thinning or crepey skin. 
 Best for: Firmness, hydration, skin texture
 How to use: Topical, microneedling
 Syn-Coll Syn-Coll can help stimulate collagen synthesis and reduce the activity of enzymes that break down collagen, which can be great for people with sagging skin or lack of skin volume. 
 Best for: Tightening, collagen 
 How to use: Topical, microneedling
 BPC-157 BPC-157 is a healing peptide that can help regenerate damaged skin and reduce inflammation. It can be beneficial for things like scarring and stretch marks. 
 Best for: Scarring, inflammation
 How to use: Injectable, topical blends
 KPV KPV is a peptide with strong anti-inflammatory benefits that can help calm skin with issues like rosacea, eczema, psoriasis, and acne. 
 Best for: Redness, inflammation, ecz

title: How to Apply for Best Results
text:
So, we know what each peptide does. But how can we apply them to maximize results? If they aren't being used the right way, you may not see maximum results and are wasting money. 
 Topical Application This is honestly the easiest way to use peptides. All you do is apply them to the skin like a serum or cream. 
 Peptides such as SNAP-8, Argireline, Leuphasyl, Syn-Ake, Matrixyl, GHK-Cu, and Syn-Coll are often found and used in topical formulations. 
 Things to remember: 
 Cleanse your skin. If you have dirty or oily skin, that is not good. WASH YO FACE!
 Apply peptides first before using thicker moisturizers and oils so they can absorb. Preferably, space them out a bit from other products. 
 A thin layer is typically sufficient. 
 Topical products are mostly going to stay in the epidermis and are great for surface-level benefits like texture, hydration, and light wrinkle reduction. They can also help with the appearance of scars. They aren't going to be life-changing for deep scars and major structural issues. 
 Microneedling Microneedling basically opens up little channels in the skin and lets the peptides go a little deeper to reach the dermis layer where the collagen and elastin actually are. They can increase the effectiveness of different peptides like GHK-Cu. 
 How to microneedle: 
 Use .25 to .5mm depth. The deeper depths are for deeper scarring and stretch marks and really should only be used if you truly know what you are doing. 
 Always use a clean and sanitized device. You wouldn't reuse dirty needles, so don't reuse dirty devices. 
 Apply the serum either in a hydropen, like the HydroDerma Pen , or immediately after using something like the DermTifix pen. 
 Avoid harsher ingredients like acids and retinoids for a couple of days after needling. 
 Microneedling can cause redness and sensitivity, so avoid long sun exposure, heavy workouts, etc immediately after. 
 Injectable Use Some peptides will work best when injected and can give systemic benefits. 
 Peptides like GHK-Cu, BPC-157, KPV, Melanotan, and Glutathione are commonly used through this method of administration. 
 Injectables can improve skin from the inside out, help with deeper healing, scars, or widespread issues, support hair and scalp health. 
 Important things to remember: 
 Only inject peptides that are intended for subcutaneous or intramuscular use. They will be either lyophilized or already liquid and typically in a vial. The exception is SNAP-8. This may come in a vial. Don't inject it please. 
 Always use sterile practices. 
 Rotate injection sites. 
 Reconstitute with bacteriostatic water and store in the fridge. 
 Timing and Frequency Topicals: 1-2x daily
 Microneedling: Once every 1-2 weeks is generally sufficient. 
 Injectables: Depending on the peptide they may be daily, every other day, or 5 on 2 off.

title: Overview
text: Semax is a peptide that was developed in Russia in the 1980s and is derived from a fragment of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTS). It is actually a registered drug in Russia and is on the Russian Ministry of Health's List of Vital and Essential Drugs and is used for things like ischemic stroke recovery, TBIs, cognitive impairment, and more. Outside of Russia though, Semax lacks approval from other regulatory agencies but is explored within the nootropic and peptide communities.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Semax works mostly through the BDNF/NGF axis as well as other areas to enhance cognition, neuroprotection, mood, and stress resilience. 
 BNDF and NGF Upregulation - This is the primary mechanism in which Semax works. It increases something called BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) which is the primary growth factor that is required for neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, dendritic growth, and long-term potentiation which is the cellular process that leads to learning and memory formation. When you increase BDNF levels, it helps with better memory, mood, and neurological recovery. 
 When you administer Semax, it increases BDNF expression in the areas of the brain that are required for learning, memory, and executive function (goal-directed behavior). This occurs through the activation of something called CREB which controls neurotrophic gene expression. 
 Alongside of that, something called NGF (nerve growth factor) is also increased. This is critical for cholinergic neurons that produce acetylcholine which are vulerable in Alzheimer's disease. Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter that helps with the communication between nerve cells and muscles and can help with new memories, attention, and adaptation in the brain. By increases NGF, it helps support the survival and function of those neurons. 
 Inhibition of Enkephalin Degradation - Enkephalins are endogenous opioid peptides that help to modulate pain, stress, and mood. They get broken down by enkephalinase enzymes, which Semax can help to inhibit , resulting in the extended action of enkephalins. This will then result in an anxiolytic effect (reducing anxiety), reducing stress response, and mood stabilization. This isn't going to act like an opioid in the normal sense where it will bind to opioid receptors, but instead can help to preserve the activity by slowing the breakdown of endogenous activity. 
 Serotonergic and Dopaminergic Modulation - max can modulate monoamine neurotransmitter systems which results in increases motivation, focus, and drive from the dopaminergic effects it produces. It also results in serotenergic modulation which can help with mood regulation and reducing anxiety which complements the enkephalin mechanism of Semax. So with Semax, people may feel more focused, motivated, and less responsive to stress.

title: Benefits of Semax
text:
Cognitive Enhancement - This is the primary benefit that most people are going for when using Semax. The increase in BDNF basically helps strengthen synapses and helps with memory consolidation. The dopaminergic component helps with working memory and issues with attention. When the two of these are combined together, people typically have better clarity, focus, recall, and mental stamina. In Russia, they actually did an fMRI study (functional MRI that tracks blood flow) and were able to observe changes within 5-20 minutes after administration of nasal Semax. You're not going to become a genius with Semax. But you will likely have a better ability to focus, stay on task, recall information, and have less mental fatigue as you're doing it. One important thing is to try to use this before completing tasks that require mental demand as that will give you increased results. Without doing that, it's like taking pre-workout and not going to the gym after. You're leaving a little bit on the table. 
 Neuroprotection - Russian clinical trials actually used Semax in ischemic stroke patients to improve their recovery and reduce the effects of the negative neurological effects afterward. BDNF upregulation can help the survival of neurons in the ischemic penumbra which is the area that is impaired due to reduced blood flow. For TBI, Semax may reduce cerebral edema, inflammatory markers, and cell death and can help with synaptic remodeling post-injury. 
 Mood and Stress - As mentioned in the mechanism section, there are enkephalinase inhibiting and serotonergic modulation components that can contribute to some mood effects alongside of the cognitive benefits like reduced anxiety, more stable mood, and a better ability to tolerate stress. A lot of times, people confuse Semax and Selank here. Semax may give some benefit in this area, but Selank is going to have more of a pronounced effect due to the GABAergic mechanism that comes with it. If your primary issue is complaint over cognition, then Selank would be the better overall choice. 
 Optic Nerve / Retina - Semax can also be used in Russia for optic nerve disease . NGF/BDNF expression can result in significant upregulation in retinal tissue after Semax administration. The retinal cells are dependent on NGF for survival and in things like glaucoma, NGF deficiency can contribute to cell death. There was a study of 36 glaucoma patients that used Semax intranasally over the course of a month and saw improvements in visual function.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Administration Routes - Semax can be used both intranasally and subcutaneously. The question often gets asked on which is better. I have asked this question to people numerous times and ultimately it seems to be split down the middle. Both may work, but generally, people are preferential towards one way or the other and they don't know until they try it. 
 Here's why nasal can work - when administered nasally, it can be absorbed through the olfactory epithelium and can leverage the olfactory and trigeminal nerve pathways which gives a direct route to increase CNS concentrations. This method would essentially allow for this increase before any type of enzymatic degradation can occur. 
 Typically, when people are using Semax, they start around 200mcg and administer it in the morning or before demanding tasks. People have worked up as high as 1mg in a single dose, but if I had worked up that high to get the effects, I would switch to Adamax as people can typically use a lesser amount which can then be more cost effective. 
 Personally, I like to use this as needed. If it's a Sunday and all I'm doing is some yard work, I'm not taking Semax. I also like to run it for a few weeks, and take a break for a few weeks before starting again. If I don't feel like I need it as much, I may wait longer before using it again.

title: Safety and Side Effects
text:
Generally speaking, the Russian literature shows a clean side effect profile. A few things that may occur: 
 Nasal Irritation - This can happen as a side effect of taking nasally administered compounds. Sometimes it may be due to concentration or too much administration. 
 Headaches - Some may experience a slight headache especially when they first start out. Often times it resolves itself over time. 
 Sleep issues - Some may feel like Semax has a slightly stimulating effect in the brain and have issues sleeping if taking too late in the day. 
 Hair Loss - You may encounter a Reddit thread expressing this concern due to the theoretical effect that BDNF can have on hair follicle cycling. I have yet to see people actually experience this in people that I have encountered.
