title: Overview
text: SS-31 is a synthetic peptide that is specifically designed to target mitochondrial function. It targets a lipid in the mitochondria called cardiolipin, which it binds to, to help restore energy efficiency, help protect from oxidative stress and damage, and preserve and restore the structure of the mitochondria. Mitochondrial dysfunction can lead to different chronic diseases and increased aging, so being able to utilize a compound like SS-31 may lead to the ability to improve health, but doing so at the cellular level.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
The primary thing that SS-31 does is interact with cardiolipin which is a phospholipid that is in the inner membrane of the mitochondria. It helps to maintain mitochondrial function and the electron transport chain, which helps to produce ATP (the cell's energy). When you encounter stressors or aging, the cardiolipin can be damaged or oxidized which messes up the electron transport chain, hurts the integrity of the membranes, reduces ATP production, and creates reactive oxygen species (ROS). When you use SS-31, it binds to the cardiolipin and helps to stabilize that inner membrane of the mitochondria and helps to protect the cardiolipin from oxidative damage. This then allows the mitochondrial membrane to have better potential which is highly important for ATP synthesis (energy production). What does all of this result in? 
 Electron Transport Chain and ATP Production: SS-31 is going to help keep the electron transport chain structured and helping to anchor them to cardiolipin. This will help the efficiency of the mitochondria and allow them to generate more ATP. One of the things that SS-31 is shown to do is increase ATP output in aged and stressed mitochondria and basically re-energize them. When doing this, it also helps to reduce the production of ROS which are harmful oxidative byproducts. 
 Antioxidation: SS-31 is different than regular antioxidants like a glutathione would be, but it can help to prevent oxidative damage. One of the ways that we already discussed is the prevention of ROS oxidation on cardiolipin. Since it's also make the electron transport chain be more efficient, there are also going to be fewer free radicals that are generated. When you're able to lower ROS in the mitochondria, it can protect the mitochondrial DNA, proteins, and lipids from damage. By preventing this damage, it can help mitigate inflammation and cell death pathways that can cause issues as we age. 
 Cell Death Prevention: When the cell is under heavy stress from things like too many free radicals, the mitochondria can undergo something called the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP). If this opens, the inner membrane loses its voltage (membrane potential), which is the component the mitochondria use to make ATP. Then you will have water and ions rush into the mitochondria causing them to swell and the internal structure will fall apart. Something called cytochrome c which can shuttle electrons to help make energy will become loose and then can trigger apoptosis or programmed cell death. With SS-31, this inner membrane is stabilized so it is less likely to open and allow the Cytochrome c to escape and instead will stay anchored to cardiolipin and help to regulate that energy production.

title: Benefits of SS-31
text:
So we know how SS-31 is improving the function of the mitochondria, but what are the benefits that you will see form this? 
 Better Cellular Energy Production: SS-31 leads to an increased ATP output in the mitochondria which can increase the energy that is available to the cells. In aged mice, they were able to see an increase in muscle ATP levels and energy reserves which basically reversed age-related energy deficits at the cellular levels. What this translated to ultimately was improved stamina and reduced fatigue. Increased cellular energy can actually be very beneficial for high-demand tissues like the heart, brain, and muscles, which is partially why SS-31 was looked at for cardiac benefits. 
 Antioxidant and Anti-Aging Benefits: Since SS-31 helps to reduce mitochondrial ROS and protect the cells from oxidative damage, this can play a role in the anti-aging process. Excess free radicals can lead to things like cellular aging, DNA damage, and tissue inflammation, so by reducing these, we're helping to slow those processes. Now these benefits haven't been fully proven through clinical studies, but based on the mechanism of action we can hypothesize that these benefits are occurring in humans as they were in animal models. 
 Vision and Eye Health: One of the things that SS-31 is being studied for is vision improvement. The retina is a tissue that is energy hungry and has a high density of mitochondria in the photoreceptor cells. With things like age-related macular degeneration, they can be associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. With SS-31, the benefits have been shown to potentially slow cell death and preserve visual function. They currently have elamipretide in Phase 3 studies for age-related macular degeneration and geographic atrophy and will be interesting to see how the results turn out. 
 Cardiac Support / Cardioprotection: Because organs like the heart are in high in energy demand, mitochondrial dysfunction can potentially lead to issues like heart disease or heart failure. In a pre-clinical studies, they saw that SS-31 therapy contributed to better heart pump function with less ejection fraction and increased cardiac output while pathological enlargement of the left ventricle was prevented . SS-31 potentially is providing the mitochondria in the heart cells with extra support during and after ischemic stress which can ultimately help with the heart's function.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
There are a few different protocols that exist for SS-31. 
 My preferred protocol is 4mg a day until I have reached 50mg total. So that results in 12 days of 4mg, and one day of 2mg. This seems to work well as a general protocol for most. 
 If looking for longer term effects, anywhere from 1-10mg a day can be an option for 2-4+ weeks. For those with severe issues, even running SS-31 for 2-4 months could prove to potentially be beneficial. For the most severe issues, even running for 6-12 months may be necessary. 
 In clinical studies, around 40mg/day seems to be the amount that is typically used, however I think this is pretty cost inefficient and seems to be more than is necessary to yield results for most.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
SS-31 has a fantastic overall safety profile with very minimal side effects that are reported. What are some of these potential side effects? 
 Injection Site Reactions: This is something that can happen with almost any injectable compound. Sometimes people may experience redness, itching, pain, or small lumps at the injection site. In the trials, pretty much every patient has some type of injection site reaction, but very few thought it was so bad that they couldn't continue treatment. 
 Systemic Side Effects: Some experience things like headaches or total body fatigue. The fatigue can be debilitating and there is really no way to fix it or overcome it. It can last for a few days for most and even longer for a smaller population of individuals. This usually resolves itself after the body goes through its reparative processes.

title: Overview
text: Tesamorelin is a peptide analog of growth hormone releasing hormone that was modified to stimulate growth hormone release in the system and was developed and approved in 2010 by the FDA to treat HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Tesamorelin is currently approved as a treatment for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, but how does it work in the body to accomplish what it does, whether treating HIV-associated lipodystrophy or providing benefits for biohackers? 
 The biggest thing that Tesamorelin is going to do in the body is agonize the GHRH receptors that are in the pituitary gland. It is going to do so by mimicking natural GHRH and binding to the GHRH receptors on the pituitary somatotroph cells to stimulate the synthesis and pulsatile release of endogenous growth hormone . Side note - the medical documentation for Tesamorelin mentions that GH is both anabolic and lipolytic. Anabolic in very simple terms means it can promote muscle repair and growth. Lipolytic is the breakdown of fats. Therefore, Tesamorelin should promote muscle growth and fat breakdown. This increase in growth hormone is going to lead to elevated levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) primarily via the liver. In the clinical studies, Tesamorelin was able to basically double (about an 81% increase on average) IGF-1 levels in the patients that were treated. 
 Once the GH and IGF-1 increased occur, this can trigger multiple things like the anabolism and lipolytic benefits mentioned above. In adipose tissue specifically, GH does a great job at stimulating lipolysis and is extremely pronounced in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) or the fat around the organs. It is going to help to deplete those visceral fat stores and can reduce circulating triglyceride levels as your body is metabolizing the freed up fatty acids that are broken down through lipolysis.

title: Benefits of Tesamorelin
text:
Based on how Tesamorelin works, what are the benefits we will get as a result of that? 
 Visceral Fat Reduction - This is probably the biggest benefit of Tesamorelin based on the data. It significantly reduces visceral adipose tissue (VAT). In the randomized trials, they observed HIV patients reducing visceral fat by about 15-20% on average over 6 months . This is an incredibly important benefit for many as the visceral fat is the most metabolically dangerous fat locations.
 Lipid Profile Improvements - Another benefit of Tesamorelin is the improvements in blood lipids, especially in patients with dylipidemia. Over the course of a 26-week trial, they were able to observe a reduction in triglyceride levels by about 50mg/dL on average vs the placebo that has a slight increase of about 9mg/dL . Total cholesterol usually decreases as well and there are even some increases in HDL which can improve total/HDL cholesterol ratio and reducing potential cardiovascular risks. There is no direct outcomes that I've found, but by doing this it could prevent cardiovascular issues in treated populations. 
 Reduction in Liver Fat (NAFLD) - In the first bullet, we discussed the visceral fat reduction benefits of Tesamorelin. It is also being seen to be effective on liver fat content as visceral fat is pretty closely linked to things like non-alcoholic fatty liver diseasee (NAFLD). In a study, one year of Tesamorelin for HIV patients with NAFLD led to a 37% relative reduction in liver fat than the patients . Tesamorelini was also able to reduce liver inflammation markers like C-reactive protein (CRP) and they observed a reduction in ALT levels through the treatment. 
 Metabolic and Body Composition - As we stated, we stated the fat loss benefits of Tesamorelin, but it can also improve lean body mass as well as provide metabolic benefits. In the trials, they did see that there was a slight increase in lean body mass in DXA scans . So, less visceral fat and a little extra muscle, which can help with metabolism. Also, there was no really significant changes to insulin sensitivity in the studies. The patients HbA1c stayed the same or slightly elevated on occasion during the course of treatment. But in the long-term data, there was no significant difference in the glucose levels between the Tesamorelin groups and the placebo groups. This is a huge benefit, because the higher dose GH therapy is likely to cause some insulin resistance, where Tesamorelin can maintain glucose control for most of the people using it.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Upon initial approval, Egrifta was available as a 1 mg per vial formulation with a recommended dose of 2mg injected subcutaneously once daily. In 2018, Egrifta SV became available as 2 mg per vial with a recommended dose of 1.4 mg subcutaneously once daily .
 The reason I linked the above information, is because I typically go with the 1mg dosage for cost effectiveness and maintaining a good cost/benefit ratio. So it doesn't HAVE to be the 2mg dosage. 
 There are a few ways that this compound could be ran. I will say that it is one of the more expensive compounds to run, so take that into consideration. 
 First, let me go into cycle length for this: 
 I think the sweet spot for a cycle of Tesamorelin is somewhere in the 12-16 week range. You will see protocols out there for 8 weeks on, 8 weeks off. I personally don't prefer that short of a cycle. Why? Because typically you don't see the results until at least 4-6 weeks in. So, if you barely start to see noticeable results at 6 weeks in, why stop 2 weeks later? You will likely continue to see more and more results as you stay on it a little bit longer, so I think going at least to 12 weeks is best. It could be ran for up to 6 months though if desired. 
 Next, let's look at the dosage options and what my thoughts are there: 
 0.5mg - There are some who say this can be a pretty effective women's dosage. I also think this could work for men. Will you get AS much results as 1mg? Maybe not. But if you're on more of a budget, this could still give some results. 
 1mg - I think this is the sweet spot dose. It will likely yield the best cost / benefit ratio out of all of the dosage options. I personally like doing this amount and have seen great results and many others do as well. If you compare costs vs. the 2mg dosage, you're saving literally 50% of the costs. Well worth it IMO. 
 2mg - Could you get more results here? Potentially. Is it enough to make it worth doubling the cost of your cycle? In my opinion, no. 
 Lastly, let's look at frequency of administration: 
 In clinical applications, it is administered every day. If you think about this over the course of a 16 week cycle, you have to take an extra 32mg at 1mg dosage or an extra 64mg at the 2mg dosage. You're adding significant costs to your cycle. So, I think using it 5 on 2 off is best to save costs and still get similar results. Either of these options can work. 
 Note: You want to take this in a fasted state. I prefer at night. It could also be done in the morning if desired.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Let's look at some of the common side effects from Tesamorelin. 
 Injection Site Reaction - This is common with a lot of injectable compounds. Common symptoms include redness, irritation, itching, pain, or swelling at the injection site. It can be a little spicy when you start using it, but usually after 1-2 weeks of using it that issue goes away and it's much more tolerable, typically with no pain or side effects. 
 Joint Pain - This is another common side effect that people can experience. It's generally due to fluid retention. Drink some extra water, reduce sodium intake slightly, and increase potassium intake slightly and it can mitigate this. It will usually resolve after a few weeks. 
 Water Retention - This is very common to have happen the first few weeks. I always tell people to expect to gain up to 10lbs. You may gain zero. You may gain two. But expect to gain up to 10 so you're at least ready for the scale to go up some. Drink some extra water, reduce sodium intake slightly, and increase potassium intake slightly and it can mitigate this. It will usually resolve after a few weeks. 
 Blood Sugar Increase - There is a slight potential for increase in blood glucose or insulin. It's usually not major and will go away after you come off of the compound. 
 Cancer - See the discussion about this in the All Things Growth Hormone Course. I think the risk is minimal, but mentioning it here because the question gets asked.

title: Overview
text: Thymosin Alpha-1 (TA-1) is a peptide that is derived from the thymus gland and is found in the thymus tissue. Early on, it was found that administering thymus extracts could actually help with immune responses in different animals and showed how important it could be for immunity. Once they realized this, they started to synthesize the compound to make sure that it was pure and safe and could control the supply of it for use. There's actually an approved version of TA-1 called thymalfasin and was developed as an actual pharmaceutical product. They did try some clinical trials in the United States in the 80s and 90s and say some potential benefits towards Hepatitis B, but faced some challenges and ultimately did not receive FDA approval for the compound. This is interesting because in China, they actually approved it in 1995 for treating Hepatitis B. It's been approved in over 35 countries since then for different usages, but mostly for Hepatitis B and C and immune system function. China is actually using it now to treat liver cancer and for things like post-surgical infection. What makes this even crazier is that even with all of these countries having it approved for multiple uses, the U.S. and many other countries especially in the west still have not approved it. But it does have orphan drug designation for certain diseases, so maybe there will one day be hope.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
Just look at the picture below and you'll understand how it all works. 
 Just kidding. But this image does give a visual depiction of how TA-1 interacts with different things in the immune cells like dendritic cells, macrophages, T cells, B cells, and NK cells. TA-1 will activate these cells and can help with cytokine production and your antibody responses. 
 So let's look at some of the things it does: 
 Activation of Dendritic Cells: TA-1 is going to activate dendritic cells which basically collect fragments of protein from antigens and show T cells what the problem is. It's going to increase the display of molecules and signals on the cell surfaces to improve the communication with the T cells and make them more effective at identifying and taking out the problem. These dendritic cells can help to release different cytokines that can drive the antiviral and anti-tumor responses as well as ones that regulate the system to prevent overreaction. 
 Regulating T Cells: TA-1 can help the immature CD8 T cells mature into cytotoxic T cells that can directly kill infected or cancerous cells. It's also going to help increase the CD4 helper T cells which are going to be ones that are responsible for coordinating a broader immune response for the body. Those helper T cells When TA-1 is involved, the helper T cells start to lean toward a Th1 response, which means they release more interferon-gamma and interleukin-2. Those two words mean nothing I know. But those are going to be cytokines that tell the killer T cells, natural killer cells, and macrophages to do more work resulting in a stronger antiviral and anti-tumor defense for the body. 
 Natural Killer (NK) Cells: The NK cells are cells that are going to quickly go in and find issues that exist in the body. So they can find the virus and bad cells and will essentially target the cell and cause it to self-destruct. They can also release cytokines to help bring in more macrophages and T cells to assist with their job. So when you look at TA-1, it's going to help increase the amount of NK cells and help them work better in getting rid of the bad cells. 
 Macrophage Activity: Macrophages are immune cells that you could compare to the sucker fish in a fish tank. They're going to eat the pathogens, dead cells, and all of the bad and help to break it down. They can also help with brining in more immune cells and shaping the body's response do different issues. Once they've essentially beaten the bad, they also help to heal and repair and bring the function back to normal. When TA-1 is introduced, the macrophages become more active and go quickly to help fight off the different issues.

title: Benefits of TA-1
text:
In the last section we broke down how TA-1 is influencing different cells that plays a role in our immune system, but what are the benefits of that? 
 Enhanced Immune Response: Thymosin Alpha-1 can help with viral infections like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and any viral infections and sicknesses that you may experience. It will help with the T-cell responses and antibody responses, which is going to make the immune system more effective at controlling the viral replication. They've even seen where it can be paired alongside of vaccines to provide stronger antibody responses and better protection than solely receiving the vaccine by itself . 
 Antiviral / Antibacterial Activity: Thymosin Alpha-1, while helping to strengthen the immune system is one amazing benefit, it can also help create a better antiviral environment in the body. Even during COVID-19, they used TA-1 in China to help with the immune responses . Especially in people who are immunosuppressed, TA-1 can help to more effectively clear different types of bacterial and fungal infections, as well viral infections. 
 Cancer Therapy Support: It is important to understand that TA-1 isn't chemotherapy, but it can help the immune system better recognize and attack tumors. Often times with cancer, the immune system is suppressed and TA-1 can help to restore some of the T-cell and NK cell activity that comes along with it. It's been studied as an adjuvant therapy (supportive treatment basically) in cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, breast cancer, and liver cancer. It's also been shown in laboratory research that TA-1 can help to slow tumor growth by promoting cancer cell death and reducing proliferation. In the U.S. TA-1 also received orphan drug status for stage II melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma . 
 Anti-Inflammatory and Autoimmune Modulation: TA-1 does activate immunity, but it also can help with regulatory pathways that will turn down excessive inflammation. It will increase IL-10 and regulatory T cells to calm the immune overreaction in the body. So in terms of managing different issues where this can be concern, TA-1 can be reasonable option to explore.

title: Dosage Strategies and Protocols
text:
Thymosin Alpha-1 Dosage protocols vary based on what may be used in clinical settings and what may be used by biohackers for different purposes. 
 For something like chronic Hepatitis, dosage protocols are 1.6mg injected subcutaneously twice weekly for 6 months. If needed it can be pushed for up to 12 months. 
 When we start to use it for treating a viral infection, typically the dosage will change to be ran in a shorter duration at a higher dosage amount. In these cases, taking somewhere between 1-2mg a day for somewhere between 7-14 days is more common. Typically, when I use TA-1, I will do 1-2mg a day for 5-10 days. I continue to take it for a period of time even after getting over the sickness to keep the benefits of immune regulation and help the bodies response to different infections. This could also be used as a short immune boosting protocol. 
 For general wellness and prevention, this protocol may look somewhat similar to the protocol for treating a viral infection. Another option would be to take it for a longer period of time and dose it a few times a week to help with the immune system's function during this time. Both of these would be within the 1-2mg dosage, just changing frequency. 
 For cancer / tumor targeting, I would run a similar protocol to how it is used for chronic Hepatitis. This protocol could vary, but at least running for a couple months may prove to be more beneficial than the acute immune response treatment protocols.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Thymosin Alpha-1 has an incredible safety profile. It is very well-tolerated and has a low occurrence of any adverse effects. It has been used in over 11,000 patients and there has been no significant concerns that arise from the usage of TA-1 . So what are some possible side effects ? 
 Injection Site Reaction: This is pretty mild and can really happen with any compound. Redness, pain, and irritation at the injection site is what is occurring and are generally mild and go away. 
 Flu-Like Symptoms: Some that use it may have fatigue, low-grade fever, or muscle aches and are usually very mild and resolve themselves easily. They usually go away as the body adjusts. 
 Immunogenicity and Allergic Reactions: This is very unlikely that it would cause an allergic reaction or be recognized as something foreign by the immune system, but it is always a potential concern. Really this would occur more so from impurities or aggregates in the compound. 
 Long-Term Safety: Since TA-1 is approved in different countries for decades, we can generally get a good idea of the long-term safety profile, especially when people are using it multiple times over the course of years. There is no significant data to support any type of organ toxicity, infection increases, or adverse effects.

title: What Happens When You Train?
text:
Training. Exercising. Working out. Whatever you want to call it. Most of the time, people think it's just moving the body or picking things up and putting them down. But what are you really doing with your body when you're doing these things? 
 Here's what's really happening: 
 Muscle damage - I know this sounds counterintuitive. But you're creating small microtears in the muscle fibers. Your body is then going to repair those tears, which results in you becoming stronger and more muscular over time. Also why recovery is so important to progress. 
 Mechanical tension - this is the force that is being exerted on the muscle that when you lift heavy loads and stretch and contract under tension, can stimulate the muscle cells to begin protein synthesis and build more muscle tissue
 Metabolic stress - As you exercise and start to feel the burn, you're going to build up metabolites which can also help trigger the muscle-building responses in the body
 Neural adaptation - You are going to get better at recruiting the muscle fibers to work. This is also why you may be able to develop a better mind-muscle connection over time. Your brain and nervous system will become more efficient in recruiting the fibers to work.

title: Cardio vs. Resistance Training
text:
The best thing is a combination of both. You don't have to do one over the other. You won't become bulky from lifting weights. It's actually incredibly hard to look like Arnold, even if you trained hard for 20 years and used steroids. That's why most people don't. Resistance training should be the foundation of what you do. 
 Resistance training: 
 Builds muscle and strength
 Improves metabolic health and insulin sensitivity
 Protects bone density (very important as you age!)
 Boosts long-term fat loss
 Cardio: 
 Improves heart and lung health
 Aids in recovery and circulation
 Helps burn calories
 How can you combine both? 
 Zone 2 cardio to help with fat burning and recovery
 HIIT for some quick, intense, fat burn
 Lifting 3-5x per week and 2-3 cardio sessions is a good general guideline for most

title: Understanding Effort
text:
The harsh reality is that most people actually don't workout as hard as they think they do. If you want to see an example of this, watch this video . 
 RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion); 
 This is a scale of 1-10 for how hard something feels. 
 RPE 10 = max effort. Can't do any more.
 RPE 8 = that was hard, but I had about 2 reps left in the tank
 RPE 6 = relatively good warm-up weight. Not the very first warm-up set, but leading up to the real working sets. 
 RIR (Reps in Reverse): 
 This is how many reps you can still do. 
 2 RIR = you could have done about 2 more reps
 Intensity doesn't always have to be training until you fall on the floor and collapse. You want to work close enough to your limits that your body has to adapt to that stimulus, but not so much that you can't recover.

title: What is a COA?
text:
A COA is a Certificate of Analysis that is basically your lab report for a compound. It is going to be a way to test the identity, purity, quantity, and generally the safety. There are further tests you can do for more "safety" measures, but the COA is the bare minimum that you want to see. 
 COAs typically are going to come from third-party testing facilities, but some companies may do their own in-house testing. While in house testing doesn't always mean that it's faked or not tested properly, third-party testing will pretty much always be the better option. The third-party testing is going to get rid of potential bias that could happen when something is tested in-house. Also, just because a company shows a COA for a product doesn't mean that it's real. Companies will continue to use the same COA for multiple batches, photoshop the results, or just use someone else's because they know that most people don't even know what they're looking for when they see these.

 Another thing to look for is the manufacturer COA. If the client info is not the same info as the company you're ordering from, then it's not their COA and they did not test the product. Plain and simple.

title: COA FAQs
text:
How recent does the COA need to be? It really just needs to be as recent as the batch is. If they're storing them properly, they will last a very long time. Now, could it be a concern if the testing date is very old? Yes. But, if a company orders very large quantities and they are selling through a specific product slower, the COA could be months old. That's fine. The product isn't degrading if storing properly. 
 How do you know if the product you receive is from the batch you're seeing? Truthfully, you don't. Trust is going to be the most important piece. I can tell you this - the companies I work with will hold batches until testing is completed. I have had conversations where they have the product for weeks ready to sell but wait until it is tested. Also, they have batches custom made for them. Then it is tested by the manufacturer. Then they test it when they receive it. So they're verifying multiple times, but always having a test once they receive it to confirm. But truthfully, you never know because bad companies will do this ALL THE TIME and sell products without testing because it's too expensive, takes too long, etc and they just want their money. I promise that happens across the industry. It's also nice to have a batch number printed on the label that ties to the COA. Could they fake this too? Yes. But it's another step to help verify.

title: General COA Thoughts
text:
COAs are important. Do you ever truly know what you're getting? No. Because it could be very easy to deceive. But it's another level of assurance that something is what it is. 
 There are very popular companies out there that do not test their batches when they receive them. They get greedy. They get lazy. 
 Never trust a vendor COA. They are the manufacturer. They can literally do whatever they want to do. They can test one good vial that they know is good, then send everyone whatever they want. They also can swap the caps and do anything to make them look the same.

But they should have some sort of refund clause to take care of you if it test poorly. Good companies will do that and stand by that typically (not always) just as another layer of confidence.

title: Overview
text: This course will break down what a unit is, what concentration is, and how to understand that as it relates to dosages.

title: What Is a Unit?
text:
When people are referring to units in regards to peptides, they are not referring to milligrams or micrograms (or they're mistakenly referring to them that way due to lack of understanding). They're talking about the volume of liquid that is being drawn up into the syringe. 
 So what exactly is one unit? 
 If you are using a standard 1ml insulin syringe, it will typically be marked with little dashes like on a ruler from 0-100. A .3ml insulin syringe will have 0-30. A .5ml insulin syringe will have 0-50. 
 100 units = 1mL
 1 unit = 0.01mL
 10 units = .1mL
 Let's just assume you have a peptide vial that you have already reconstituted. If you draw up 10 units on the syringe, you are drawing out .1mL of the liquid. How much actual peptide that's in that .1mL is going to depend on the concentration of that liquid in the vial.

title: What Is Concentration?
text:
Concentration basically tells you how much peptide is in each mL of liquid once it is mixed. 
 I like to compare this to adding sugar to tea:
 The more sugar you add to the tea, the sweeter it will be. 
 The same with peptides. The more mg per mL, the stronger the dose will be per spray or injection in the same volume of liquid. 
 How do you calculate this concentration? 
 Peptide amount (in mg) / bac water (in mL) = Concentration (mg/mL)
 For example: 
 You add 2ml of bac water to a 5mg vial. 
 5mg / 2mL = 2.5 mg/mL. 
 Every 1mL of liquid contains 2.5mg of the peptide.
 How does this correlate to units? 
 If your concentration is 2.5 mg/mL and your injection is .1 mL: 
 0.1 mL x 2.5 mg/mL = .25mg or 250 mcg

title: Understanding Dose Based on Concentration
text:
Once you know the concentration, you are then able to calculate the units based on the dosage. 
 Lets say that you reconstituted a 5mg vial with 2.5mL of liquid. That is going to give you a concentration of 2 mg per mL. You need to determine how much liquid is going to give you .5 mg (your dosage). 
 .5mg / 2 mg / mL = 0.25 mL
 Since 1 mL = 100 units, then: 
 0.25 mL = 25 units
 You can also use a peptide calculator to assist with this, but this is explaining the concept behind it. 
 The most important formula to remember: 
 Volume to inject = Desired dose / Concentration
 To determine the units based on volume, you need to remember this: 
 Since 100 units = 1 mL, multiple the mL amount by 100 to determine the units
 0.1 mL = 10 units
 0.2 mL = 20 units
 0.25 mL = 25 units
 0.5 mL = 50 units

title: Overview
text: Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) is a 28-amino acid peptide hormone that acts as a neurotransmitter and hormone in the body. It is produced in many tissues like the gut, pancreas, and brain. This is one of my favorite peptides as it is almost a Swiss Army Knife with all of the things that it can do for, and throughout, the body.

title: Mechanism of Action
text:
VIP binds to two class B G-protein-coupled receptors, VPAC1 and VPAC2, which are expressed across a lot of tissues within the body. This gives an explanation to why it may have such a broad spectrum of benefits as well. These receptors are found in the pulmonary vascular smooth muscle layer and in airway smooth muscle of large airways, sub-mucosal glands, airway epithelium, alveolar walls, innate immune cells like human mast cells, neutrophils, peripheral blood monocytes, and murine macrophages , within the CNS in piriform cortex, cerebral cortex, suprachiasmatic nucleus, hippocampus, and pineal gland, as well as the liver, intestine, pancreas, skeletal muscle, heart, kidney, adipose tissues, testis, and the stomach . Apologies for the long list, but that gives you an understanding of how broadly those VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors may be spread throughout the body and how VIP may be able to exert its benefits by it's affinity to bind to those receptors and lead to it's benefits throughout the body. Once VIP hits those receptors, it can activate adenylyl cylase and raise intracellular cAMP levels, which activates protein kinase A (PKA), influences gene expression like increasing clock genes Per1 and Per2, synchronizing circadian rhythms, among other effects. So because of this, what are some things that VIP does downstream once it activates those receptors? 
 Side note, we know that VIP has a very short half life (see half-life course). However, the important thing here is that once VIP activates those receptors, it can create a cascading physiological effect throughout the body, which are listed below. However, the short half-life really seems to be the biggest challenge with VIP, as finding a way to leverage a potential longer half-life analog or derivative may yield even better benefits. 
 Smooth Muscle Relaxation and Vasodilation - Elevated cAMP (which VIP raises intracellularly as stated above) in smooth muscle cells causes relaxation. Therefore, VIP produces quite strong bronchodilation in airways and vasodilation in blood vessels that are independent of cholinergic and adrenergic pathways (basically, some pathways that act as signaling systems within the autonomic nervous system to regulate bodily functions through neurotransmitters and their receptors). The bronchodilator effects of VIP is about 100-fold more potent than isoproterenol (beta-1 and beta-1 adrenergic receptor agonist) and about 50x more in the vasodilatory effect on pulmonary arteries than prostacyclin (vasodilator). Ultimately, these actions are going to lead to bronchospasm relief, increased airflow, and reduced vascular resistance. VIP also can increase the secretion of pulmonary surfactant ( a lipoprotein complex produced in the lungs that reduces surface tension at the air-fluid interface and allows expansion of alveoli and allow for gas exchange ) and improves blood flow to the heart and lungs. 
 Immune Modulation and Anti-Inflammation - VIP also has a pretty significant r

title: Benefits of VIP
text:
Gastrointestinal Motility and Digestion - Since VIP plays a role on the enteric nervous system, it is a strong regulator of digestive function. It induces relaxation of smooth muscle in the GI like the lower esophageal sphincter, stomach, and gallbladder and stimulates fluid and electrolyte secretion within the intestinal lumen. So, what it will do is help to lubricate the gut and coordinate something called peristalsis which basically helps to promote intestinal motility and the movement of contents within it. Loss of VIP signaling can actually lead to sluggish bowel transit . Clinically, this would suggest that VIP or other VPAC agonist might be able to be used to treat certain motility disorders like ileus or constipation be leveraging those smooth muscle relaxant and secretory effects to bring back gastrointestinal flow to where it needs to be. 
 Sleep and Circadian Rhythm - Within the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which is basically the circadian pacemaker within your brain, there are a set of neurons that use VIP as a neurotransmitter to synchronize daily rhythms. VIP that is released within the SCN will bind to VPAC2 receptors, activating cAMP/PKA pathways that help to align the cells clocks with the 24-hour light/dark cycle. This hypothalamic VIP signaling is important for maintaining the circadian rhythm as it ensures proper hormone release, body temperature, and your sleep-wake cycle. Disruption of VIP or the receptors ultimately will result in fragmented, desynchronized circadian patterns. When they looked at mice lacking VIP or VPAC2, they saw chaotic SCN neuronal rhythms and blunted daily behavioral cycles. So, adequate VIP activity can help to support all of this. They also are studying the VIP-VPAC2 pathway for its potential in treating circadian rhythm disorders . So, by enhancing VIP signaling in the SCN, it could improve circadian misalignment or poor sleep by helping to synchronize your internal clock. 
 Anti-Inflammatory and Autoimmune Modulation - In the mechanism of action section we discussed a bit how it worked, and because of that, it could be a potential therapeutic anti-inflammatory agent for conditions like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), rheumatoid arthritis, sepsis, and other autoimmune disorders. To short summarize some of the mechanism, it basically shifts your body from producing the inflammatory cytokines and promoting the anti-inflammatory cytokines so it puts your body in more of a regulatory state. It could potentially be used in situations to try to dampen inflammation in situations where the immune system is overactive. They've looked at this some in experimental models of colitis and arthritis and seen reductions in severity due to the immune-calming effect of VIP. Unfortunately, it's just not made it through with VIP or a VIP-derived compound to be more widely available.

title: Dosage and Protocols
text:
Intranasal - This is actually a common method of administration for VIP . It is also pretty commonly used for conditions like CIRS. It allows it to go across the nasal mucosa and reach the brain via olfactory region. 
 Subcutaneous Injection - VIP analogues are most commonly used for subcutaneous use as they were designed to be used in this manner, but VIP also can be used subcutaneously. One major difference between the two is that SC injection does seem to give users more of the "flushing" feeling that may be felt with VIP. One difficulty with this method as well is that you may have to use a sterile 10mL vial to transfer it into in order to dilute it enough to easily draw the small dosages. 
 Dosages - The most common dosage range is 50 - 100 mcg per administration. In certain cases, 50mcg may even me administered up to 4x daily (200 mcg total/day), especially in the beginning of some treatments, before reducing down to 1-2x daily. From what I've seen, typically 1-2x daily can be sufficient for most cases. Most don't need to go over the 200 - 300 mcg range typically per day. 
 The length of time on this peptide can vary. Some stay on for 6+ months straight. It can also be ran in cycles. Ultimately, it depends on what and why someone is deciding to use it. I've seen some who use it continuously and had to lower their dosage due to continuous BP control and a lesser need for VIP to regulate things such as that. 
 It has been used IV and via nebulizer, but for our purposes, IN and SC are the most common routes.

title: Side Effects and Safety
text:
Overall VIP has a pretty good safety profile and is pretty well tolerated. 
 Flushing - This is hands down the most common side effect. People typically experience flushing, warmth, and even some transient low blood pressure after administering a dose. It seems to be mitigated via intranasal administration as well as adaptation to the compound. 
 Stomach Issues - In certain rarer cases, some may get stomach cramps or nausea. This makes sense as it stimulates some activity in the digestive tract. 
 Pancreatitis - This would be extremely rare, but I at least want to mention it. There are some case reports in VIP therapy. This seems to only be in HIGH AMOUNTS as it may hyperstimulation the pancreas. Understand that in some of the testing they were doing near-constant IV administration and other dosages and methods. There were no major, overt cases reported so far to date, but I want to at least mention it. You likely won't want to overdo / overdose VIP anyways, but just pay attention to that. If you're someone with chronic pancreatitis or something else going on with the pancreas, maybe keep an eye of caution or decide against potential use. 
 Low Blood Pressure - VIP can reduce blood pressure. If you already have low blood pressure, VIP may not be a great option for you. It's at least worth monitoring if you use it to make sure you're not crashing or exacerbating low blood pressure.

title: Introduction
text:

Every time they see a video on Instagram or TikTok about magnesium supplements to add to the cart, then they see a post about vitamin D and they add that too.  what your body is actually going to need

 That means that you need to understand the science well enough to be able to make your own decisions, know what to test for, and understand how these pieces can interact with each other, especially when it comes to being paired with things like peptides and other compounds that this community might use.

title: Testing First
text:
If you want to get results with supplementation, then the most important thing you can do before buying any is get blood work done. The reason for this is pretty simple. Deficiency and sufficiency are going to look very different when it comes to supplementation. Taking vitamin D when you are already at optimal levels is probably going to do very little for you but taking it when you are severely deficient can literally change your life. It's still the same compound but you have significantly different outcomes depending on where your baseline is. 
 Most people don't test any of this stuff and they just guess that they're deficient in something based on symptoms, which is really not reliable especially when there's a lot of similarity between different causal factors. So by assuming that most people are deficient in a certain thing and taking it because of that isn't necessarily wrong as a place to start but it's not really a strategized approach to it. In this course you will see that there is a testing guide that covers exactly what to test, what those results might mean, and then the ranges you might be targeting instead of the broad reference ranges that doctors might say are normal.

title: What Supplements Can and Can't Do
text:
Supplements can not override a poor diet, chronic sleep deprivation, lack of exercise, or high stress. What they can do is fill genuine gaps in nutrition that the diet doesn't cover. Whether it's because some of the modern food is less nutrient-dense than it used to be, because you have some type of genetic variant that affects how you process certain nutrients (the MTHFR section covers this in depth), or because your lifestyle creates demands that food alone doesn't meet. 
 Some of these compounds do have some legitimate longevity, performance, and neuroprotective effects that go beyond just correcting a deficiency but again these things are still going to want to have a foundation that is solid.

title: Understanding Cognitive Function
text:
One of the toughest questions I get is "what is good for cognitive function"? It's tough because cognitive function is really a broad range of things. Anywhere from memory, learning, attention, problem-solving, etc. There are a lot of things that go on in the brain that can allow these things to occur. 
 Neurotransmitters: These are chemical messengers that transmit signals between neurons that are fundamental to cognition. Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter and plays a role in learning and memory, where acetylcholine is involved in memory formation and learning. Dopamine can modulate motivation, focus, and reward-based learning behaviors. You really need to have the right balance between the excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters to have clear thinking, attention, and memory. Imbalances with these neurotransmitter systems can cause cognitive impairments like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ADHD, etc. 
 Neurogenesis: This is the process of generating new neurons. For adults, neurogenesis is thought to contribute to learning and memory formation. If you're able to enhance neurogenesis, then you can improve cognitive resilience. You can do this through things like increasing brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). 
 Synaptic Plasticity: Cognitive function depends a lot on your brain's ability to strengthen and form new synaptic connections which is known as synaptic plasticity. Long-term potentiation is sustained strengthening of synapses that allows for learning and memory storage. If you lose synaptic connections or your brain isn't able to adapt, it can impair memory. Neurotrophic factors such as BDNF and nerve growth factor (NGF) can support synaptic plasticity. 
 Inflammation and Oxidative Stress: Neuroinflammation, which is the activation of immune cells in the release of inflammatory cytokines, can be a double-edged sword. Acute inflammatory responses can help to aid in injury repair, but chronic inflammation in the brain can cause damage to neurons and synapses which an lead to cognitive impairment and neurodegeneration. Oxidative stress (excess free radicals) can injure brain cells and impair cognitive function like memory. Elevated inflammatory markers and oxidative damage are observed in many neurodegenerative diseases. Reducing this is important to preserving cognition. 
 Neurodegeneration: Over the course of your life, your neurons can become dysfunctional or die. Neurodegeneration often involves excitotoxicity (neuronal damage from excess glutamate signaling), mitochondrial dysfunction, and chronic inflammation. Protecting neurons and clearing / preventing toxic protein aggregates are the key to prevent cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases. 
 So how can peptides help in these areas? 
 Some peptides can stimulate growth factors in the brain, which will promote neurogenesis and synaptic repair. Some peptides can increase BDNF and NGF expression which can lead to the growth of new neurons and synapses.

title: P21
text:
P21 is a synthetic tetra-peptide that comes from the active piece of CTNF, which is a large neurotrophic protein that can't cross the blood-brain barrier, so they focused on this active piece of it in order to leverage its benefits. The goal of P21 was to be used as a therapy for things like Alzheimer's or other neurodegenerative conditions. 
 What can it help with? 
 BDNF Upregulation: P21 can significantly increase levels of BDNF in the brain, which is highly important for neuron survival, growth of new neurons, and formation of neural synapses. This can lead to increases neurogenesis and they even saw the birth of new neurons in animal studies that matured into functional cells. 
 Reduced Neurodegeneration: Similarly to Cerebrolysin, P21 can actually help to reduce the accumulation of toxic proteins that are associated with Alzheimer's. In mouse models, they saw Tau protein buildup reduced and a reduction in the b-amyloid plaques. It seems like it can either inhibit or reverse the process that can lead to the tangles and plaque formation. This is one of the major reasons it seems promising for Alzheimer's disease. 
 Synaptic Repair and Plasticity: P21 can help to preserve and restore synapses in the brain. There are things called dendritic spines which are protrusions where synapses occur, and P21 maintained healthier spine counts and synaptic marker levels in animal models. By doing this, it can help to support memory and cognitive function. 
 PAK Pathway Support: It seems like P21 might intersect with the P21-activated kinase (PAK) pathway in neurons. Alzheimer's disease is associated with defects in PAK signaling. So, by improving overall neuron health and possible engaging those related pathways, P21 might indirectly help to normalize PAK signaling to protect the dendritic spines (see previous bullet point).
